title: All Patches Matter, More Patches Better: Enhance AI-Generated Image Detection via Panoptic Patch Learning
submission:
The rapid proliferation of AI-generated images (AIGIs) highlights the pressing demand for generalizable detection methods. In this paper, we establish two key principles for AIGI detection task through systematic analysis:
**(1) All Patches Matter**, since the uniform generation process ensures that each patch inherently contains synthetic artifacts, making every patch a valuable detection source; and
**(2) More Patches Better**, as leveraging distributed artifacts across more patches improves robustness by reducing over-reliance on specific regions.
However, counterfactual analysis uncovers a critical weakness: naively trained detectors display **Few-Patch Bias**, relying disproportionately on *minority patches*.
We identify this bias to **Lazy Learner** effect, where detectors to limited patch artifacts while neglecting distributed cues.
To address this, we propose **Panoptic Patch Learning** framework, which integrates: 
(1) *Randomized Patch Reconstruction*, injecting synthetic cues into randomly selected patches to diversify artifact recognition; 
(2) *Patch-wise Contrastive Learning*, enforcing consistent discriminative capability across patches to ensure their uniform utilization.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that PPL enhances generalization and robustness across datasets.

title: Visual Jigsaw Post-Training Improves MLLMs
submission: Reinforcement learning based post-training has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for improving alignment and reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). While vision-centric post-training is important for enhancing MLLMs’ intrinsic understanding of visual signals, current paradigms remain heavily text-centric. We introduce Visual Jigsaw, a general self-supervised post-training task that strengthens visual understanding by partitioning and shuffling visual inputs and asking the model to reconstruct the correct permutation in natural language. Visual Jigsaw is formulated as an ordering task that aligns well with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) and requires no extra visual generative components or annotations. We instantiate Visual Jigsaw across images, videos, and 3D data and report modest improvements on internal perception and reasoning probes. These improvements are observed on our held-out tests, however we do not provide systematic comparisons to established baselines or large-scale public benchmarks in this manuscript, and the observed gains are relatively small, suggesting further study is needed to establish broader significance.

title: Conformal Prediction with Corrupted Labels: Uncertain Imputation and Robust Re-weighting
submission: We study conformal prediction in the presence of corrupted labels, building on tools for generating prediction sets with prescribed coverage. Standard conformal validity assumes i.i.d. labels, which can fail under label noise or missingness. Prior work suggested using privileged information (PI) to re-weight the data distribution to recover validity. We analyze robustness of such privileged conformal prediction (PCP) to weight inaccuracies and propose uncertain imputation (UI), a conformal method that imputes corrupted labels while preserving uncertainty rather than relying on precise weight estimates. Our presentation outlines theoretical intuitions and sketch proofs that these procedures can control coverage under various corruption regimes. Finally, we describe how the components can be integrated into a triply robust framework that combines re-weighting, imputation, and an additional correction to mitigate failures of any single component. Concrete experimental protocols and detailed empirical results are deferred to the full version.

title: Coupled Transformer Autoencoder for Disentangling Multi-Region Neural Latent Dynamics
submission: Simultaneous recordings from thousands of neurons across multiple brain areas reveal rich mixtures of activity that are shared between regions and dynamics that are unique to each region. Existing alignment or multi-view methods neglect temporal structure, whereas dynamical latent-variable models capture temporal dependencies but are usually restricted to a single area, assume linear read-outs, or conflate shared and private signals. We introduce Coupled Transformer Autoencoder (CTAE)—a sequence model that addresses both (i) non-stationary, non-linear dynamics and (ii) separation of shared versus region-specific structure, in a single framework. CTAE employs Transformer encoders and decoders to capture long-range neural dynamics, and explicitly partitions each region’s latent space into orthogonal shared and private subspaces. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CTAE on a controlled synthetic dataset and two high-density electrophysiology datasets of simultaneous recordings from multiple regions, one from motor cortical areas and the other from sensory areas. CTAE extracts meaningful representations that better decode behavior variables compared to existing approaches.

title: OneTwoVLA: A Unified Vision-Language-Action Model with Adaptive Reasoning
submission: General-purpose robots need synergistic reasoning and acting. Dual-system approaches that separate high-level reasoning from low-level acting suffer from limited mutual understanding and latency. We introduce OneTwoVLA, a unified vision-language-action model that performs both System One (acting) and System Two (reasoning), adaptively switching between explicit reasoning at critical moments and action generation otherwise. We design a scalable pipeline to synthesize embodied reasoning-centric vision-language data for co-training with robot data. OneTwoVLA demonstrates extremely strong performance: it matches or exceeds prior modular systems across long-horizon planning, error detection and recovery, natural human-robot interaction, and visual grounding, achieving near-perfect task success rates on several long-horizon manipulation benchmarks and substantially reducing latency. This unified formulation enables long-horizon, highly dexterous behaviors such as making hotpot or mixing cocktails.

title: Extending Sequence Length is Not All You Need: Effective Integration of Multimodal Signals for Gene Expression Prediction
submission: Gene expression prediction, which predicts mRNA expression levels from DNA sequences, presents significant challenges. Prior work has emphasized extending input sequence length to locate distal enhancers that may influence target genes over hundreds of kilobases. We observe, however, that for current models naive long sequence modeling can decrease performance, and that algorithmic fixes only partially mitigate this degradation. Instead, proximal multimodal epigenomic signals near target genes appear more important, motivating a focus on how best to integrate these signals. We note that different signal types play distinct biological roles: some mark active regulatory elements while others reflect background chromatin patterns that can introduce confounding associations. To address these issues, we propose Prism, a framework aimed at better integrating multimodal epigenomic features to reduce confounding effects. While details of the internal representation and adjustment strategies are omitted here, experiments indicate that careful multimodal modeling can enable competitive gene expression prediction using relatively short sequences.

title: SumRA: Parameter Efficient Fine-tuning with Singular Value Decomposition and Summed Orthogonal Basis
submission: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) seeks to adapt large pretrained speech models with few trainable parameters while retaining performance. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) decomposes weight updates into two low-rank matrices A and B so that W' = W0 + BA. Prior work found that freezing A and only updating B can reduce trainable parameters when A is initialized from singular vectors of W0 via SVD, but initializing A with only leading singular vectors limits its representational reach. We propose SumRA, which initializes each row of A as a sum of multiple singular vectors sampled beyond the leading components, allowing A to span a wider subspace of the pretrained weights. We apply SumRA to adapt a large pretrained speech model to several low-resource language settings and report consistent improvements in adaptation behavior while using fewer updated parameters than full fine-tuning. The approach is simple, incurs little overhead, and offers a tunable trade-off between parameter efficiency and coverage of the model’s knowledge subspace.

title: Partition Generative Modeling: Masked Modeling Without Masks
submission:
Masked generative models (MGMs) can generate tokens in parallel and in any order, unlike autoregressive models (ARMs), which decode one token at a time, left-to-right. However, MGMs process the full-length sequence at every sampling step, including \mask tokens that carry no information. In contrast, ARMs process only the previously generated tokens.
We introduce ``Partition Generative Models'' (PGMs), which replace masking with partitioning. Tokens are split into two groups that cannot attend to each other, and the model learns to predict each group conditioned on the other, eliminating mask tokens entirely. Because the groups do not interact, PGMs can process only the clean tokens during sampling, like ARMs, while retaining parallel, any-order generation, like MGMs.
On OpenWebText, PGMs achieve $5-5.5\times$ higher throughput than MDLM while producing samples with lower Generative Perplexity. On ImageNet, PGMs reach comparable FID to MaskGIT with a $7.5\times$ throughput improvement. With twice as many steps, the FID improves to 4.56 while remaining $3.9\times$ faster than MGMs. Finally, PGMs remain compatible with existing MGM samplers and distillation methods.

title: LucidFlux: Caption-Free Photo-Realistic Image Restoration via a Large-Scale Diffusion Transformer
submission: Universal image restoration (UIR) seeks to recover images degraded by unknown mixtures while preserving semantics. We present LucidFlux, a caption-free UIR framework that adapts a large diffusion transformer (Flux.1) to restoration with minimal parameter overhead. LucidFlux introduces a lightweight dual-branch conditioner that injects signals from the degraded input and a lightly restored proxy to respectively anchor geometry and suppress artifacts. A timestep- and layer-adaptive modulation schedule routes these cues across the backbone’s hierarchy, yielding updates that aim to protect global structure while recovering texture. To avoid the latency and instability of text prompts or VLM captions, we enforce a caption-free semantic alignment via SigLIP features extracted from the proxy. A scalable curation pipeline filters large-scale data for structure-rich supervision. Across benchmarks, LucidFlux shows favorable behavior compared to several baselines. Ablations explore where and when conditioning matters for large DiTs, and suggest conditioning choices are important for robust, prompt-free restoration.

title: Traceable Evidence Enhanced Visual Grounded Reasoning: Evaluation and Method
submission: Existing visual grounded reasoning models can reference image regions dynamically, resembling human "thinking with images", but a holistic diagnostic benchmark for this capability is lacking. We introduce TreeBench, a traceable-evidence evaluation benchmark built on three guiding principles: focused perception of subtle targets in complex scenes, traceable evidence via bounding-box-based evaluation, and second-order reasoning that tests object interactions and spatial hierarchies beyond simple localization. We sample high-quality, densely packed images and enlist multiple multimodal experts to annotate questions, candidate options, and answers, followed by iterative quality control to produce a curated set of challenging visual QA pairs. Current models still struggle on these cases, indicating gaps in traceable visual reasoning. To address this, we propose TreeVGR, a training paradigm that jointly supervises localization and reasoning pathways, using reinforcement-style objectives to encourage explainable evidence traces. Initial results suggest promise for improved traceability, but the overall benefits and generalization remain to be more comprehensively characterized.

title: Echoes as Anchors: Probabilistic Costs and Attention Refocusing in LLM Reasoning
submission: Test-time compute allocation in large reasoning models (LRMs) is widely used and has applications in mathematical problem solving, code synthesis, and planning. Recent approaches scale self-consistency and parallel thinking, add generic thinking tokens, or prompt models to re-read the question, but these either inject task-agnostic tokens or rely on heuristics that do not address the spontaneous repetition many LRMs show at the start of their internal traces. We analyze and exploit this tendency to restate the question, which we term the Echo of Prompt (EOP), as a front-loaded, compute-shaping mechanism. We formalize echo removal as rejection-based conditioning and define the Echo Likelihood Gap ΔL as a proxy linking early repetition to likelihood behavior. To exploit EOP, we develop Echo-Distilled SFT (ED-SFT) to encourage an "echo-then-reason" pattern and Echoic Prompting (EP) to re-ground the model mid-trace without training. Length-controlled likelihood analyses and layer-wise attention studies suggest attention refocusing in middle layers. We evaluate on GSM8K, MathQA, Hendrycks-MATH, AIME24, and MATH-500 and report preliminary improvements under matched compute, with mixed gains across settings.

title: Time-Gated Multi-Scale Flow Matching for Time-Series Imputation
submission: We address multivariate time-series imputation by learning the velocity field of a data-conditioned ordinary differential equation (ODE) via flow matching. Our method, Time-Gated Multi-Scale Flow Matching (TG-MSFM), conditions the flow on an endpoint comprising observed values, a per-time visibility mask, and short left/right context, processed by a time-aware Transformer whose self-attention is masked to aggregate only from observed timestamps. To reconcile global trends with local details we introduce time-gated multi-scale velocity heads on a fixed 1D pyramid and blend them through a time-dependent gate; a mild anti-aliasing filter stabilizes the finest branch. At inference we use a second-order Heun integrator with a per-step data-consistency projection that keeps observed coordinates exactly on the straight path from the initial noise to the endpoint. Training uses gap-only supervision of the velocity on missing coordinates. Across standard benchmarks we report competitive MSE/MAE and discuss ablations that isolate contributions of the time-gated heads, masked attention, and the data-consistent integration, with implementation and broader comparisons deferred to the main manuscript.

title: FastGRPO: Accelerating Policy Optimization via Concurrency-aware Speculative Decoding and Online Draft Learning
submission: Group relative policy optimization (GRPO) can improve reasoning capabilities of large language models via reinforcement learning. We propose FastGRPO, a concurrency-aware speculative decoding framework that dynamically adjusts drafting and verification strategies according to real-time concurrency, and an online draft learning mechanism that continuously adapts the draft model using feedback from the target model. The concurrency-aware design maximizes generation acceleration by selecting drafting strategies that better match running concurrency levels, while online draft learning mitigates performance degradation due to distributional drift between the fixed draft and evolving target. Experimental evaluation across multiple mathematical reasoning datasets shows end-to-end speedups of 2.35x to 2.72x compared to prior decoding strategies, with the code released at https://github.com/yedaotian9/FastGRPO.

title: Reading Images Like Texts: Sequential Image Understanding in Vision-Language Models
submission: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong performance across many tasks. Existing VLMs typically process visual information by serializing images, a method that diverges from the parallel nature of human vision. Inspired by the dual-stream hypothesis distinguishing "what" and "where" pathways, we deconstruct visual processing in VLMs into object recognition and spatial perception for separate study. For object recognition, we convert images into text token maps and observe a two-stage unfolding from shallow to deep layers: attribute recognition followed by semantic disambiguation. For spatial perception, we derive and empirically check a geometric structure underlying positional representation in VLMs. Based on these findings, we introduce a token compression algorithm implemented as a plug-and-play visual decoder to improve decoding efficiency, and a RoPE scaling technique to enhance spatial reasoning. Through experiments we validate these analyses and propose design principles for future architectures, though we do not report comparisons to established baselines and the practical advantage remains described in qualitative terms.

title: Lightweight Transformer for EEG Classification via Balanced Signed Graph Algorithm Unrolling
submission: EEG signals recorded by scalp sensors exhibit inherent anti-correlations that can be modeled by negative edges in a finite graph. Motivated by this, we propose a lightweight, interpretable transformer-like architecture derived by unrolling a spectral denoising algorithm for signals on a balanced signed graph — a graph with no cycles containing an odd number of negative edges. A balanced signed graph admits well-defined frequencies that map to a corresponding positive graph via a similarity transform of the graph Laplacian. We realize an efficient implementation of an ideal low-pass filter on the mapped positive graph using a Lanczos approximation, and we let the cutoff frequency be learned from data. During training, two balanced signed graph denoisers are trained that implicitly capture posterior-like information for two signal classes, and we compare their reconstruction errors for binary classification of EEG. Experiments indicate classification performance comparable to representative deep learning schemes while using substantially fewer parameters, though the exact regimes of superiority require further clarification.

title: Dual Randomized Smoothing: Beyond Global Noise Variance
submission: Randomized Smoothing (RS) uses global noise variance to certify robustness, but a single global variance cannot simultaneously perform well at small and large radii. To address this limitation, we propose a dual RS framework that allows input-dependent noise variances. We show conceptually that RS can remain valid with locally constant, input-dependent variances, and build a two-component approach: a variance estimator that proposes a variance per input, and a classifier that uses the estimated variance. The variance estimator is treated to promote local constancy, and we outline iterative training strategies to coordinate the two components. This paper focuses on the formulation and potential benefits of input-adaptive variance for improved certified robustness across radii. Detailed proofs, implementation specifics, and exhaustive empirical protocols are deferred to future work; here we present the framework and discuss design trade-offs and practical considerations for deployment.

title: Watermark-based Attribution of AI-Generated Content
submission: Several companies have deployed watermark-based detection to identify AI-generated content. However, attribution—the ability to trace back to the user of a generative AI (GenAI) service who created given AI-generated content—remains largely unexplored despite its growing importance. In this work, we present a systematic study on watermark-based, user-level attribution of AI-generated content. Our core idea is to assign a unique watermark to each GenAI user and embed this watermark into that user’s generated content, then attribute by identifying the user whose watermark best matches the one extracted from the content. We address the key challenge of how to select watermarks for users to improve attribution. To do so, we derive probabilistic lower bounds on detection and attribution performance for arbitrary watermark sets, and propose a selection procedure that optimizes these bounds. We discuss the implications of robustness and post-processing on attribution accuracy and provide qualitative examples illustrating typical behavior under common post-processes such as compression and simple edits.

title: Cost-of-Pass: An Economic Framework for Evaluating Language Models
submission: AI systems must generate value that exceeds inference costs, and we argue this tradeoff needs economically grounded metrics. Building on Farrell's productive efficiency, we propose a framework that combines accuracy and inference cost to assess language models' productivity. We introduce the idea of a cost-of-pass, informally described as the expected monetary cost to obtain a correct solution, and we discuss a frontier notion as the minimal such cost across available models or human experts using approximate hiring costs. Our discussion touches on lightweight, large, and reasoning models and their relative roles for different task types, and we sketch how tracking the frontier over time may reveal progress. We also outline counterfactual frontiers that omit particular model classes to attribute drivers of progress, and we briefly consider inference-time techniques including majority voting, self-refinement, and a budget-aware approach. Overall, we present an economic perspective intended to guide measurement and deployment decisions, though concrete deployment recommendations are left open.

title: Revisiting Sharpness-Aware Minimization: A More Faithful and Effective Implementation
submission: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) improves generalization by minimizing the maximum training loss within a neighborhood around parameters. SAM is typically implemented by taking gradient ascent steps to find an ascent point and then applying the gradient at that shifted point to update the current parameters. This common practice can be interpreted as approximating the SAM objective while neglecting the full derivative of the ascent point with respect to parameters. Yet a clear, intuitive account of why the gradient at the ascent point works better than the local gradient is still lacking. We propose a new interpretation: the gradient at the single-step ascent point, when applied back at the current parameters, can better align with the direction toward the local maximum than the plain local gradient. At the same time, this approximation can be inaccurate, and its quality may deteriorate with more ascent steps. To address these issues, we introduce eXplicit Sharpness-Aware Minimization (XSAM), which explicitly estimates the direction of the maximum during training and defines a search space that leverages gradient information at multi-step ascent points. XSAM unifies single- and multi-step settings and incurs negligible overhead; experiments across models and datasets show consistent improvements over existing methods.

title: Cambrian-S: Towards Spatial Supersensing in Video
submission: We argue that progress in true multimodal intelligence calls for a shift from reactive, task-driven systems and brute-force long context towards a broader paradigm of supersensing. We frame spatial supersensing as four stages beyond linguistic-only understanding: semantic perception (naming what is seen), streaming event cognition (maintaining memory across continuous experiences), implicit 3D spatial cognition (inferring the world behind pixels), and predictive world modeling (creating internal models that filter and organize information). Current benchmarks largely test only the early stages, offering narrow coverage of spatial cognition and rarely challenging models in ways that require true world modeling. To drive progress in spatial supersensing, we present VSI-SUPER, a two-part benchmark: VSR (long-horizon visual spatial recall) and VSC (continual visual spatial counting). These tasks require arbitrarily long video inputs yet are resistant to brute-force context expansion. We then test data scaling limits by curating VSI-590K and training Cambrian-S, achieving +30% absolute improvement on VSI-Bench without sacrificing general capabilities. Yet performance on VSI-SUPER remains limited, indicating that scale alone is insufficient for spatial supersensing. We propose predictive sensing as a path forward, presenting a proof-of-concept in which a self-supervised next-latent-frame predictor leverages surprise (prediction error) to drive memory and event segmentation. On VSI-SUPER, this approach substantially outperforms leading proprietary baselines, showing that spatial supersensing requires models that not only see but also anticipate, select, and organize experience.

title: LightRetriever: A LLM-based Text Retrieval Architecture with Extremely Faster Query Inference
submission: LLM-based text retrieval ranks documents by vector similarity with documents pre-encoded offline and queries encoded online. While large LLMs improve retrieval quality, serving deep models slows query inference and increases online resource demands. We propose LightRetriever, an LLM-based retriever that keeps a full-sized LLM for document encoding but reduces query handling to an extremely lightweight process resembling an embedding lookup. title: WSVD: Weighted Low-Rank Approximation for Fast and Efficient Execution of Low-Precision Vision-Language Models
submission: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) has become an important technique for reducing the computational burden of vision–language models (VLMs), which play a central role in tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering. Although multiple prior works have proposed efficient SVD variants to enable low-rank operations, it remains challenging to translate low-rank approximations into consistent latency reductions in practice. To address this, we introduce a finer-grained computational pattern and apply SVD at a more local granularity, while also adapting relative importance across weight elements during the decomposition to better preserve accuracy. We further combine this decomposition strategy with quantization of weights and activations to produce a compact VLM execution approach. Collectively, we present Weighted SVD (WSVD), an integrated low-rank and quantization recipe that aims to reduce execution cost of VLMs while retaining task performance. Implementation details and code are available to reproduce the described procedure.

title: Source-Guided Flow Matching
submission: Guidance of generative models is commonly achieved by modifying the probability flow vector field with an added guidance term. We propose Source-Guided Flow Matching (SGFM), which instead adjusts the source distribution while keeping a pre-trained vector field unchanged. This reduces guidance to sampling from an altered source distribution. We outline theoretical statements suggesting SGFM can recover a target distribution under certain idealized conditions, and we provide informal discussion about errors when using approximate samplers or vector fields. The approach is compatible with optimal flow matching models since the transport map implied by the vector field is left intact. We compare several sampling strategies and discuss practical considerations; experiments on synthetic and applied tasks are used to illustrate the framework at a conceptual level.

title: FlexLoRA: Entropy-Guided Flexible Low-Rank Adaptation
submission: Large pre-trained models achieve strong performance across domains, but full fine-tuning is often costly in compute and memory. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become common, and Low-Rank Adaptation introduces trainable low-rank matrices that perform well. However, fixed-rank designs can lack flexibility. We propose FlexLoRA, an entropy-guided flexible low-rank adaptation framework that evaluates matrix importance via spectral energy entropy, supports rank pruning and expansion under a global budget, and uses zero-impact initialization for newly added singular directions to promote stability. FlexLoRA is intended to address granularity, flexibility, and stability concerns in PEFT via a more principled mechanism for allocating capacity. In practice, experiments across benchmarks show that FlexLoRA can match or sometimes improve over contemporary baselines in various settings, though improvements are not uniformly large. We present design choices and ablations that highlight where flexible rank allocation tends to be most beneficial, leaving broader adoption and more extensive tuning to future work.

title: Stochastic Self-Organization in Multi-Agent Systems
submission: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable multi-agent systems (MAS) where agents collaborate to solve tasks beyond a single model. Most existing approaches rely on fixed topologies, pretrained graph generators, optimization over edges, or external LLM judges, adding complexity. We introduce a response-conditioned framework that adapts communication on the fly. Agents independently generate answers and assess peer contributions using a Shapley-inspired approximation. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is constructed to route information from high-contribution agents to others, enabling stable and efficient message passing without additional supervision or training. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that multiple agents can increase the chance of correctness and that correct answers tend to dominate information flow. Experiments with both strong and weak LLM backends indicate robust behavior in many settings; gains are modest and task-dependent. Direct, comprehensive comparisons with all prior graph-based or judge-based methods are left to future work.

title: Sampling-aware Adversarial Attacks Against Large Language Models
submission: Assessing adversarial robustness of large language models (LLMs) requires careful methodology because LLMs are deployed at scale and can produce harmful outputs under various conditions. Prior work studies adversarial attacks, jailbreaks, and robustness, often focusing on single-point greedy generations; these approaches come from a long literature on robustness evaluation, stochastic sampling behaviors, and safety practices in model deployment. In this context we emphasize that repeated sampling complements prompt optimization: by allocating compute between optimization and sampling one can often find harmful outputs more reliably. Casting the attack as a resource allocation problem yields practical trade-offs between optimization and sampling effort. Integrating sampling into existing attacks improves success rates and efficiency in our experiments, and we further analyze how distributions of output harmfulness evolve during attacks and introduce an entropy-maximization objective as a label-free target. These findings highlight the often-overlooked role of sampling when assessing and improving LLM safety.

title: MesaNet: Sequence Modeling by Locally Optimal Test-Time Training
submission: Sequence modeling is dominated by causal transformers using softmax self-attention, and recent work has produced linearized alternatives that behave like efficient recurrent neural networks (RNNs). These methods, such as DeltaNet, Mamba, or xLSTM, can be unified by noting their recurrent layer dynamics arise from an in-context regression objective approximately optimized online. Here we join that line and introduce a chunkwise parallelizable variant of the Mesa layer that was previously only sequential, hoping to scale the approach. The layer stems from an in-context loss that we now minimize to optimality at each time point using a conjugate gradient solver, and we describe implementation details and stability considerations. Through an extensive suite of experiments up to large parameter counts we compare performance, and we observe trade-offs between inference flops and downstream benchmark results. The presentation mixes implementation notes, empirical observations, and motivations in an overlapping way.

title: ReactID: Synchronizing Realistic Actions and Identity in Personalized Video Generation
submission: Personalized video generation faces a trade-off between identity consistency and action realism: rigid identity preservation can cause unnatural motion, while focusing on action can compromise subject fidelity. This arises from imprecise subject-video alignment, unstable training due to varying sample difficulties, and insufficient fine-grained action modeling. We present ReactID, a framework that aims to harmonize identity accuracy and motion naturalness via coordinated advances in data, training, and action modeling. We assemble ReactID-Data using an annotation pipeline that mixes vision-based label extraction, MLLM-based detection, and post-verification to improve subject-video correspondence. We analyze learning difficulty across subject size, appearance similarity, and sampling strategy, and propose a progressive curriculum from easy to hard samples to stabilize training. ReactID also introduces timeline-based conditioning that supplements text prompts with multi-action sequences, integrating per-sub-action timestamps via a subject-aware cross-attention module and a temporally-adaptive RoPE. We claim improved balance between identity preservation and action realism, though specific metric details and ablations are not fully delineated.

title: VideoNSA: Native Sparse Attention Scales Video Understanding
submission: Video understanding in multimodal language models remains limited by context length: models often miss key transition frames and struggle to maintain coherence across long time scales. To address this, we adapt Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to video-language models. Our method, VideoNSA, adapts Qwen2.5-VL through end-to-end training on a 216K video instruction dataset. We employ a hardware-aware hybrid approach to attention, preserving dense attention for text, while employing NSA for video. Compared to token-compression and training-free sparse baselines, VideoNSA achieves improved performance on long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial benchmarks. Further ablation analysis reveals four key findings: (1) reliable scaling to 128K tokens; (2) an optimal global–local attention allocation at a fixed budget; (3) task-dependent branch usage patterns; and (4) the learnable combined sparse attention help induce dynamic attention sinks. While these results indicate promise for NSA in video-language settings, the overall improvements are moderate and additional work is needed to understand trade-offs across more diverse tasks and hardware constraints.

title: Consistent Text-to-Image Generation via Scene De-Contextualization
submission: Consistent text-to-image (T2I) generation seeks to produce identity-preserving images of the same subject across diverse scenes, yet it often fails due to identity (ID) shift. We show that a key source of ID shift is the native correlation between subject and scene context, called scene contextualization, which arises as T2I models fit large natural-image distributions. We formally prove near-universality of this scene–subject correlation and derive theoretical bounds on its strength. Building on this, we propose Scene De-Contextualization (SDeC), a training-free prompt embedding editing approach that imposes an inversion process of T2I’s built-in scene contextualization. SDeC identifies and suppresses the latent scene–subject correlation within the ID prompt embedding by quantifying SVD directional stability and adaptively re-weighting eigenvalues. Crucially, SDeC allows per-scene use (one prompt per scene) without requiring prior access to all target scenes. Experiments suggest SDeC can improve identity preservation in many cases while generally maintaining scene diversity, though effects vary by model and setting.

title: Fusing Pixels and Genes: Spatially-Aware Learning in Computational Pathology
submission: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in multimodal learning within computational pathology. Existing models primarily rely on vision and language modalities; however, language alone lacks molecular specificity and offers limited pathological supervision, leading to representational bottlenecks. In this paper, we propose STAMP, a Spatial Transcriptomics-Augmented Multimodal Pathology representation learning framework that integrates spatially-resolved gene expression profiles to enable molecule-guided joint embedding of pathology images and transcriptomic data. Our study shows that self-supervised, gene-guided training provides a robust and task-agnostic signal for learning pathology image representations. Incorporating spatial context and multi-scale information further enhances model performance and generalizability. To support this, we constructed SpaVis-6M, the largest Visium-based spatial transcriptomics dataset to date, and trained a spatially-aware gene encoder on this resource. Leveraging hierarchical multi-scale contrastive alignment and cross-scale patch localization mechanisms, STAMP effectively aligns spatial transcriptomics with pathology images, capturing spatial structure and molecular variation. We validate STAMP across six datasets and four downstream tasks, where it consistently achieves strong performance. These results highlight the value and necessity of integrating spatially resolved molecular supervision for advancing multimodal learning in computational pathology. The code is included in the supplementary materials. The pretrained weights and SpaVis-6M are available at: https://github.com/Hanminghao/STAMP.

submission: We introduce Weak-to-Strong Diffusion (W2SD), a framework that leverages the estimated gap between an existing weak model and a stronger model to drive sampling trajectories toward regions of the real data distribution. W2SD uses a reflective operation that alternates between denoising and inversion augmented by the weak-to-strong gap; this steers latents along refined sampling paths. The framework is flexible in its choice of weak-to-strong model pairs (e.g., DreamShaper vs. SD1.5, different experts in MoE) and can be applied across architectures. We apply W2SD to image and video generation, and report consistent improvements in human preference, aesthetic quality, and prompt adherence across UNet- and DiT-based architectures and MoE setups. The additional computation is modest compared to the observed gains, and combining multiple weak-to-strong gaps yields cumulative improvements that enhance practical deployability.

title: BRIDGING THE GAP BETWEEN HUMAN MOTION AND ACTION SEMANTICS VIA KINEMATIC PHRASES
submission: The goal of motion understanding is to establish a reliable mapping between motion and action semantics, while it is a challenging many-to-many problem. An abstract action semantic (i.e., walk forwards) could be conveyed by perceptually diverse motions (walk with arms up or swinging), while a motion could carry different semantics w.r.t. its context and intention. This makes an elegant mapping between them difficult. Previous attempts adopted direct-mapping paradigms with limited reliability. Also, current automatic metrics fail to provide reliable assessments of the consistency between motions and action semantics. We identify the source of these problems as the significant gap between the two modalities. To alleviate this gap, we propose Kinematic Phrases (KP) that take the objective kinematic facts of human motion with proper abstraction, interpretability, and generality characteristics. Based on KP as a mediator, we can unify a motion knowledge base and build a motion understanding system. Meanwhile, KP can be automatically converted from motions and to text descriptions with no subjective bias, inspiring Kinematic Prompt Generation (KPG) as a novel automatic motion generation benchmark. In extensive experiments, our approach shows superiority over other methods, but quantitative improvements are inconsistent and on several standard benchmarks we observe no clear advantage, suggesting limited practical gains.

title: Equivariant Splitting: Self-supervised learning from incomplete data
submission: Self-supervised learning for inverse problems allows training a reconstruction network from noise and/or incomplete data alone. These methods have the potential of enabling learning-based solutions when obtaining ground-truth references for training is expensive or impossible. We introduce a new definition of equivariance in the context of reconstruction networks, and show that the combination of self-supervised splitting losses and equivariant reconstruction networks results in unbiased estimates of the supervised loss. In this work we propose Equivariant Splitting, a self-supervised strategy devised for settings with a single incomplete observation model. Experiments include image inpainting, accelerated magnetic resonance imaging, sparse-view computed tomography, and compressive sensing. The proposed loss achieves state-of-the-art performance in settings with highly rank-deficient forward models. Related discussions and limitations are interleaved with the description of experiments and design choices, and some method components are presented after the results, which may obscure the central motivation.

title: VeriEquivBench: An Equivalence Score for Ground-Truth-Free Evaluation of Formally Verifiable Code
submission: Formal verification is the next frontier for ensuring the correctness of code generated by Large Language Models (LLMs). While co-generation of code and formal specifications in languages like Dafny promises alignment with user intent, progress is constrained by how specification quality is evaluated. We introduce VeriEquivBench, a new benchmark comprising 2,389 algorithmic problems designed to probe limitations of current models in code generation and formal reasoning. Rather than relying on a small set of ground-truth specifications, VeriEquivBench is intended to support formally grounded evaluation at scale. The benchmark includes diverse, complex tasks and accompanying artifacts intended for use with formally verifiable workflows. We describe the benchmark composition and intended usage scenarios, and discuss directions for future work to improve specification generation and verification practices for model-driven code.

title: GuirlVG: Incentivize GUI Visual Grounding via Empirical Exploration on Reinforcement Learning
submission: Graphical user interface visual grounding (GUI-VG)—a core capability for GUI agents—has primarily relied on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), demanding extensive data curation and significant training costs. However, as MLLMs continue to advance and even cover GUI domains during pretraining, the necessity of exhaustive SFT post-training becomes increasingly questionable. Meanwhile, the recent successes of rule-based reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) suggest a more efficient alternative. However, despite its promise, the optimal manner of RFT for GUI-VG remains unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce GuirlVG, a reinforcement learning–based GUI-VG method built on a systematic empirical study and a novel stabilization technique. Preliminarily, we find that naive application of RFT underperforms the SFT baseline, motivating a deeper exploration of RFT. First, we decompose RFT into its core components and analyze the optimal formulation of each. Second, as part of this exploration, we propose a novel Adversarial KL Factor that dynamically stabilizes training to mitigate reward over-optimization. Third, we further explore the training configurations of RFT to enhance the effectiveness. Extensive experiments show that GuirlVG, with only 5.2K training samples, outperforms SFT methods trained on over 10M samples, achieving a +7.7% improvement on ScreenSpot, a +17.2% improvement on ScreenSpotPro and 91.9% accuracy on ScreenSpotV2.

title: How hard is learning to cut? Trade-offs and sample complexity
submission: In recent years, branch-and-cut algorithms have been the target of data-driven approaches designed to enhance decision making in phases such as branching or cut selection. For cutting plane selection two score functions have been proposed: branch-and-cut tree size and gap closed. In this paper we present new sample complexity lower bounds that apply to both scores for broad families of classes mapping an instance to a cut. We show that learning to minimize those scores over an unknown instance distribution requires sample complexity comparable to learning generic target functions, and we argue these bounds extend to cuts from the Simplex tableau. To our knowledge these constitute the first lower bounds in the learning-to-cut framework. We compare the theoretical picture to prior upper bounds and discuss implications for designing learning-based cut selectors; empirical validation is presented only at a preliminary level.

title: VenusX: Unlocking Fine-Grained Functional Understanding of Proteins
submission: Deep learning models have driven significant progress in predicting protein function and interactions at the protein level. While these advancements have been invaluable for many biological applications such as enzyme engineering and function annotation, a more detailed perspective is essential for understanding protein functional mechanisms and evaluating the biological knowledge captured by models. This study introduces VenusX, a benchmark designed to assess protein representation learning with a focus on fine-grained intra-protein functional understanding. VenusX comprises task categories covering residue-level binary classification, fragment-level multi-class classification, and pairwise functional similarity scoring to target active sites, binding sites, conserved sites, motifs, domains, and epitopes, curated from major open-source resources. By providing mixed-family and cross-family evaluation settings, the benchmark aims to support assessment of models on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. For baseline evaluation, we assess a range of popular open-source models and report their performance across the benchmark using multiple metrics. Our code, data, and a leaderboard are provided as open-source resources.

title: Explaining Grokking and Information Bottleneck through Neural Collapse Emergence
submission: The training dynamics of deep networks often defy expectations. Two examples are grokking—where test performance improves long after training loss plateaus—and the information bottleneck, where models discard input information as training proceeds. The mechanisms and relations between these phenomena remain unclear. In this work we offer a unified explanation through neural collapse, a characterization of learned representation geometry. We show that contraction of within-class population variance is closely related to both grokking and information bottleneck, and we relate this contraction to a neural collapse measure computed on the training set. By studying the dynamics of neural collapse we argue that different time scales between fitting and collapse progression can account for late-phase behavior. We validate these ideas on several datasets and architectures, although some aspects of the setup and motivation are presented non-linearly and with limited emphasis on the original empirical puzzles.

title: Computational Bottlenecks for Denoising Diffusions
submission: Denoising diffusions sample from a distribution mu in R^d by constructing a stochastic process whose terminal distribution approximates mu. The drift of this diffusion is typically learned via score-matching objectives. We revisit the question of whether every distribution for which sampling is tractable is also amenable to diffusion-based sampling. Prior work suggests broad families of distributions where sampling is easy but learning an appropriate drift may be hard. In this work we connect those phenomena to information–computation gaps in statistical estimation and argue that, under certain computational limitations, diffusion sampling can fail to recover the target distribution even when score-matching objectives appear well optimized. We illustrate these limitations on a sparse low-rank matrix sampling task and discuss implications for choosing sampling approaches in practice.

title: Flow Caching for Autoregressive Video Generation
submission: Autoregressive models built on Transformer architectures remain a natural paradigm for generating very long videos by synthesizing content in sequential chunks, but the sequential generation loop is slow. Prior caching strategies accelerate diffusion-based video models by assuming uniform denoising across frames; this assumption does not hold for autoregressive chunked generation where different chunks can behave differently at the same timestep. We propose FlowCache, a caching framework designed for autoregressive video generation that treats each chunk with independent caching policies so chunks can avoid unnecessary recomputation. We introduce a chunkwise caching strategy that adapts to per-chunk denoising characteristics and a joint importance–redundancy KV cache compression mechanism that enforces fixed memory bounds while attempting to preserve quality. Empirically, FlowCache achieves substantial speedups on standard benchmarks with only minor changes to visual quality. The code is available at https://github.com/mikeallen39/FlowCache.

title: NI Sampling: Accelerating Discrete Diffusion Sampling by Token Order Optimization
submission: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive approaches, offering the flexibility to generate tokens in arbitrary orders and the potential for parallel decoding. However, existing heuristic sampling strategies are inefficient: they choose only a small subset of tokens at each step, leaving substantial room for improvement. We study token sampling order optimization and show that fully leveraging correct predictions at each step can reduce the number of sampling iterations by orders of magnitude without compromising task performance. Based on this, we introduce Neural Indicator Sampling (NI Sampling), a general sampling order optimization framework that uses a neural indicator to decide which tokens to sample at each step, trained with a trajectory-preserving objective. Experiments on LLaDA and Dream across multiple benchmarks show dramatic speedups: NI Sampling attains up to 100× acceleration over full-step sampling with no measurable performance drop, and consistently dominates confidence-threshold sampling in the accuracy–step trade-off.

title: RLAP-CLIP: Continual Multimodal Learning with Prototype Adaptation and Difficulty-Aware Routing
submission: Vision-language models such as CLIP achieve strong zero-shot performance through contrastive pre-training but still face substantial challenges in class-incremental image classification. When learning tasks sequentially, prototype quality can degrade and visual adaptation capabilities are often underutilized. We propose RLAP-CLIP to address these issues with three complementary components. First, a reinforcement-learning-based prototype optimization module aims to construct prototypes more deliberately than simple averaging. Second, a difficulty-aware cross-modal fusion mechanism routes samples through different processing pathways according to estimated complexity. Third, a dual-modal prompting scheme attempts to balance visual and textual adaptation. We evaluate RLAP-CLIP on a range of image classification benchmarks and observe consistent improvements over prior approaches, indicating that actively optimized prototypes and adaptive routing can mitigate common class-incremental failures. Code and experimental details are provided in the paper.

title: Robust Fine-tuning of Vision-Language-Action Robot Policies via Parameter Merging
submission: Generalist robot policies trained on large, diverse datasets can generalize across many behaviors, yet they often struggle when finetuned on a small number of demonstrations for a novel task, suffering from overfitting and loss of prior abilities. We seek a simple strategy that preserves a generalist policy's broad competencies while enabling robust learning of a new skill. We show that interpolating the weights of a finetuned model with those of the pretrained model provides such a trade-off: a merged model can inherit generalist behaviors while incorporating the new task skill. We describe practical considerations for weight interpolation and discuss how to apply it across simulated and real-world robot tasks. We also sketch how this approach can be applied incrementally to enable continual skill acquisition without catastrophic loss. Extensive empirical work underpins these claims, but specific numerical comparisons and baseline details are omitted here.

submission: We study the statistical performance of continual learning for two linear regression tasks in a well-specified random design. We consider a structural regularization algorithm that incorporates a generalized ℓ2-regularization tailored to the Hessian of the previous task to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. We establish upper and lower bounds on the joint excess risk for this algorithm, highlighting a trade-off between memory complexity and statistical efficiency: memory complexity is measured by the number of vectors needed to define the structural regularization. Increasing the number of vectors worsens memory complexity but improves excess risk, and vice versa. Our theory suggests naive continual learning without regularization suffers from forgetting, while structural regularization mitigates it. These findings are theoretical and are presented without extensive empirical baselines for comparison, and thus their practical impact may be limited.

title: IceCache: Memory-Efficient KV-cache Management for Long-Sequence LLMs
submission: Key-Value (KV) cache accelerates inference in LLMs by storing intermediate attention states during autoregressive generation. Prior work has offloaded KV-cache to CPU while keeping subsets on GPU, and we propose IceCache, a KV-cache management strategy that combines semantic token clustering with PagedAttention. IceCache organizes semantically related tokens into contiguous memory regions managed by a hierarchical, dynamically updatable structure to enable more efficient token selection and better CPU–GPU transfers. Our description alternates between design choices and implementation notes, and does not foreground a single, concrete problem statement about memory bottlenecks. We report experiments on LongBench indicating that IceCache can maintain accuracy with a reduced token budget and compare it qualitatively to other offloading methods. Code and examples are provided on the project page for readers to reproduce and interpret the trade-offs.

title: Unlocking the Essence of Beauty: Advanced Aesthetic Reasoning with Relative-Absolute Policy Optimization
submission: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are promising for image aesthetic assessment because they can capture high-level aesthetic features through cross-modal understanding. The scarcity of multimodal aesthetic reasoning data and the subjective nature of aesthetics make it challenging for MLLMs to produce accurate judgments with interpretable rationales. We propose Aes-R1, a general aesthetic reasoning framework that combines a pipeline, AesCoT, to produce chain-of-thought style reasoning data for initial training, and a reinforcement learning phase to refine scoring and ranking behavior. After teaching the model to generate structured explanations before scoring, the framework applies a policy optimization approach that jointly considers absolute scores and relative preferences to improve both per-image scoring and cross-image ranking. Aes-R1 enables MLLMs to output explanations alongside scores, improving aesthetic reasoning in a unified manner. Extensive experiments show improved performance over comparable models and ablations validate robustness under limited supervision and some out-of-distribution scenarios, though details of datasets and exact gains are described in the paper.

title: Reasoning Models Can be Accurately Pruned Via Chain-of-Thought Reconstruction
submission: Reasoning language models such as DeepSeek-R1 produce long chain-of-thought traces during inference time which make them costly to deploy at scale and, as we note, standard pruning can hurt reasoning more than it does usual LM tasks. We show that pruning sometimes causes larger performance drops and can even slow down end-to-end latency because the model emits more thinking tokens with degraded reasoning. This stems in part from pruning approaches that prioritize input reconstruction even though reasoning is decode-dominated. We introduce a simple, drop-in fix: during pruning we jointly reconstruct activations from the input and the model’s on-policy chain-of-thought traces. This Reasoning-Aware Compression (RAC) integrates with existing pruning workflows like SparseGPT and, in our experiments, substantially improves retained reasoning quality after compression. Anonymized code is available at: https://github.com/RyanLucas3/Reasoning-Aware-Compression

title: Unveiling the Potential of Diffusion Large Language Model in Controllable Generation
submission: Controllable generation is a task in NLP with many applications. Even state-of-the-art autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) can be unreliable when required to generate structured output. Inspired by diffusion-based large language models (dLLM), we suggest that architectural differences, especially global information-sharing, might be relevant for controllable generation. To explore this, we propose Self-adaptive Schema Scaffolding (S^3), a framework that enables dLLM to more stably generate structured outputs (e.g., JSON) by utilizing reverse reasoning and global context. S^3 initiates a schematic template directly in the output context as a starting state for dLLM, offering a simpler alternative to complex prompt optimization. Experiments indicate that our method improves structure adherence, content fidelity, and faithfulness for some setups, suggesting practical pathways for deploying dLLMs in controllable generation tasks.

title: Neyman-Pearson Classification under Both Null and Alternative Distributions Shift
submission: We study transfer learning for Neyman–Pearson classification, where the goal is to minimize error under distribution μ1 while constraining error under μ0 below a given threshold. Transfer in imbalanced settings like Neyman–Pearson classification has received limited attention, and controlling both types of errors under shift is challenging. Prior work typically considers shift only in μ1, but in practice both μ0 and μ1 can shift. We propose an adaptive procedure that aims to leverage informative sources to improve Type-I and Type-II errors while attempting to avoid negative transfer when the source is uninformative. The method is designed to adapt to varying degrees of source relevance, and we sketch statistical conditions under which improvements can be expected. We also describe practical algorithmic choices to make the procedure computationally efficient and discuss scenarios where adaptation may be limited.

title: A Progressive Training Framework for Spiking Neural Networks with Learnable Multi-hierarchical Model
submission: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have garnered considerable attention due to their energy efficiency and unique biological characteristics. However, the widely adopted Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model, as the mainstream neuron model in current SNN research, has been revealed to exhibit significant deficiencies in deep-layer gradient calculation and in capturing global information along the time dimension. In this paper, we propose the Learnable Multi-hierarchical (LM-H) model to address these issues by dynamically regulating its membrane-related factors. We point out that the LM-H model fully encompasses the information representation range of the LIF model while offering the flexibility to adjust the extraction ratio between historical and current information. We also provide some theoretical arguments for the effectiveness of the LM-H model and discuss the functionality of its internal parameters to some extent, and we propose a progressive training algorithm tailored specifically for the LM-H model. Furthermore, we devise an efficient training framework for our model, encompassing hybrid training and time-slicing online training. Through experiments on various datasets, we validate the advantages of our model and training algorithm compared to previous approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/hzc1208/STBP_LMH

title: SPECS: Decoupling Multimodal Learning via  Self-distilled Preference-based Cold Start
submission:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently catalyzed a wave of "MLLM-r1" approaches that bring RL to vision language models. Most representative paradigms begin with a cold start, typically employing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), to initialize the policy before RL. However, SFT-based cold start adopts the reasoning paradigm intertwined with task solution and output format, which may induce instruction-style overfitting, weakens out-of-distribution generalization, and ultimately affects downstream RL. We revisit the cold start along two views, its training method and data construction, and introduce the Generalization Factor (GF) coefficient to quantify the generalization capability under different methods. Our empirical study finds that preference–based training methods (e.g. DPO) generalizes better than SFT-based methods in cold start. Motivated by this, we propose $\textbf{SPECS}$—a $\textbf{S}$elf-distilled, $\textbf{P}$r$\textbf{e}$ference-based $\textbf{C}$old $\textbf{S}$tart framework that decouples multimodal learning: (1) generates introspective preference data pairs via self-distillation, avoiding reliance on larger teachers or manual annotation; (2) performs preference–based training to learn, focusing on shallow, transferable surface-form criteria (format, structure, style) rather than memorizing content; and (3) hands off to RLVR for deep reasoning results. Experimental results across multiple multimodal benchmarks show that our decoupling learning framework yields consistent performance gains over strong baselines, improving MEGA-Bench by 4.1\% and MathVista by 12.2\%. Additional experiments indicate that SPECS contributes to reducing in-distribution "stuckness," improving exploration, stabilizing training, and raising the performance ceiling.

title: Jailbreaking the Matrix: Nullspace Steering for Controlled Model Subversion
submission: Large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak-style interventions that attempt to bypass safety mechanisms, despite advances in alignment and instruction tuning. Existing attacks often rely on prompt rewrites, dense optimization, or ad hoc heuristics and can lack interpretability. We propose Head-Masked Nullspace Steering (HMNS), a circuit-level intervention that (i) identifies attention heads most causally responsible for a model’s baseline routing, (ii) suppresses their write paths via targeted column masking, and (iii) injects a perturbation constrained to the orthogonal complement of the muted subspace. This geometry-aware intervention is intended to preserve fluency while steering certain aspects of model routing, though the exact objectives and safety implications vary across models and deployment contexts. HMNS operates in a closed-loop detection–intervention cycle, re-identifying causal heads and reapplying interventions across decoding attempts. We present experiments that probe HMNS design choices and behavior across several benchmarks and defenses, and highlight directions for further study of geometry-informed circuit interventions for controlled model steering.

title: MMR-V: What's Left Unsaid? A Benchmark for Multimodal Deep Reasoning in Videos
submission: The sequential nature of videos challenges multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to locate multi-frame evidence and perform multimodal reasoning. Existing video benchmarks mainly emphasize understanding tasks that match frames mentioned in the question and rely on a few adjacent frames. To address this gap, we introduce MMR-V: A Benchmark for Multimodal Deep Reasoning in Videos. MMR-V emphasizes long-range, multi-frame reasoning where evidence frames may be far from the question frame; tasks require reasoning beyond direct perception, involving hidden information; annotations are manually curated to reflect common real-world perceptions; and distractor strategies are used to reduce shortcuts. MMR-V comprises several hundred videos and over a thousand tasks. Our evaluations indicate current models struggle with multi-modal reasoning and that common reasoning enhancements provide limited improvements. We hope MMR-V will stimulate research on improving multimodal reasoning capabilities.

title: KITS: Inductive Spatio-Temporal Kriging with Increment Training Strategy
submission: Sensors are commonly deployed to perceive the environment. However, due to the high cost, sensors are usually sparsely deployed. Kriging is the tailored task to infer the unobserved nodes (without sensors) using the observed source nodes (with sensors). The essence of kriging task is transferability. Recently, several inductive spatio-temporal kriging methods have been proposed based on graph neural networks, being trained based on a graph built on top of observed nodes via pretext tasks such as masking nodes out and reconstructing them. However, the graph in training is inevitably much sparser than the graph in inference that includes all the observed and unobserved nodes. The learned pattern cannot be well generalized for inference, denoted as graph gap. To address this issue, we first present a novel Increment training strategy: instead of masking nodes (and reconstructing them), we add virtual nodes into the training graph so as to mitigate the graph gap issue naturally. Nevertheless, the empty-shell virtual nodes without labels could have bad-learned features and lack supervision signals. To solve these issues, we pair each virtual node with its most similar observed node and fuse their features together; to enhance the supervision signal, we construct reliable pseudo labels for virtual nodes. As a result, the learned pattern of virtual nodes could be safely transferred to real unobserved nodes for reliable kriging. We name our new Kriging model with Increment Training Strategy as KITS. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KITS consistently outperforms existing kriging methods by large margins, e.g., the improvement over MAE score could be as high as 18.33\%.

title: R2PS: Worst-Case Robust Real-Time Pursuit Strategies under Partial Observability
submission: Computing worst-case robust strategies in pursuit-evasion games (PEGs) is time-consuming, especially when real-world factors like partial observability are considered. Real-time applicable pursuit strategies for graph-based PEGs are missing when pursuers only have imperfect information about the evader. Although methods like Equilibrium Policy Generalization (EPG) and Grasper guide learning GNN policies robust to different dynamics, they assume perfect information and ignore cases where the evader can anticipate pursuers' actions. We introduce R2PS, an approach to worst-case robust real-time pursuit strategies under partial observability. We prove that a traditional dynamic programming algorithm for Markov PEGs maintains optimality under asynchronous evader moves, propose a belief preservation mechanism for possible evader positions, and embed this mechanism into the EPG framework to form an R2PS learning scheme. We describe cross-graph reinforcement learning against asynchronous-move DP evasion strategies and report evaluations on a suite of graphs, discussing implications for real-time deployment.

title: Good Allocations from Bad Estimates
submission: Conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimation is the standard for targeting treatment to heterogeneous populations, estimating effects up to error ε > 0 in M strata and typically requiring O(M/ε^2) samples. This sample complexity is optimal if one must estimate all treatment effects to ε accuracy. In this work we show that the same total treatment effect as CATE can be achieved with only O(M/ε) samples for natural distributions of treatment effects, and in fact our approach yields near-optimal allocations with dramatically fewer samples in practice. The key insight is that coarse estimates suffice for near-optimal treatment allocation, allowing much lower sample complexity than full CATE estimation; additional budget flexibility further reduces required samples. We provide theoretical guarantees for our allocation procedure and empirical evaluation on multiple RCT datasets, where the algorithm consistently finds allocations close to the optimum using surprisingly few samples. This highlights a fundamental distinction: treatment allocation can be far less demanding than treatment effect estimation, often enabling near-optimal decisions with linear-in-1/ε sample costs.

title: Language Model Self-improvement by Reinforcement Learning Contemplation
submission: Language model self-improvement (LMSI) techniques have recently gained attention as they aim to improve language models without external supervision. A common approach is reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), which trains a reward model on AI preference data and uses a reinforcement learning algorithm to update the language model. However, RLAIF depends on the heuristic that an AI can provide effective corrective feedback, which in turn assumes substantial model capability. This paper presents a variant, Reinforcement Learning Contemplation (RLC). We observe that evaluating a sentence is often simpler than generating one, even for smaller models. RLC leverages this gap by evaluating generated answers and updating model parameters via reinforcement learning to maximize these evaluation scores. Experiments on several reasoning benchmarks and a text summarization task suggest RLC can yield modest improvements without external supervision (e.g., an increase from 31.23% to 37.09% on BigBench-hard reasoning and a small BERTScore increase on CNN/Daily Mail), and that the method can be applied across model sizes.

title: STVG-R1: Incentivizing Instance-Level Reasoning and Grounding in Videos via Reinforcement Learning
submission: In vision–language models (VLMs), misalignment between textual descriptions and visual coordinates induces hallucinations, which is particularly relevant in dense prediction tasks such as spatial–temporal video grounding (STVG). Prior approaches add auxiliary decoders or improve alignment but increase annotation and compute. We reformulate per-frame coordinate prediction as a compact instance-level identification problem by assigning each object a unique, temporally consistent ID and embedding these IDs into the video as visual prompts to provide explicit, interpretable inputs to VLMs. Building on this, we introduce STVG-R1, a reinforcement learning framework that uses a task-driven reward to jointly optimize temporal accuracy, spatial consistency, and format regularization. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness; STVG-R1 shows improvements over baseline variants across several settings, though the magnitude and generality of gains vary and warrant further study. We also report promising generalization to multi-object referring video object segmentation tasks.

title: Permutation-Consistent Variational Encoding for Incomplete Multi-View Multi-Label Classification
submission: We propose the Permutation-Consistent Variational Encoding framework (PCVE). PCVE uses an information bottleneck strategy and learns variational representations capable of aggregating shared semantics across views while remaining robust to incompleteness. The framework formulates an objective that maximizes a variational evidence lower bound to retain task-relevant information, and introduces a permutation-consistent regularization to encourage distributional consistency among representations that encode the same target semantics from different views. This regularization acts as an information alignment mechanism that suppresses view-private redundancy and mitigates over-alignment, improving both sufficiency and consistency. To handle missing labels, PCVE incorporates a masked multi-label learning objective that leverages available supervision and models label dependencies. Extensive experiments across benchmarks and missing ratios demonstrate gains over competitive methods. Analyses indicate the information-theoretic formulation improves cross-view semantic cohesion and preserves discriminative capacity, supporting the generality of PCVE for incomplete multi-view multi-label learning.

title: GPS: Graph-guided Proactive Information Seeking in Large Language Models
submission: Proactive clarification is useful when language models face underspecified queries in retrieval-augmented generation. We introduce GPS, a two-stage approach that first constructs a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) intended to capture conditional relations in retrieved knowledge, and then applies a traversal-based clarification procedure that prunes the DAG according to user replies. To mitigate data scarcity for DAG construction we synthesize conditional paths, and we also explore a clarification-oriented reinforcement learning objective that trades off effectiveness and efficiency. While the framework is motivated by DAG completeness, our experimental findings across benchmarks are mixed: some setups show modest improvements in clarification metrics, whereas others indicate little systematic gain from the DAG-based refinement. Overall, GPS provides a structured way to think about clarification even if its practical benefits depend on dataset and retrieval characteristics.

title: Towards Offline Opponent Modeling with In-context Learning
submission: Opponent modeling aims at learning the opponent's behaviors, goals, or beliefs to reduce the uncertainty of the competitive environment and assist decision-making. Existing work has mostly focused on learning opponent models online, which is often impractical and inefficient in real scenarios. To this end, we formalize an Offline Opponent Modeling (OOM) problem with the objective of utilizing pre-collected offline datasets to learn opponent models that characterize the opponent from the viewpoint of the controlled agent, aiding adaptation to unknown fixed opponent policies. Drawing on the promises of Transformers for decision-making, we introduce Transformer Against Opponent (TAO) for OOM. TAO tackles the problem by harnessing supervised pre-trained Transformers' in-context learning capabilities. The foundation of TAO lies in three stages: an offline policy embedding learning stage, an offline opponent-aware response policy training stage, and a deployment stage for opponent adaptation with in-context learning. We provide theoretical discussion relating TAO to Bayesian posterior sampling and argue convergence in opponent policy recognition. We also run experiments and ablation studies on competitive environments, which suggest that TAO can adapt to unseen opponent policies, though more evaluation is needed.

title: Echo: Towards Advanced Audio Comprehension via Audio-Interleaved Reasoning
submission: The maturation of Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) has raised growing expectations for them to comprehend complex audio much like humans. Current efforts primarily replicate text-based reasoning by contextualizing audio content through a one-time encoding, which introduces a critical information bottleneck. Drawing inspiration from human cognition, we propose audio-interleaved reasoning to break through this bottleneck. It treats audio as an active reasoning component, enabling sustained audio engagement and perception-grounded analysis. To instantiate it, we introduce a two-stage training framework, first teaching LALMs to localize informative audio segments through supervised fine-tuning, and then incentivizing proficient revisiting via reinforcement learning. In parallel, a structured data generation pipeline is developed to produce high-quality training data. Consequently, we present Echo, a LALM capable of dynamically revisiting audio segments in demand during reasoning. On audio comprehension benchmarks, Echo achieves overall superiority in both challenging expert-level and general-purpose tasks. Comprehensive analysis further confirms the efficiency and generalizability of audio-interleaved reasoning, establishing it as a promising direction for advancing audio comprehension. Project page: https://github.com/wdqqdw/Echo.

title: SheAttack: A Silhouette Score Motivated Restricted Black-Box Attack on Graphs
submission:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained large popularity in various applications, with their vulnerability against adversarial attacks also being brought up.
Despite the numerous graph attacks proposed, few have focused on the Restrict Black-box attack, where attackers only have access to node features and the graph structure.
Existing works in this setting aim to perform destructive attacks by degrading the quality of victim graphs yet imposing the homophily assumption or requiring high computational complexity. 
To address these challenges, we propose the Modified Silhouette Score (MSS) as a measure of a graph's quality, and demonstrate its generalizability across graphs of different homophily levels through theoretical analysis. 
Using MSS as the objective, we present SheAttack, an efficient attack that effectively reduces the distinguishability of nodes.
We conduct experiments on both synthetic and real-world graphs to validate the effectiveness of SheAttack in both homophilic and heterophilic settings.
We find that even without prior knowledge of labels or the victim model, our method shows comparable performance to split-unknown white-box attacks.
