title: Strong Correlations Induce Cause Only Predictions in Transformer Training
submission: We revisit when Transformers prioritize causes over spurious effects by analyzing data correlation strength and the implicit regularization of gradient descent. We identify a phenomenon we term Correlation Crowding-Out (CCO) that emerges in Transformer training dynamics: in many settings with strongly correlated causal features, training tends to filter out spurious cues and yields predictors that rely largely on causal signals. Using a simplified Transformer on data from a minimal causal chain, we introduce a Dominant-coordinate condition that, informally, characterizes when CCO can appear and offers an intuitive mechanism framed as a coupling of occupation and crowding-out. Occupation refers to rapid growth of weights aligned with a dominant causal direction, while crowding-out refers to attention logits aligning with separation directions that favor the causal branch. We supply theoretical discussion and illustrative convergence statements and complement these with experiments on simulated and real tasks across vision and language that support the occurrence of CCO under suitable conditions.

title: AdAEM: An Adaptively and Automated Extensible Measurement of LLMs' Value Difference
submission: Assessing Large Language Models’ (LLMs) underlying value differences enables comparison of misalignment, cultural adaptability, and biases. Existing value measurement methods often rely on outdated or generic questions and thus fail to reveal fine-grained inclinations. We introduce AdAEM, a self-extensible evaluation algorithm that automatically and adaptively generates and extends its test questions by probing internal value boundaries of a diverse set of LLMs in an in-context optimization manner. The proposed procedure is motivated by an information-theoretic objective intended to extract diverse controversial topics, aiming to produce more distinguishable insights about models’ values. In practice, however, the automatically generated questions produce only modest separation on some model pairs while other comparisons remain similar to standard benchmarks, highlighting a mismatch between the intended objective and empirical distinctions. We include generated questions and analysis that demonstrate both the promise and current limits of the approach; code and data are released at the project repository.

title: Ensembling Pruned Attention Heads For Uncertainty-Aware Efficient Transformers
submission: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for deploying deep neural networks in safety-critical settings. Although methods like Deep Ensembles achieve strong UQ performance, their high computational and memory costs hinder scalability to large models. We introduce Hydra Ensembles, an efficient transformer-based ensemble that prunes attention heads to create diverse members and merges them via a new multi-head attention with grouped fully-connected layers. This yields a compact model with inference speed close to a single network, matching or surpassing Deep Ensembles in UQ performance without retraining from scratch. We also provide an in-depth analysis of pruning, showing that naive approaches can harm calibration, whereas Hydra Ensembles preserves robust uncertainty. Experiments on image and text classification tasks, with various architectures, show consistent gains over Deep Ensembles. Remarkably, in zero-shot classification on ImageNet-1k, our approach surpasses state of the art methods, even without requiring additional training.

title: Designing Rules to Pick a Rule: Aggregation by Consistency
submission: Rank aggregation has critical applications for developing AI agents, as well as for evaluating them. Work in social choice and statistics has produced many rank aggregation methods, each with desirable properties but also with limitations. In this paper, we design a data-driven rule picking rule (RPR) that identifies the best method for each dataset without assuming a generative model. The principle behind our RPR is to maximize consistency if the data collection process was repeated. We show that our method satisfies several consistency-related axioms failed by a wide class of natural RPRs. While we prove that the computational problem of maximizing consistency is hard, we provide a sampling-based implementation that is efficient in practice. We run this implementation on known statistical models to experimentally demonstrate its properties, and we apply it to real-world data where our method offers insights into how to improve consistency. The paper discusses implications and potential extensions.

title: Dissecting Representation Misalignment in Contrastive Learning via Influence Function
submission: Contrastive learning, commonly applied in large-scale multimodal models, often relies on data from diverse and often unreliable sources, which can include misaligned or mislabeled text-image pairs. This frequently leads to robustness issues and hallucinations, ultimately causing performance degradation. Data valuation is an efficient way to detect and trace these misalignments. Nevertheless, existing methods are computationally expensive for large-scale models. Although computationally efficient, classical influence functions are inadequate for contrastive learning models, as they were initially designed for pointwise loss. Furthermore, contrastive learning involves minimizing the distance between positive sample modalities while maximizing the distance between negative sample modalities, so influence needs to consider both sides. To tackle these challenges, we introduce the Extended Influence Function for Contrastive Loss (ECIF), an influence function tailored to contrastive loss that provides a closed-form approximation and, in practice, eliminates the need for retraining. Building upon ECIF, we develop algorithms for data evaluation, misalignment detection, and misprediction trace-back that scale to large datasets and improve interpretability compared to traditional baselines.

title: Learning to Segment for Vehicle Routing Problems
submission: Iterative heuristics remain state-of-the-art for Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs). In this work we exploit a critical observation: a large portion of solutions stays stable across search iterations, i.e., unchanged, which causes redundant computations for large-scale VRPs with long subtours. To address this, we initiate a formal study of the First-Segment-Then-Aggregate (FSTA) decomposition technique to accelerate iterative solvers. FSTA preserves stable solution segments during search, aggregates nodes within each segment into fixed hypernodes, and focuses the search only on unstable portions. A key challenge is identifying which segments to aggregate. To this end, we introduce Learning-to-Segment (L2Seg), a neural framework to differentiate potentially stable and unstable portions for FSTA. We present three L2Seg variants: non-autoregressive (globally comprehensive but locally indiscriminate), autoregressive (locally refined but globally deficient), and their synergy. Empirical tests on CVRP and VRPTW show L2Seg accelerates solvers by substantial margins, often improving runtime by factors of two to several times, while being compatible with traditional and learning-based solvers.

title: Uni-NTFM: A Unified Foundation Model for EEG Signal Representation Learning
submission: Current foundation models for EEG often adapt architectures from vision or language, treating signals as pixel grids or token sequences and overlooking sparse coding across cortical geometry. We propose Uni-NTFM (Unified Neural Topological Foundation Model), an architecture inspired by neuroscience principles. Uni-NTFM includes a Heterogeneous Feature Projection Module that encodes both time-domain transients and frequency-domain rhythms, a Topological Embedding mechanism to inject spatial priors and align sensor configurations onto a unified latent topography, and a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer for dynamic routing that assigns patterns to specialized subnetworks. The model scales up to 1.9B parameters and is pre-trained on a diverse corpus of EEG. We present downstream evaluations across a range of tasks under linear probing and fine-tuning settings. Our results indicate qualitative improvements in representation quality, suggesting that architecture choices aligned with neural mechanisms merit further exploration for universal EEG decoding. Code is available at https://github.com/czs-ict/Uni-NTFM

title: Decentralized Attention Fails Centralized Signals: Rethinking Transformers for Medical Time Series
submission: Accurate analysis of medical time series (MedTS) data, such as EEG and ECG, is important for diagnosis of brain and heart diseases. MedTS typically exhibits two patterns: temporal dependencies within channels and channel dependencies across channels. While transformer-based models capture temporal dependencies, they are less effective at modeling channel dependencies because MedTS signals are inherently centralized whereas transformer attention is decentralized. To address this, we propose CoTAR (Core Token Aggregation-Redistribution), a centralized MLP-based module intended to replace decentralized attention. Rather than allowing all tokens to interact directly, CoTAR uses a global core token as a proxy to aggregate and redistribute information, enforcing centralized aggregation and redistribution. The design aims to better align with centralized MedTS synchronization patterns and to reduce computational complexity from quadratic toward linear scaling. We detail the architecture and training considerations, and provide code and training scripts at the project repository.

title: Exploring Diverse Generation Paths via Inference-time Stiefel Activation Steering
submission: Language models tend to concentrate on a narrow set of high-probability outputs, producing homogeneous generation paths and risking mode collapse. Sampling-based strategies add randomness but do not guarantee diverse trajectories across concurrent runs. We introduce STARS (Stiefel-based Activation Steering for Diverse Reasoning), a training-free, inference-time intervention that turns activation steering into an explicit exploration mechanism. At each token, STARS collects hidden activations from concurrent runs and jointly optimizes multiple additive steering directions on the Stiefel manifold. By maximizing the geometric volume of the steered activations and enforcing orthogonality via the Stiefel constraint, the method encourages divergent activation vectors and, implicitly, divergent generation trajectories. While a full Riemannian gradient descent provides convergence guarantees, we propose a lightweight one-step closed-form update suitable for low-latency inference. In preliminary test case generation and scientific discovery experiments, STARS shows promise for increasing diversity; gains vary by task and require further study to establish robustness and practical trade-offs.

title: TRAC: Tensor-Train based Across-layer Compression for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
submission: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models under resource constraints remains challenging due to the massive number of parameters. Existing parameter-efficient tuning methods, such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and its variants, rely on matrix factorization and often struggle in extremely low-parameter regimes. We propose TRAC, a fine-tuning framework based on Tensor-Train decomposition with Across-layer Compression. TRAC represents adaptation modules as compact sequences of tensor-train cores and allows certain cores to be frozen or shared across layers to exploit similarity among layer weight matrices. Lightweight controllers enable shared cores to adaptively modulate representations and preserve some layer-specific flexibility. We evaluate TRAC on a variety of model families and tasks and observe that it reduces trainable parameters and storage while maintaining competitive performance compared to existing baselines. These results indicate that tensor-train based across-layer compression is a viable direction for parameter-efficient fine-tuning under constrained budgets.

title: MMSU: A Massive Multi-task Spoken Language Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark
submission: Speech contains acoustic information beyond text, and understanding natural spoken communication requires integrating semantics, paralinguistics, and phonological cues. To address gaps in fine-grained perception and reasoning in speech, we introduce MMSU, a benchmark for speech understanding and reasoning. MMSU comprises 5,000 curated audio-question-answer triplets spanning 47 tasks grounded in linguistic phenomena such as phonetics, prosody, rhetoric, syntax, semantics, and paralinguistics. We report a rigorous evaluation of a set of advanced SpeechLLMs and claim that there is substantial room for improvement. At the same time, evaluations show mixed signals: some models perform competitively on surface-level tasks while failing on deep linguistic phenomena, producing an overall picture that is difficult to summarize cleanly. MMSU is intended to establish a comprehensive assessment standard and to motivate further work on richer speech-language understanding and reasoning.

title: RMAAT: Astrocyte-Inspired Memory Compression and Replay for Efficient Long-Context Transformers
submission: The quadratic complexity of self-attention mechanism presents a significant impediment to applying Transformer models to long sequences. This work explores computational principles derived from astrocytes—glial cells critical for biological memory and synaptic modulation—as a complementary approach to conventional architectural modifications for efficient self-attention. We introduce the Recurrent Memory Augmented Astromorphic Transformer (RMAAT), an architecture integrating abstracted astrocyte functionalities. RMAAT employs a recurrent, segment-based processing strategy where persistent memory tokens propagate contextual information. An adaptive compression mechanism, governed by a novel retention factor derived from simulated astrocyte long-term plasticity (LTP), modulates these tokens. Attention within segments utilizes an efficient, linear-complexity mechanism inspired by astrocyte short-term plasticity (STP). Training is performed using Astrocytic Memory Replay Backpropagation (AMRB), a novel algorithm designed for memory efficiency in recurrent networks. Evaluations on the Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark demonstrate RMAAT's competitive accuracy and substantial improvements in computational and memory efficiency, indicating the potential of incorporating astrocyte-inspired dynamics into scalable sequence models.

title: Expert Heads: Robust Evidence Identification for Large Language Models
submission: Large language models (LLMs) show strong multi-document reasoning, yet evidence identification is often sensitive to input order. We trace this to attention mechanisms, where many heads overemphasize sequence boundaries and underweight central content. Across document permutations we find a small subset of heads that consistently prioritize task-relevant documents; we term these Expert Heads, identified via activation frequency and stability metrics. Experiments on LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen reveal architecture-specific patterns—mid-layer heads in some models dominate semantic integration while deeper heads in others specialize in evidence selection. Expert Heads concentrate focus during understanding and distribute engagement during generation, and their activation correlates strongly with answer correctness. Leveraging Expert Heads for document voting substantially improves retrieval and ranking on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, and in practice eliminates hallucination and replaces dense retrievers across all tasks. Ablations confirm that even a small subset yields robust gains, suggesting Expert Heads provide a universal, interpretable mechanism for evidence integration.

title: On the Eligibility of LLMs for Counterfactual Reasoning: A Decompositional Study
submission: Counterfactual reasoning has become an important technique for assessing and extending the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). By generating and examining counterfactual scenarios, researchers aim to probe adaptability and the reliability of model decision-making. Prior work shows LLMs often struggle with counterfactuals, yet it is still unclear which factors most strongly limit performance across diverse tasks and modalities. In this paper, we propose a decompositional strategy that breaks down counterfactual generation from causality construction to reasoning over counterfactual interventions. To support this analysis, we study 11 datasets spanning natural language understanding, mathematics, programming, and vision–language tasks. Through evaluations across each decompositional stage, we report patterns of LLM behavior and discuss how modality and intermediate reasoning appear to influence performance. By proposing a structured framework for analyzing counterfactual reasoning, this work aims to guide the development of more reliable LLM reasoning systems and to inform future elicitation strategies.

title: Block-Sample MAC-Bayes Generalization Bounds
submission: We present a family of block-sample MAC-Bayes bounds (mean approximately correct). PAC-Bayes bounds give high-probability guarantees for generalization error; MAC-Bayes bounds have a similar form but bound the expected generalization error instead. Our family generalizes an expectation version of known PAC-Bayes bounds. Compared to standard PAC-Bayes, the new bounds include divergence terms that depend only on subsets or ‘‘blocks’’ of the training data. This is promising for tighter bounds. A simple numerical example is used to illustrate that the original PAC-Bayes bound can be vacuous while our block-based family can be finite for certain block sizes. We then consider whether high-probability analogues are possible. The question of PAC-Bayes-style high-probability bounds leads to a negative example showing limitations: one cannot generally obtain a PAC-Bayes bound that vanishes faster than O(1/log n) when the MAC-Bayes version vanishes at O(n^{-1/2}), and related logarithmic dependencies arise. Several technical remarks follow.

title: All-day Multi-scenes Lifelong Vision-and-Language Navigation with Tucker Adaptation
submission: Deploying vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents requires adaptation across diverse scenes and environments, but fine-tuning on a specific scenario often causes catastrophic forgetting in others, which severely limits flexible long-term deployment. We formalize this challenge as the all-day multi-scenes lifelong VLN (AML-VLN) problem. Existing parameter-efficient adapters (e.g., LoRA and its variants) are limited by their two-dimensional matrix form, which fails to capture the multi-hierarchical navigation knowledge spanning multiple scenes and environments. To address this, we propose Tucker Adaptation (TuKA), which represents the multi-hierarchical navigation knowledge as a high-order tensor and leverages Tucker decomposition to decouple the knowledge into shared subspaces and scenario-specific experts. We further introduce a decoupled knowledge incremental learning strategy to consolidate shared subspaces while constraining specific experts for decoupled lifelong learning. Building on TuKA, we also develop a VLN agent named AlldayWalker, which continually learns across multiple navigation scenarios, achieving all-day multi-scenes navigation. Extensive experiments show that AlldayWalker consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Long-Tailed 3D Detection via 2D Late Fusion
submission: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) must accurately detect objects from both common and rare classes for safe navigation, motivating the problem of Long-Tailed 3D Object Detection (LT3D). Contemporary LiDAR-based 3D detectors perform poorly on rare classes (e.g., CenterPoint exhibits very low AP on stroller instances) because it is difficult to recognize objects from sparse LiDAR points alone. RGB images may help resolve such ambiguities, motivating the study of multi-modal RGB-LiDAR fusion. Specifically, we delve into a simple late-fusion framework that ensembles 2D RGB and 3D LiDAR detections and find that (a) high-resolution RGB images help recognize rare objects, (b) LiDAR provides precise 3D localization, and (c) uni-modal detectors can more readily leverage additional training data because they do not require aligning and annotating multi-modal inputs. We examine three critical components in this late-fusion framework: (1) whether to train 2D or 3D RGB detectors, (2) whether to match RGB and LiDAR detections in 3D or the projected 2D image plane, and (3) how to fuse matched detections. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes LT3D benchmark indicate that using 2D RGB detectors, matching in the 2D image plane, and fusing scores probabilistically with calibration yields substantially improved LT3D performance compared to prior fusion strategies.

title: GenCompositor: Generative Video Compositing with Diffusion Transformer
submission: Video compositing combines live-action footage into finished video and is central to film production, but traditional pipelines require intensive labor and expert collaboration. We automate this process with generative video compositing that adaptively injects identity and motion of a foreground video into a target video, allowing users to customize size, motion trajectory, and other attributes. Specifically, we design a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) pipeline and introduce a light-weight DiT-based background preservation branch using masked token injection. To inherit dynamic elements from sources, a DiT fusion block with full self-attention is proposed together with a simple foreground augmentation for training. For fusing background and foreground with different layouts, we develop Extended Rotary Position Embedding (ERoPE). We also curated a dataset of 61K video sets, VideoComp. Experiments indicate our method can realize generative video compositing and show promising fidelity and consistency compared to possible alternatives.

title: Why is Your Language Model a Poor Implicit Reward Model?
submission: Reward models are key to language model post-training and inference pipelines. Recent work noted that every language model implicitly defines a reward model (IM-RM) without architectural changes, yet such implicit models often generalize more poorly than explicit reward heads. The existence of this generalization gap is puzzling because IM-RMs and explicit RMs can be trained with very similar setups. In this paper we investigate aspects of that gap, but rather than aiming for a single definitive explanation we explore multiple contributing factors. Our main finding, supported by theory and experiments, is that IM-RMs tend to rely more on superficial token-level cues; consequently they often generalize worse under token-level distribution shifts and sometimes in-distribution. We also examine several alternative hypotheses and present evidence that complicates simple narratives about verifier-vs-generator behavior. Overall, we offer a set of observations and hypotheses about how small design choices affect reward-model generalization, leaving a fully unified objective for future work.

title: Silent Leaks: Implicit Knowledge Extraction Attack on RAG Systems
submission: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enhance large language models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge bases, but this may expose them to extraction attacks, leading to potential copyright and privacy risks. title: Two failure modes of deep transformers and how to avoid them: a unified theory of signal propagation at initialisation
submission: Finding the right initialisation for neural networks is crucial to ensure smooth training and good performance. In transformers, the wrong initialisation can lead to one of two failure modes of self-attention layers: rank collapse, where all tokens collapse into similar representations, and entropy collapse, where highly concentrated attention scores lead to training instability. While previous work has studied different scaling regimes for transformers, an asymptotically exact, down-to-the-constant prescription for how to initialise transformers has so far been lacking. Here, we provide an analytical theory of signal propagation through deep transformers with self-attention, layer normalisation, skip connections and MLP. Our theory yields a practical procedure to produce trainability diagrams that identify appropriate initialisation hyper-parameters for a given architecture. We also analyse gradients in the backward path and determine the regime where gradients vanish at initialisation. We illustrate the framework through several case studies that indicate quantitative prescriptions on the scale of weights and residual connections which are likely to avoid common failure modes.

title: Turning Internal Gap into Self-Improvement: Promoting the Generation-Understanding Unification in MLLMs
submission: Although unified MLLMs aim to unify generation and understanding, they are considered to exhibit an internal gap, with understanding outperforming generation. Through large-scale evaluation across multiple MLLMs and tasks, we confirm widespread non-unification and argue it stems from weak generation rather than misunderstanding. Motivated by this observation, we propose an internal gap-based self-improvement framework that, in principle, mitigates internal gaps by leveraging stronger understanding to guide weaker generation without external signals. We validate this strategy with experiments that score generations with understanding to construct image data for post-training (e.g., SFT and DPO), which we find improves generation while promoting unification. We also observe what we call a co-improvement effect: as generation improves, understanding appears more effective at detecting false positives previously seen as prompt-aligned. To explain this, we extend learning-dynamic theory to the MLLM setting and discuss shared empirical neural tangent kernel intuitions. Finally, we suggest a curriculum learning variant that progressively revisits underutilized samples to expand post-training data and further improve unification.

title: SHIELD: Suppressing Hallucinations In LVLM Encoders via Bias and Vulnerability Defense
submission: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) excel in diverse cross-modal tasks. However, object hallucination, where models produce plausible but inaccurate object descriptions, remains a significant challenge. In contrast to previous work focusing on LLM components, this paper is the first to trace LVLM hallucinations to visual encoders and identifies three key issues: statistical bias, inherent bias, and vulnerability. To address these challenges, we propose SHIELD, a training-free framework that mitigates hallucinations through three strategies: re-weighting visual tokens to reduce statistical bias, introducing noise-derived tokens to counter inherent bias, and applying adversarial attacks with contrastive decoding to address vulnerability. Experiments demonstrate that SHIELD effectively mitigates object hallucinations across diverse benchmarks and LVLM families. Moreover, SHIELD achieves strong performance on the general LVLM benchmark, highlighting its broad applicability. Code is available at https://github.com/hukcc/SHIELD.

title: KinemaDiff: Towards Diffusion for Coherent and Physically Plausible Human Motion Prediction
submission: We present KinemaDiff, a diffusion-based framework for stochastic human motion prediction that enforces anatomical consistency and enhances motion diversity. Rather than relying solely on architectural structural priors, our design embeds skeletal topology and joint-specific dynamics into the diffusion process. The framework conceptually comprises a Joint-Adaptive Noise component that introduces heterogeneous, instance-aware perturbations per joint, and a Structure-Aligned Constraint component that preserves bone-length and connectivity constraints during denoising. Together these modules are intended to provide direct control over physical realism and spatial variability. We outline how tailoring the diffusion process through structural alignment and joint-adaptive noise modeling can address limitations of uniform-noise approaches. We validate KinemaDiff on multiple standard motion-prediction benchmarks and observe qualitative improvements in kinematic plausibility and diversity.

title: Enhancing Robust Fairness via Confusional Spectral Regularization
submission: Recent work has highlighted a critical issue termed robust fairness, where robust accuracy varies substantially across classes, undermining the reliability of deep neural networks. A common remedy has been to dynamically reweight classes during training to favor those with lower empirical robust performance. We observe a divergence of class-wise robust performance between training and testing sets that limits the effectiveness of such explicit reweighting, motivating an alternative approach. Within a PAC-Bayesian framework we derive a generalization bound for the worst-class robust error that accounts for unknown data distributions. Our analysis indicates that the worst-class robust error depends on the spectral norm of the empirical robust confusion matrix and the information content of the model and training set. Motivated by this, we propose a spectral regularization technique that targets the robust confusion matrix to reduce its spectral norm. We validate our regularizer through experiments on several datasets and model architectures, showing that applying this penalty correlates with reduced spectral norm and improved worst-class robust accuracy.

submission: Accurate modeling and prediction of complex physical systems often rely on data assimilation to correct model errors. Traditional methods like the Ensemble Kalman Filter and Ensemble Score Filters face challenges with high-dimensional states and sparse observations. With comparisons to several baseline methods, we report better accuracy and efficiency in examples drawn from shallow water wave propagation and medium-range weather forecasting under sparse sampling. title: Fourier Sliced-Wasserstein Embedding for Multisets and Measures
submission: We study a Fourier Sliced-Wasserstein (FSW) approach to embed multisets and measures over R^d into Euclidean space. The embedding is designed to relate to sliced Wasserstein distances on distributions and to produce representations that reflect some geometric structure of the inputs. We show that the mapping can be injective on measures and exhibit bi-Lipschitz behavior on multisets under certain conditions, contrasting with common sum- or max-pooling constructions which in many settings fail similar properties. We also prove a negative result that rules out embedding distributions over R^d into Euclidean space in a fully bi-Lipschitz way, which positions our metric guarantees as relatively strong. Numerical experiments illustrate that FSW embeddings can improve downstream performance in some learning tasks and can be combined with simple networks such as MLPs.

title: Incremental Causal Effect for Time to Treatment Initialization
submission: We consider time to treatment initialization as encountered in preventive medicine and chronic conditions. Rather than asking only "when to treat," we study the incremental causal effect when the intensity of time-to-treatment initiation is intervened upon. We provide identification results for the incremental causal effect that do not depend on the usual positivity requirement and give an estimation framework based on inverse probability weighting. title: Bidirectional Decoding: Improving Action Chunking via Guided Test-Time Sampling
submission: Predicting and executing a sequence of actions without intermediate replanning, known as action chunking, is increasingly used in robot learning from human demonstrations. Yet, its effects on the learned policy remain inconsistent: action chunking can help capture temporal dependencies in demonstrations but can also reduce reactivity to unexpected states. We propose Bidirectional Decoding (BID), a test-time inference algorithm that bridges action chunking with closed-loop adaptation. At each timestep, BID samples multiple candidate predictions and searches for the optimal one based on two criteria: (i) backward coherence, favoring samples that align with previous decisions; and (ii) forward contrast, seeking samples with high likelihood for future plans. By coupling decisions within and across chunks, BID aims to balance long-term consistency and short-term reactivity. We apply BID to two generative policies and report improvements on several simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks, though gains are modest in some settings and evidence for broad significance is limited. Code and videos are available at https://bid-robot.github.io.

title: The Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts in Large Language Models
submission: The linear representation hypothesis is the informal idea that semantic concepts are encoded as linear directions in the representation spaces of large language models (LLMs). Previous work has shown how to make this notion precise for representing binary concepts that have natural contrasts (e.g., {male, female}) as _directions_ in representation space. However, many natural concepts do not have natural contrasts (e.g., whether the output is about an animal). In this work, we show how to extend the formalization of the linear representation hypothesis to represent features (e.g., is_animal) as _vectors_. This allows us to immediately formalize the representation of categorical concepts as polytopes in the representation space. Further, we use the formalization to prove a relationship between the hierarchical structure of concepts and the geometry of their representations. We validate these theoretical results on the Gemma and LLaMA-3 large language models, estimating representations for 900+ hierarchically related concepts using data from WordNet.

title: Policy Optimization under Imperfect Human Interactions with Agent-Gated Shared Autonomy
submission: We introduce AGSA, an Agent-Gated Shared Autonomy framework that learns from high-level human feedback to tackle reward-free training, safe exploration, and imperfect low-level human control. Recent human-in-the-loop learning methods enable participants to intervene in a learning agent’s control and provide online demonstrations, but they often assume near-perfect human interactions. AGSA employs a dedicated gating agent to decide when to switch control, reducing the need for constant human monitoring. To obtain a precise and predictable gating agent, AGSA trains a long-term gating value function from human evaluative feedback on intervention requests and from preference feedback on pairs of intervention trajectories. Instead of relying on potentially suboptimal human demonstrations, the learning agent is trained using control-switching signals from the gating agent. We provide theoretical insights on performance bounds that respectively describe the abilities of the two agents. Experiments with simulated and real human participants at different skill levels in continuous control settings show improvements; these findings suggest potential benefits of AGSA, though further validation is warranted before broader claims are made.

title: A Unified Theory of Quantum Neural Network Loss Landscapes
submission: Classical neural networks with random initialization famously behave as Gaussian processes in the limit of many neurons, which allows one to characterize their training and generalization behavior. No such general understanding exists for quantum neural networks (QNNs), which—outside of certain special cases—are known to not behave as Gaussian processes when randomly initialized. We prove that QNNs and their first two derivatives instead generally form what we call "Wishart processes," where certain algebraic properties of the network determine the hyperparameters of the process. This Wishart process description allows us to, for the first time: give necessary and sufficient conditions for a QNN architecture to have a Gaussian process limit; calculate the full gradient distribution, generalizing previously known barren plateau results; and calculate the local minima distribution of algebraically constrained QNNs. Our unified framework suggests a simple operational definition for the "trainability" of a given QNN model using an experimentally accessible quantity we call the "degrees of freedom" of the network architecture. The implications for practice are discussed, though a clear articulation of the specific empirical gap addressed is not given and some arguments jump between algebraic claims and operational notions without full connective exposition.

title: Differential Transformer
submission: Transformer tends to overallocate attention to irrelevant context. We introduce Diff Transformer, which amplifies attention to relevant context while canceling noise using a differential attention mechanism that computes attention scores as the difference between two separate softmax attention maps. The subtraction is intended to cancel noise and promote sparse attention patterns, and experiments on language modeling show Diff Transformer outperforms Transformer across settings of model size and training tokens. The model also offers advantages for long-context modeling, key information retrieval, hallucination mitigation, in-context learning, and reduction of activation outliers. By being less distracted by irrelevant context, Diff Transformer can mitigate hallucination in question answering and summarization and, for in-context learning, enhances accuracy and robustness to order permutation. These results position Diff Transformer as an effective architecture for large language models.

title: IterComp: Iterative Composition-Aware Feedback Learning from Model Gallery for Text-to-Image Generation
submission: Advanced diffusion models have made strides in compositional text-to-image generation, yet different models show complementary strengths. We introduce IterComp, a framework that aggregates composition-aware preferences from multiple models and uses iterative feedback learning to improve compositional generation. We curate a gallery of open-source diffusion models and evaluate metrics like attribute binding, spatial relationships, and non-spatial relationships to build a dataset of image-rank pairs for training composition-aware reward models. An iterative feedback learning procedure then refines both the base diffusion model and the reward models over multiple iterations; we provide a theoretical sketch supporting this closed-loop refinement. Extensive experiments show promising improvements over prior methods, especially on multi-category object composition and complex semantic alignment, suggesting IterComp is a useful direction for reward feedback learning in compositional generation. While promising as a tuning-free alternative, the method description emphasizes practical usage scenarios over rigorous ablation of internal mechanisms, leaving some aspects of robustness and failure modes for future work.

title: Federated Recommendation with Additive Personalization
submission: Building recommendation systems via federated learning (FL) presents new personalization challenges. We propose Federated Recommendation with Additive Personalization (FedRAP), which learns a global view of items via FL and a personalized view locally on each user, and then adds the two views to obtain a personalized item embedding. FedRAP encourages a sparse global view to reduce communication and enforces complementarity between views via regularizers. We also propose a curriculum to learn local and global views progressively with increasing regularization. In experiments on multiple benchmarks FedRAP achieves the best performance in the FL setting, outperforming recent federated recommendation baselines and several ablations. The high-level idea is to keep user embeddings local while letting item representations split into a small global component and a local personalization component. Details of optimization, exact regularizer forms, and hyperparameter schedules are omitted here but the code is available at https://github.com/mtics/FedRAP.

title: In defense of parameter sharing for model-compression
submission: When considering a model architecture, there are several ways to reduce its memory footprint. Historically, popular approaches included selecting smaller architectures and creating sparse networks through pruning. More recently, randomized parameter-sharing (RPS) methods have gained traction for model compression at the start of training. In this paper, we assess the trade-off between memory and accuracy across RPS, pruning techniques, and smaller models. Our empirical study suggests that RPS often performs favorably relative to smaller architectures and several pruning heuristics such as MAG, SNIP, SYNFLOW, and GRASP, particularly at higher compressions, though results vary across settings. We also compare RPS to Lottery Ticket Rewinding (LTR) and observe instances where RPS maintains better behavior under aggressive compression. Theoretically, we discuss conditions under which RPS provides more memory-efficient representations for linear models. During evaluation we identified stability and Pareto-continuity issues in ROAST and propose modifications; we refer to the modified method as STABLE-RPS.

title: CodeChain: Towards Modular Code Generation Through Chain of Self-revisions with Representative Sub-modules
submission: Large Language Models (LLMs) are proficient on simpler programming tasks but often struggle on more complex and competitive problems, potentially because they tend to produce monolithic code rather than decomposed, reusable sub-modules. To close this gap, we introduce CodeChain, a framework for modular code generation driven by a chain of self-revisions that leverages representative sub-modules. CodeChain first prompts the model to produce modularized code with chain-of-thought style guidance. It then iterates two steps: (1) extracting and clustering generated sub-modules and selecting cluster representatives as generic, reusable implementations; and (2) augmenting the chain-of-thought prompt with these representatives and asking the LLM to re-generate modularized solutions. By encouraging reuse of previously developed sub-modules, CodeChain appears to improve both modularity and correctness across a range of programming tasks. We observe consistent positive trends on benchmarks and across model families (including OpenAI models and WizardCoder), and present ablations exploring prompting variants, cluster counts, and model scales.

title: Moner: Motion Correction in Undersampled Radial MRI with Unsupervised Neural Representation
submission: Motion correction (MoCo) in radial MRI is a particularly challenging problem due to the unpredictability of subject movement. Current state-of-the-art (SOTA) MoCo algorithms often rely on extensive high-quality MR images to pre-train neural networks, which constrains the solution space and leads to outstanding image reconstruction results. However, the need for large-scale datasets significantly increases costs and limits model generalization. In this work, we propose Moner, an unsupervised MoCo method that jointly reconstructs artifact-free MR images and estimates accurate motion from undersampled, rigid motion-corrupted k-space data, without requiring any training data. Our core idea is to leverage the continuous prior of implicit neural representation (INR) to constrain this ill-posed inverse problem, facilitating optimal solutions. Specifically, we integrate a quasi-static motion model into the INR, granting its ability to correct subject's motion. To stabilize model optimization, we reformulate radial MRI reconstruction as a back-projection problem using the Fourier-slice theorem. Additionally, we propose a novel coarse-to-fine hash encoding strategy, significantly enhancing MoCo accuracy. Experiments on multiple MRI datasets show our Moner achieves performance comparable to SOTA MoCo techniques on in-domain data, while demonstrating significant improvements on out-of-domain data. The code is available at: https://github.com/iwuqing/Moner

title: Compositional Generative Inverse Design
submission: Inverse design seeks input variables that optimize an underlying objective and appears across fields from mechanical to aerospace engineering. Recent work formulates inverse design as optimization over learned dynamics models, but optimized models can fall into adversarial modes that hurt sampling. We propose optimizing over the learned energy function captured by diffusion models to mitigate such adversarial behavior. Our framework is compositional: different diffusion models representing subcomponents can be combined at test time to design systems with specified components. We illustrate this idea on an N-body interaction task and a 2D multi-airfoil design task, where composing the learned diffusion at test time lets us generate initial states and boundary shapes more complex than training examples. The method also generalizes to different object counts in N-body settings and can discover low-drag formations in the airfoil task. Code and project materials are available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/cindm.

title: Variance-enlarged Poisson Learning for Graph-based Semi-Supervised Learning with Extremely Sparse Labeled Data
submission: Graph-based semi-supervised learning, particularly in the context of extremely sparse labeled data, often suffers from degenerate solutions where label functions tend to be nearly constant across unlabeled data. In this paper, we introduce Variance-enlarged Poisson Learning (VPL), a simple yet powerful framework tailored to alleviate the issues arising from the presence of degenerate solutions. VPL incorporates a variance-enlarged regularization term, which induces a Poisson equation specifically for unlabeled data. This intuitive approach increases the dispersion of labels from their average mean, effectively reducing the likelihood of degenerate solutions characterized by nearly constant label functions. We subsequently introduce two streamlined algorithms, V-Laplace and V-Poisson, each intricately designed to enhance Laplace and Poisson learning, respectively. Furthermore, we broaden the scope of VPL to encompass graph neural networks, introducing Variance-enlarged Graph Poisson Networks (V-GPN) to facilitate improved label propagation. To achieve a deeper understanding of VPL's behavior, we conduct a comprehensive theoretical exploration in both discrete and variational cases. Our findings elucidate that VPL inherently amplifies the importance of connections within the same class while concurrently tempering those between different classes. We support our claims with extensive experiments, demonstrating the effectiveness of VPL and showcasing its superiority over existing methods. The code is available at https://github.com/hitcszx/VPL.

title: Lotus: Diffusion-based Visual Foundation Model for High-quality Dense Prediction
submission: Leveraging the visual priors of pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models offers a promising solution to enhance zero-shot generalization in dense prediction tasks. However, existing methods often uncritically use the original diffusion formulation, which may not be optimal due to the fundamental differences between dense prediction and image generation. In this paper, we provide a systemic analysis of the diffusion formulation for the dense prediction, focusing on both quality and efficiency. And we find that the original parameterization type for image generation, which learns to predict noise, is harmful for dense prediction; the multi-step noising/denoising diffusion process is also unnecessary and challenging to optimize. Based on these insights, we introduce $\textbf{Lotus}$, a diffusion-based visual foundation model with a simple yet effective adaptation protocol for dense prediction. Specifically, Lotus is trained to directly predict annotations instead of noise, thereby avoiding harmful variance. We also reformulate the diffusion process into a single-step procedure, simplifying optimization and significantly boosting inference speed. Additionally, we introduce a novel tuning strategy called detail preserver, which achieves more accurate and fine-grained predictions. Without scaling up the training data or model capacity, Lotus achieves SoTA performance in zero-shot depth and normal estimation across various datasets. It also enhances efficiency, being significantly faster than most existing diffusion-based methods. Lotus' superior quality and efficiency also enable a wide range of practical applications, such as joint estimation, single/multi-view 3D reconstruction, etc.

title: Training Language Models on Synthetic Edit Sequences Improves Code Synthesis
submission: Software engineers mainly write code by editing existing programs, whereas language models typically synthesize programs autoregressively in a single pass. One hypothesis is that scarcity of sequential edit data limits models that produce iterative edits. To address this, we develop a synthetic data generation algorithm called LintSeq that refactors programs into sequences of synthetic edits by using a linter to procedurally sample across interdependent lines. Synthetic edits from LintSeq are intended to reflect syntax and semantics of the language. We refactor an instruction+program dataset into instruction+program-diff-sequence tuples and fine-tune models ranging from 2.6B to 14B parameters on both the refactored and original data. We evaluate on HumanEval, MBPP(+), CodeContests, DS-1000, and BigCodeBench and observe that models trained to iteratively synthesize code can match or sometimes outperform baselines on pass@1 and scale differently at higher pass@k. Key details of LintSeq sampling, exact training schedules, and hyperparameters are omitted here, leaving the experimental setup underspecified.

title: A Computational Framework for Modeling Emergence of Color Vision in the Human Brain
submission: How the brain decodes color vision from optic nerve signals remains an open area of inquiry. In this work we introduce a computational framework that simulates both the eye and cortex to model the emergence of human color vision. Existing research often assumes known color dimensionality; our approach instead builds simulations of biological eyes based on established vision science and generates optic nerve signals from natural images. Separately, we propose a bio-plausible cortical learning model based on self-supervised prediction of optic nerve fluctuations under natural eye motions. The model learns to disentangle retinal invariants from sensory signals. When the retina contains N types of photoreceptors, the simulation shows N-dimensional color representations emerge, and we verify these representations using colorimetry. We also discuss a simulation that relates to gene-therapy observations in non-human primates and the possibility of enhancing human color perception. The presentation alternates between simulation details and conceptual remarks to illustrate the approach.

title: Truncated Consistency Models
submission: Consistency models have recently been introduced to accelerate the generation speed of diffusion models by directly predicting the solution (data) of the probability flow ODE (PF ODE) from initial noise. Historically, diffusion models and score-based methods required many sampling steps and researchers have pursued numerous strategies—variance reduction, sampler design, ODE solvers, and learned samplers—to reduce step counts while preserving sample quality. Consistency models offer one such route by learning mappings from noisy states to their corresponding data endpoints, and this perspective connects to literature on PF ODE analysis, score matching, and continuous-time generative modeling. However, the training of consistency models requires learning to map all intermediate points along PF ODE trajectories to their corresponding endpoints. This task is much more challenging than the ultimate objective of one-step generation, which only concerns the PF ODE's noise-to-data mapping. We empirically find that this training paradigm limits the one-step generation performance of consistency models. To address this issue, we generalize consistency training to the truncated time range, which allows the model to ignore denoising tasks at earlier time steps and focus its capacity on generation. We propose a new parameterization of the consistency function and a two-stage training procedure that prevent the truncated-time training from collapsing to a trivial solution. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 64x64 datasets show that our method achieves better one-step and two-step FIDs than the state-of-the-art consistency models such as iCT-deep, using more than 2x smaller networks.

title: CapeX: Category-Agnostic Pose Estimation from Textual Point Explanation
submission:
Conventional 2D pose estimation models are constrained by their design to specific object categories. This limits their applicability to predefined objects. To overcome these limitations, category-agnostic pose estimation (CAPE) emerged as a solution. CAPE aims to facilitate keypoint localization for diverse object categories using a unified model, which can generalize from minimal annotated support images.
Recent CAPE works have produced object poses based on arbitrary keypoint definitions annotated on a user-provided support image. Our work departs from conventional CAPE methods, which require a support image, by adopting a text-based approach instead of the support image. 
Specifically, we use a pose-graph, where nodes represent keypoints that are described with text. This representation takes advantage of the abstraction of text descriptions and the structure imposed by the graph.
Our approach effectively breaks symmetry, preserves structure, and improves occlusion handling.
We validate our novel approach using the MP-100 benchmark, a comprehensive dataset covering over 100 categories and 18,000 images. MP-100 is structured so that the evaluation categories are unseen during training, making it especially suited for CAPE.  Under a 1-shot setting, our solution achieves a notable performance boost of 1.26\%, establishing a new state-of-the-art for CAPE. Additionally, we enhance the dataset by providing text description annotations for both training and testing. We also include alternative text annotations specifically for testing the model's ability to generalize across different textual descriptions, further increasing its value for future research. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/matanr/capex.

title: How Much is a  Noisy Image Worth? Data Scaling Laws for Ambient Diffusion.
submission: The quality of generative models depends on the quality of training data. Ambient Diffusion trains diffusion models with corrupted data only, which can be cheaper to acquire, but ambient models generally underperform models trained on clean data. We study this at scale by training many models on data with different corruption levels across three datasets ranging from 30,000 to about 1.3M samples. We find that training only on noisy data does not match clean-data performance at these sample sizes, yet combining a small set of clean examples (for instance 10% of the data) with a large set of noisy examples can approach the performance of clean-data-trained models. We also develop sample complexity bounds for learning from Gaussian mixtures with heterogeneous variances and argue that noisy samples have substantially lower marginal utility than clean samples. Implications for dataset design are discussed.

title: GrabS: Generative Embodied Agent for 3D Object Segmentation without Scene Supervision
submission: We study 3D object segmentation in complex point clouds without requiring human labels of 3D scenes. Relying on pretrained 2D features or external signals alone often limits unsupervised methods to simple categories or yields inferior objectness. We propose GrabS, a two-stage pipeline that first learns generative and discriminative object-centric priors from object datasets, and then trains an embodied agent to discover objects by querying against these pretrained generative priors. The method is designed to leverage object-centric priors to guide segmentation proposals and refine masks in cluttered scenes. We evaluate GrabS on two real-world datasets and a newly created synthetic dataset and report qualitative and quantitative improvements in segmentation quality. While results indicate promising gains in challenging scenarios, the quantitative significance varies across datasets and further benchmarking against established baselines is needed to fully characterize the advantages.

title: ImagineNav: Prompting Vision-Language Models as Embodied Navigator through Scene Imagination
submission: Visual navigation is essential for home-assistance robots to search for objects and accomplish long-horizon daily tasks, and many recent methods use large language models for commonsense inference to improve exploration. However, planning in LLMs is text-limited and does not naturally capture spatial occupancy or geometry, which matters for rational navigation. We explore whether a vision-language model (VLM), using only on-board RGB/RGB-D streams, can perform mapless visual navigation by imagining future observations. We present ImagineNav, an imagination-powered navigation framework that imagines likely future observation images at candidate robot views and reduces planning to best-view image selection for a VLM. Where2Imagine generates candidate views and is distilled to align with human navigation habits, while an off-the-shelf point-goal policy moves the robot to chosen views. We report experiments on open-vocabulary object navigation benchmarks; while some qualitative examples show the system selecting sensible views, quantitative comparisons are mixed and the overall contribution is primarily a practical exploration of VLM-based scene imagination rather than a definitive performance gain.

title: Deep Kernel Posterior Learning under Infinite Variance Prior Weights
submission: Neal (1996) proved that infinitely wide shallow Bayesian neural networks converge to Gaussian processes when weights have bounded prior variance, and Cho & Saul (2009) provided recursive relations for deep kernel processes. Subsequent work has connected these perspectives and characterized layer-wise covariance kernels for several activations. Recent authors have noted that such covariance kernels are deterministic in wide limits, limiting representation learning, and have proposed various fixes. In this paper we study Bayesian deep networks in an alternative limiting regime where layer widths grow and prior weight distributions are elliptically distributed with heavy tails. We analyze the resulting layer-wise processes which exhibit stable marginal behavior and discuss a conditional representation that relates to recursive kernel constructions. We also outline generalizations to multi-layer settings and comment on computational implications, while leaving some motivations and application-specific goals open for further exploration.

title: TeaserGen: Generating Teasers for Long Documentaries
submission: Teasers are an effective tool for promoting content in entertainment, commercial and educational fields. However, creating an effective teaser for long videos is challenging for it requires long-range multimodal modeling capability for the input videos, while necessitating maintaining audiovisual alignments, managing scene transitions and preserving factual accuracy for the output teasers. Due to the lack of a publicly-available dataset, progress along this research direction has been hindered. In this work, we present DocumentaryNet, a collection of 1,269 documentaries paired with their teasers, featuring multimodal data streams of video, speech, music, sound effects and narrations. With DocumentaryNet, we propose a new two-stage system for generating teasers from long documentaries. The proposed TeaserGen system first generates the teaser narration from the transcribed narration from the documentary using a pretrained large language model, and then selects the most relevant visual content to accompany the generated narration through language-vision models. For narration-video matching, we explore two approaches: a pretraining-based model using pretrained contrastive language-vision models and a deep sequential model that learns the mapping between the narrations and visuals. Our experimental results show that the pretraining-based approach is more effective at identifying relevant visual content than directly trained deep autoregressive models.

title: Are Bert Family Good Instruction Followers?  A Study on Their Potential And Limitations
submission: Language modeling at scale has brought unprecedented success to natural language models. Many decoder-only and encoder-decoder models have exhibited strong instruction-following capabilities and emergent skills. The potential of the BERT family, which are encoder-only models, deserves attention. We adopt XML-R to explore the effectiveness of the BERT family for instruction following and zero-shot learning. After multi-task instruction tuning, our fine-tuned model, Instruct-XMLR, outperforms Bloomz on all evaluation tasks and matches mT0 on most tasks. Instruct-XMLR also shows strong task and language generalization and accelerates decoding due to its non-autoregressive generation manner, achieving around 3× speedup compared with current autoregressive large language models. We observe limitations such as declines in long-generation tasks and length prediction shortcomings. Overall, Instruct-XMLR can serve as a capable instruction follower and zero-shot learner.

title: Tight Time Complexities in Parallel Stochastic Optimization with Arbitrary Computation Dynamics
submission: In distributed stochastic optimization, parallel and asynchronous methods must operate under widely varying and unpredictable computation dynamics, including hardware and network delays, time-varying computation powers, and worker disconnections. To capture these realistic behaviors we formalize a universal computation model that describes virtually any computation behavior of workers/devices/CPUs/GPUs. Leveraging this model and new proof techniques, we establish tight lower bounds that apply broadly to synchronous and asynchronous methods, including Minibatch SGD, Asynchronous SGD, and Picky SGD. We then show matching upper bounds (up to constants) by analyzing Rennala SGD and Malenia SGD methods. Alongside these theoretical results, we provide extensive discussion of how the universal computation model relates to practical system heterogeneity, straggler effects, and resource variability, highlighting implications for algorithm design under realistic parallel computation dynamics.

title: Scaling Optimal LR Across Token Horizons
submission: Scaling model size, training tokens, and cluster size underpins modern LLM progress, yet it is impractical to extensively tune hyperparameters for the largest runs. We study how the approximately optimal learning rate (LR) varies with the token horizon and present empirical observations suggesting that optimal LR tends to change as training length increases, with longer horizons favoring smaller LRs. We propose that the optimal LR follows a predictable relationship across token horizons and offer a rule-of-thumb for transferring LR from shorter to longer runs with minimal overhead. We discuss methodology, assumptions, and limitations, and we note indications that some large-scale runs may have used higher LRs than would be suggested by this perspective. Detailed controlled baselines and extensive comparisons are deferred to future, more comprehensive studies.

title: Field-DiT: Diffusion Transformer on Unified Video, 3D, and Game Field Generation
submission: Probabilistic fields model distributions of continuous functions over metric spaces and promise to unify generation across images, videos, and 3D geometry, but they struggle with long-context generation beyond toy examples. This limitation is due in part to their MLP-based architecture which lacks strong inductive biases to capture global structure from uniform sampling, so we propose a simple model to address this. We adopt a view-wise sampling algorithm to focus learning on local structure, and combine this with autoregressive generation to preserve global geometry. The model adapts cross-modality conditions like text prompts for text-to-video, camera poses for 3D view synthesis, and control actions for game generation. Our experiments across modalities show the approach is effective, and with about 675M parameters it demonstrates potential as a unified framework for scalable, architecture-consistent visual content generation for different modalities with shared weights. See project page at https://kfmei.com/Field-DiT/.

title: Programming Refusal with Conditional Activation Steering
submission: LLMs have shown remarkable capabilities, but precise control of their response behavior remains challenging. Existing activation steering methods alter behavior indiscriminately, which is limiting in settings that require selective responses like content moderation or domain-specific assistants. We propose Conditional Activation Steering (CAST), which analyzes activation patterns during inference to selectively apply or withhold steering conditioned on the input. The method is based on the observation that different prompt categories elicit distinct hidden-state patterns. With CAST one can specify rules such as "if input is about hate speech or adult content, then refuse" or "if input is not about legal advice, then refuse," enabling selective modification of responses while leaving other outputs unchanged. CAST operates without weight optimization and we release an open-source implementation of the framework.

title: Generating Pragmatic Examples to Train Neural Program Synthesizers
submission: Programming-by-example is the task of synthesizing a program consistent with a set of user-provided input-output examples. As examples are often under-specifications of intent, a good synthesizer must choose the intended program from many consistent candidates. Prior work frames program synthesis as a cooperative game between a listener (that synthesizes programs) and a speaker (a user choosing examples), showing that models of computational pragmatic inference can be effective at selecting the intended programs. However, these models require counterfactual reasoning over large program and example spaces, which is infeasible in realistic settings. We propose PraX, a way to amortize this search with neural networks. We sample pairs of programs and examples via self-play between listener and speaker models, and use pragmatic inference to choose informative training examples from this sample. We then use the informative dataset to train models that better disambiguate user-provided examples without human supervision. We validate PraX on the challenging task of synthesizing regular expressions from example strings and observe improvements in practice.

title: Quantitative Approximation for Neural Operators in Nonlinear Parabolic Equations
submission: Neural operators are studied as universal approximators for continuous operators arising from PDEs. title: Democratic Training Against Universal Adversarial Perturbations
submission: Despite their advances, deep neural networks remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Universal adversarial perturbations (UAPs), which are input-agnostic, are particularly concerning because a single perturbation can deceive a model across many inputs. We observe that UAPs often coincide with an abnormal entropy spectrum in hidden layers, which suggests that predictions become dominated by a small number of features rather than being democratically distributed. Motivated by this, we propose "Democratic Training", an entropy-based model enhancement intended to suppress the influence of universal perturbations and promote a more balanced feature contribution. Democratic Training is efficient to apply and is evaluated across multiple network architectures, datasets, and current universal attack methods. Empirical results indicate reductions in attack effectiveness alongside preserved accuracy on clean samples, though the exact mechanisms and limits of the approach are discussed at a conceptual level and left for more detailed follow-up work.

title: LoRA-Pro: Are Low-Rank Adapters Properly Optimized?
submission: Low-rank adaptation, also known as LoRA, has emerged as a prominent method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of foundation models. Despite its computational efficiency, LoRA often performs differently than full fine-tuning. In this paper, we first uncover a fundamental connection between the optimization processes of LoRA and full fine-tuning: using LoRA for optimization is mathematically equivalent to full fine-tuning using a low-rank gradient for parameter updates. This low-rank gradient can be expressed in terms of the gradients of the two low-rank matrices in LoRA. Leveraging this insight, we introduce LoRA-Pro, a method that enhances LoRA by strategically adjusting the gradients of these low-rank matrices so that the resulting low-rank gradient more closely reflects the structure of the full fine-tuning gradient. We theoretically derive optimal adjustments for the low-rank matrices and describe how to apply them during fine-tuning. We release our implementation at https://github.com/mrflogs/LoRA-Pro for reproducibility and further study.

title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF
submission: Language models can produce errors that are hard for humans to detect. RLHF, the most popular post-training method, may make models better at persuading humans. We study this under a standard RLHF pipeline and name the phenomenon U-Sophistry. Specifically, we ask time-constrained human subjects to judge model outputs and measure their accuracy against gold labels. On a reading-style question set and a code-writing task, RLHF makes models more convincing to our subjects without improving task correctness. The false positive rate of participants increases substantially on both tasks. Probing methods designed for other forms of intentional deception do not generalize to this behavior. Our findings point to a failure mode of RLHF and motivate further work on assisting human evaluators.

title: Structural-Entropy-Based Sample Selection for Efficient and Effective Learning
submission: Sample selection improves the efficiency and effectiveness of machine learning models by providing informative and representative samples. Samples can be modeled as a sample graph, where nodes are samples and edges indicate similarities. title: Rethinking Classifier Re-Training in Long-Tailed Recognition: Label Over-Smooth Can Balance
submission: In long-tailed recognition, the Decoupled Training paradigm separates representation learning and classifier re-training. Prior work has attempted to improve both stages simultaneously, complicating isolation of classifier re-training effects. Motivated by recent findings that simple regularization yields strong features, we revisit classifier re-training methods using a unified feature representation and re-evaluate their performance. We propose two metrics, Logits Magnitude and Regularized Standard Deviation, to compare differences between methods. Using these metrics, we argue that balancing Logits Magnitude across classes and reducing its overall value can reduce training errors. From this analysis we develop a simple label over-smoothing approach that adjusts logits by softening one-hot labels, assigning a probability slightly higher than 1/K to the true class and slightly lower than 1/K to other classes. Implementation details, exact hyperparameters, and experimental outcomes across datasets are omitted here, but we emphasize that the approach requires no prior knowledge of class distribution.

title: Instance-dependent Early Stopping
submission: We propose an Instance-dependent Early Stopping (IES) method that adapts early stopping from the entire training set to the instance level, based on the principle that once the model has mastered an instance, training on it should stop. IES considers an instance as mastered if the second-order differences of its loss remain within a small range around zero. This offers a more consistent measure of an instance's learning status compared with directly using the loss value, and hence allows a unified threshold to determine when an instance can be excluded from further backpropagation. Excluding mastered instances from backpropagation can increase gradient norms and thereby accelerate the decrease of training loss. In machine learning practice, early stopping is widely used to regularize models and save computation when validation stops improving; conventional early stopping applies the same criterion to all instances without considering individual learning status, which motivates our instance-level approach. We empirically observe meaningful reductions in backpropagation while maintaining test accuracy.

title: Provable Memory Efficient Self-Play Algorithm for Model-free Reinforcement Learning
submission: The thriving field of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) studies how a group of interacting agents make decisions autonomously in a shared dynamic environment. Existing theoretical studies in this area suffer from at least two of the following obstacles: memory inefficiency, the heavy dependence of sample complexity on the long horizon and the large state space, the high computational complexity, non-Markov policy, non-Nash policy, and high burn-in cost. In this work, we take a step towards settling this problem by designing a model-free self-play algorithm \emph{Memory-Efficient Nash Q-Learning (ME-Nash-QL)} for two-player zero-sum Markov games, which is a specific setting of MARL. We prove that ME-Nash-QL can output an $\varepsilon$-approximate Nash policy with remarkable space complexity $O(SABH)$, sample complexity $\widetilde{O}(H^4SAB/\varepsilon^2)$, and computational complexity $O(T\mathrm{poly}(AB))$, where $S$ is the number of states, $\{A, B\}$ is the number of actions for the two players, $H$ is the horizon length, and $T$ is the number of samples. Notably, our approach outperforms in terms of space complexity compared to existing algorithms for tabular cases. It achieves the lowest computational complexity while preserving Markov policies, setting a new standard. Furthermore, our algorithm outputs a Nash policy and achieves the best sample complexity compared with the existing guarantee for long horizons, i.e. when $\min \\{ A, B \\} \ll H^2$. Our algorithm also achieves the best burn-in cost $O(SAB\,\mathrm{poly}(H))$, whereas previous algorithms need at least $O(S^3 AB\,\mathrm{poly}(H))$ to attain the same level of sample complexity with ours.

title: What Makes a Good Diffusion Planner for Decision Making?
submission: Diffusion models have recently shown promise for decision-making by generating behavior plans, a paradigm often called diffusion planning. Despite many strong empirical results, the design principles that make a diffusion planner effective are inconsistently applied across prior work. Here we present a systematic empirical study of diffusion planning in an offline reinforcement learning setting: we trained and evaluated over 6,000 diffusion models to probe components such as guided sampling, network architecture, action generation, and planning strategy. Our experiments reveal several surprising trends—for example, unconditional sampling with selection can sometimes outperform guided sampling, and Transformers can be preferable to U-Nets in some settings. Based on these observations we propose a simple diffusion planning baseline and provide practical recommendations; we leave open whether this baseline is uniformly superior across all benchmarks and encourage replication via our code.

title: SecureGS: Boosting the Security and Fidelity of 3D Gaussian Splatting Steganography
submission: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a leading method for 3D representation due to its real-time rendering and high-quality outputs, highlighting the need to protect the privacy of 3D assets. Traditional NeRF steganography methods do not adequately address explicit 3DGS representations since point cloud files are publicly accessible. Existing GS steganography approaches mitigate some issues but still suffer from reduced rendering fidelity, higher computational cost, and security weaknesses, particularly around the geometry of visualized point clouds. To address these demands, we propose SecureGS, a secure and efficient 3DGS steganography framework inspired by scaffold anchor designs and neural decoding. SecureGS uses a hybrid decoupled Gaussian encryption mechanism to embed offsets, scales, rotations, and RGB attributes of hidden Gaussians into anchor features, retrievable only by authorized users via privacy-preserving neural decoders. We further introduce density region-aware anchor growing and pruning to locate hiding regions adaptively. Extensive experiments indicate SecureGS vastly outperforms existing GS steganography in fidelity, speed, and security and effectively eliminates common structural leaks.

title: Controlled LLM Decoding via Discrete Auto-regressive Biasing
submission: Discrete Auto-regressive Biasing is a controlled decoding algorithm that leverages gradients while operating entirely in the discrete text domain. Specifically, we introduce a new formulation by defining a joint distribution over the generated sequence and an auxiliary bias sequence, and we propose a Langevin-within-Gibbs sampling algorithm using gradient-based discrete MCMC. Our method significantly improves constraint satisfaction while maintaining comparable or better fluency, all with lower computational costs. One common approach uses energy-based decoding, which defines a target distribution through an energy function that combines multiple constraints; these methods often struggle to balance fluency with constraint satisfaction. However, the precise problem statement motivating the shift from continuous to discrete sampling is not laid out clearly, and the logical flow between the identified shortcomings of prior work and our algorithmic choices is uneven. We demonstrate the method on sentiment control, detoxification, and keyword-guided generation, but parts of the narrative jump between concepts without a tight connection.
