title: CLIPure: Purification in Latent Space via CLIP for Adversarially Robust Zero-Shot Classification
submission: Adversarial robustness and zero-shot generalization are central challenges for deploying vision models in safety-critical settings. In this paper, we aim to build an adversarially robust zero-shot image classifier that can accurately and efficiently classify unseen examples while defending against unforeseen adversarial attacks, addressing critical challenges in real-world safety-sensitive scenarios. To achieve this, we focus on two key challenges: zero-shot classification and defense against unforeseen attacks. We ground our work on CLIP, a vision-language pre-trained model to perform zero-shot classification. To defend against unforeseen attacks, we adopt a purification approach, as it is independent of specific attack types. We then define a purification risk as the KL divergence between the joint distributions of the purification and attack process. The derived lower bound of purification risk inspires us to explore purification in CLIP's multi-modal latent space. We propose a CLIP-based purification method called CLIPure, with CLIPure-Diff modeling image likelihood via a generative latent process and CLIPure-Cos modeling likelihood via similarity to a blank template. Extensive experiments show robustness close to clean accuracy, outperforming prior robustness by large margins (e.g., CIFAR10 91.1%, ImageNet 72.6%) with modest extra inference cost.

title: Fine-Tuned Language Models Generate Stable Inorganic Materials as Text
submission: We propose fine-tuning large language models for generation of stable materials. Large pretrained LLMs have proven highly effective across many text and multimodal tasks, and their sequence modeling inductive biases suggest they may be a natural fit for text-encoded atomistic data; this background motivates our approach. Fine-tuning large language models on text representations of atomic structures is simple to implement and, empirically, surprisingly reliable: around 90% of sampled structures obey basic physical constraints on atom positions and charges. Using energy-above-hull estimates from both learned ML potentials and gold-standard DFT, our strongest model (fine-tuned LLaMA-2 70B) generates materials predicted to be metastable roughly twice as often (49% vs 28%) as CDVAE, a competing diffusion model. Because text prompting is inherently flexible, the same models support unconditional generation, infilling of partial structures, and text-conditional generation. We also observe that model scale tends to improve capture of crystal symmetries.

title: Reconstructive Visual Instruction Tuning
submission: We introduce reconstructive visual instruction tuning (ROSS), a family of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) that exploit vision-centric supervision signals. ROSS prompts LMMs to supervise visual outputs by reconstructing input images, and it uses a denoising objective to reconstruct latent representations of input images rather than regressing raw RGB values. This intrinsic activation design encourages models to retain image detail and reduce hallucination. Implementation uses a single SigLIP visual encoder with a denoising latent target and integrates with standard language model backbones. Empirically, ROSS consistently brings improvements across different visual encoders and language models. Evaluation in our experiments, however, concentrates on instruction-following and text-centric metrics and qualitative human judgments of outputs rather than detailed pixel- or latent-space fidelity measures. In comparison with extrinsic assistance alternatives that aggregate multiple visual experts, ROSS provides competitive behavior with a single encoder. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

title: CodePlan: Unlocking Reasoning Potential in Large Language Models by Scaling Code-form Planning
submission: We introduce CodePlan, a scalable paradigm that has models generate and follow code-form plans—pseudocode that outlines structured reasoning processes. By leveraging code’s structure, CodePlan aims to capture semantics and control flows for multi-step tasks. It also permits automatic extraction of code-form plans from large text corpora without curated, task-specific datasets, which enables scaling. To train CodePlan we build a dataset of roughly 2M examples that combine code-form plans with standard prompt–response pairs from existing corpora. With modest computation overhead, CodePlan yields improvements versus directly generating responses, averaged across a suite of multi-step reasoning benchmarks; we observe a 25.1% relative improvement in our evaluation. Additional analyses show larger gains on more complex tasks and improved data efficiency, though behavior varies by benchmark and setup.

title: Towards Robust and Efficient Cloud-Edge Elastic Model Adaptation via Selective Entropy Distillation
submission: The conventional deep learning paradigm often involves training a model on a server and then deploying the model or its distilled versions to resource-limited edge devices. Usually, models remain fixed once deployed due to the cost of model adaptation for both server and edge. Yet, test environments can change dynamically, producing distribution shifts that degrade performance and require prompt adaptation. Moreover, increasing data collected at the edge motivates adapting the cloud model as well. We propose a Cloud-Edge Elastic Model Adaptation (CEMA) paradigm in which edge models only need to perform forward propagation and can be adapted online. To reduce communication, we devise two criteria to exclude samples from uploading: dynamic unreliable and low-informative sample exclusion. Based on uploaded samples, we update and distribute affine normalization parameters by distilling from a stronger foundation model to the edge model with a sample replay strategy. Preliminary experiments on ImageNet-C and ImageNet-R indicate that CEMA can yield modest improvements in some settings, though broader evaluation and baseline comparisons remain necessary.

title: Revisiting Convolution Architecture in the Realm of DNA Foundation Models
submission:
In recent years, A variety of methods based on Transformer and state space model (SSM) architectures have been proposed, advancing foundational DNA language models. 
However, there is a lack of comparison between these recent approaches and the classical architecture—convolutional networks (CNNs)—on foundation model benchmarks.
This raises the question: are CNNs truly being surpassed by these recent approaches based on transformer and SSM architectures? In this paper, we develop a simple but well-designed CNN-based method, termed ConvNova. ConvNova identifies and proposes three effective designs: 1) dilated convolutions, 2) gated convolutions, and 3) a dual-branch framework for gating mechanisms.

For example, in histone-related tasks, ConvNova exceeds the second-best method by an average of 5.8\%, while generally utilizing fewer parameters and enabling faster computation.  In addition, the experiments observed findings that may be related to biological characteristics. This indicates that CNNs are still a strong competitor compared to Transformers and SSMs. We anticipate that this work will spark renewed interest in CNN-based methods for DNA foundation models.

title: SINGER: Stochastic Network Graph Evolving Operator for High Dimensional PDEs
submission: We introduce SINGER, a StochastIc Network Graph Evolving operatoR, for learning evolution operators of high-dimensional PDEs. The framework uses a sub-network to approximate the initial-time solution and stochastically evolves sub-network parameters over time via a graph neural network, aiming to inherit desirable properties of parametric solution operators such as topology awareness, semigroup structure, and stability, with theoretical guarantees. We apply SINGER to a collection of evolution PDEs in varying dimensions and study generalization to unseen initial conditions, dimensions, sub-network width, and time steps. Empirically, performance is mixed: SINGER exhibits strong generalization in some settings but fails to consistently outperform baselines across all tasks, indicating a discrepancy between the theoretical properties and practical gains. We analyze possible causes for these mixed results and discuss directions to better align the method's theoretical advantages with robust empirical performance.

title: Training One-Dimensional Graph Neural Networks is NP-Hard
submission: We initiate the study of the computational complexity of training graph neural networks (GNNs). We consider the classical node classification setting; there, the intractability of training multidimensonal GNNs immediately follows from known lower bounds for training classical neural networks (and holds even for trivial GNNs). However, one-dimensional GNNs form a crucial case of interest: the computational complexity of training such networks depends on both the graphical structure of the network and the properties of the involved activation and aggregation functions. As our main result, we establish the NP-hardness of training ReLU-activated one-dimensional GNNs via a highly non-trivial reduction. We complement this result with algorithmic upper bounds for the training problem in the ReLU-activated and linearly-activated settings.

title: Neuron Platonic Intrinsic Representation From Dynamics Using Contrastive Learning
submission: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that behind different modalities of data (what we sense or detect), there exists a universal, modality-independent representation of reality. Inspired by this, we treat each neuron as a system, where we can detect the neuron’s multi-segment activity data under different peripheral conditions. We believe that, similar to the Platonic idea, there exists a time-invariant representation behind the different segments of the same neuron, which reflects the intrinsic properties of the neuron’s system. Intrinsic properties include the molecular profiles, brain regions and morphological structure, etc. The optimization objective for obtaining the intrinsic representation of neurons should satisfy two criteria: (I) segments from the same neuron should have a higher similarity than segments from different neurons; (II) the representations should generalize well to out-of-domain data. To achieve this, we employ contrastive learning, treating different segments from the same neuron as positive pairs and segments from different neurons as negative pairs. During implementation we chose VICReg, which uses only positive pairs for optimization but indirectly separates dissimilar samples via regularization terms. We evaluate the approach on simulated Izhikevich dynamics and two real-world neuron dynamics datasets and report observations on representation structure and generalization across datasets.

title: PEARL: Parallel Speculative Decoding with Adaptive Draft Length
submission:
Speculative decoding (SD), where an extra draft model is employed to provide multiple **draft** tokens first and then the original target model verifies these tokens in parallel, has shown great power for LLM inference acceleration.
However, existing SD methods suffer from the mutual waiting problem, i.e., the target model gets stuck when the draft model is *guessing* tokens, and vice versa. This problem is directly incurred by the asynchronous execution of the draft model and the target model, and is exacerbated due to the fixed draft length in speculative decoding.
To address these challenges, we propose a conceptually simple, flexible, and general framework to boost speculative decoding, namely 
**P**arallel sp**E**culative decoding with **A**daptive d**R**aft **L**ength (PEARL). 
Specifically, PEARL proposes *pre-verify* to verify the first draft token in advance during the drafting phase, and *post-verify* to generate more draft tokens during the verification phase.
PEARL parallels the drafting phase and the verification phase via applying the two strategies, and achieves adaptive draft length for different scenarios, which effectively alleviates the mutual waiting problem.
Experiments on various text generation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our PEARL, leading to a superior speedup performance up to **4.43$\times$** and **1.50$\times$**, compared to auto-regressive decoding and vanilla speculative decoding, respectively.

title: FreqPrior: Improving Video Diffusion Models with Frequency Filtering Gaussian Noise
submission: Text-driven video generation with diffusion models has advanced, and recent work started to explore the effect of noise priors in frequency space. Prior Fourier-based manipulations can lead to outputs that lack motion dynamics and fine imaging detail. We analyze a variance decay phenomenon in these approaches that may contribute to loss of detail and motion, and argue that the choice of noise distribution across frequencies influences generation quality. Based on this, we propose FreqPrior, a noise initialization strategy that refines noise in the frequency domain using a filtering approach designed to treat different frequency bands while keeping an overall Gaussian-like prior. We also introduce a partial sampling schedule that perturbs latents at intermediate timesteps when searching for the noise prior, which can reduce inference time. Preliminary experiments indicate qualitative improvements in motion and detail, suggesting frequency-aware priors are a promising direction for video diffusion.

title: ShortcutsBench: A Large-Scale Real-world Benchmark for API-based Agents
submission: Recent advances in integrating large language models (LLMs) with application programming interfaces (APIs) have attracted interest in both academia and industry. In this work we introduce ShortcutsBench, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating API-based agents on real-world complex tasks. ShortcutsBench aggregates real APIs from Apple Inc., refined user queries, human-annotated high-quality action sequences, and detailed parameter-filling values including parameters that may request input from the system or the user. We discuss limitations of existing datasets in capturing the multi-dimensional difficulty of API tasks and provide the benchmark and tooling to support future research. We also report preliminary evaluations of a set of agents to illustrate common failure modes in API selection, parameter filling, and input solicitation; these initial tests suggest potential gaps rather than definitive rankings, and are intended to motivate more systematic baselines and comparisons. All datasets, code, experimental logs, and results are available at https://github.com/EachSheep/ShortcutsBench.

title: Progressive Token Length Scaling in Transformer Encoders for Efficient Universal Segmentation
submission: A common architecture for universal segmentation uses a transformer encoder to aggregate multi-scale backbone features and a decoder that maps object queries to masks. We propose PROgressive Token Length SCALing for Efficient transformer encoders (PRO-SCALE), a plug-in strategy for Mask2Former-style architectures that progressively scales token length across encoder layers. PRO-SCALE gradually reduces token counts at deeper encoder layers while preserving multi-scale information for the decoder. The method can be configured in multiple ways and integrates with existing multi-scale encoders. PRO-SCALE reduces encoder computation and overall model cost while aiming to keep segmentation quality close to the baseline. We present ablations that explore different scaling schedules and show the approach generalizes across segmentation settings and can be extended toward detection tasks. Code is available at the project repository.

title: PhysPDE: Rethinking PDE Discovery and a Physical Hypothesis Selection Benchmark
submission: Recovering PDE expressions from experimental observations has long relied on symbolic regression, which often produces formulas lacking clear physical interpretation. There is substantial prior work on combining data-driven approaches with physical priors, machine learning for science (ML4Sci) efforts to extract governing laws, and various strategies to regularize and constrain discovery. Motivated by the desire to emphasize interpretability and theory-driven analysis, we introduce a novel ML4Sci task paradigm that frames PDE recovery as interpretation within the space of prior physical hypotheses. Concretely, we formulate the problem as a nonlinear mixed-integer programming (MIP) instance and tackle it with an efficient search scheme developed for this purpose. Experiments on designed Fluid Mechanics and Laser Fusion datasets illustrate the feasibility and interpretability of the approach, and highlight how prior hypotheses can narrow the search space for PDE discovery.

title: Towards 3D Molecule-Text Interpretation in Language Models
submission: Language models (LMs) have greatly influenced diverse domains, but their limited ability to reason about 3D molecular structure constrains their use in biomolecular tasks. To address this, we present 3D-MoLM: 3D-Molecular Language Modeling, a framework that integrates a 3D molecular encoder with a language model. The integration is performed by introducing a 3D molecule–text projector that maps the encoder’s representation space into inputs compatible with an LM. To improve cross-modal understanding and instruction following, we construct a 3D molecule-centric instruction tuning collection and use it during alignment. Through 3D molecule–text alignment and instruction tuning, 3D-MoLM establishes an end-to-end connection between 3D encoders and LMs. We report consistent improvements on a range of downstream tasks including molecule–text retrieval, molecule captioning, and open-text molecular QA that emphasize 3D-dependent properties. Code and datasets will be released at the project repository.

title: Controllable Blur Data Augmentation Using 3D-Aware Motion Estimation
submission: Existing realistic blur datasets provide insufficient variety in scenes and blur patterns to be trained, while expanding data diversity demands considerable time and effort due to complex dual-camera systems. To address the challenge, data augmentation can be an effective way to artificially increase data diversity. However, existing methods on this line are typically designed to estimate motions from a 2D perspective, e.g., estimating 2D non-uniform kernels disregarding 3D aspects of blur modeling, which leads to unrealistic motion patterns due to the fact that camera and object motions inherently arise in 3D space. In this paper, we propose a 3D-aware blur synthesizer capable of generating diverse and realistic blur images for blur data augmentation. Specifically, we estimate 3D camera positions within the motion blur interval, generate the corresponding scene images, and aggregate them to synthesize a realistic blur image. Since the 3D camera positions projected onto the 2D image plane inherently lie in 2D space, we can represent the 3D transformation as a combination of 2D transformation and projected 3D residual component. This allows for 3D transformation without requiring explicit depth measurements, as the 3D residual component is directly estimated via a neural network. Furthermore, our blur synthesizer allows for controllable blur data augmentation by modifying blur magnitude, direction, and scenes, resulting in diverse blur images. As a result, our method significantly improves deblurring performance, making it more practical for real-world scenarios.

title: Learning Multi-Agent Communication with Contrastive Learning
submission: Communication is a powerful tool for coordination in multi-agent RL, yet inducing an effective common language is challenging, particularly in decentralized settings. We introduce an alternative perspective where communicative messages between agents are treated as different incomplete views of the environment state. By examining relationships between messages sent and received, we propose to learn to communicate using contrastive learning to maximize mutual information between messages within a trajectory. In environments where communication is important, our approach often improves coordination and can accelerate learning in several cases. Using qualitative metrics and representation probing, we show that the method tends to induce more symmetric communication and to capture more global state information than simple baselines. Overall, these findings suggest that contrastive objectives applied to messages are a promising direction for emergent multi-agent communication.

title: Storybooth: Training-Free Multi-Subject Consistency for Improved Visual Storytelling
submission: Consistent text-to-image generation of the same subjects across multiple images is important for visual storytelling and multi-shot video generation. Existing methods often require costly fine-tuning per subject and struggle with multi-character consistency. We analyze this limitation and identify self-attention leakage as a primary factor that grows when enforcing consistency across multiple characters. Motivated by this, we propose a training- and optimization-free approach to improve multi-subject consistency. title: CR2PQ: Continuous Relative Rotary Positional Query for Dense Visual Representation Learning
submission: Dense visual contrastive learning (DRL) shows promise for learning localized information in dense prediction tasks, but struggles with establishing pixel/patch correspondence across different views (cross-contrasting). Existing methods mostly rely on self-contrasting the same view with variations, which limits input variance and can hinder downstream performance. We analyze self-contrasting and cross-contrasting and identify a key issue: transforming discrete positional embeddings to continuous representations. To address correspondence, we propose a Continuous Relative Rotary Positional Query (CR2PQ) that is intended to enable patch-level representation learning. We provide implementation details and report experiments on standard datasets that suggest improvements in convergence and downstream tasks. The contribution is primarily a continuous positional query mechanism for cross-view matching; while our results are encouraging, the exact scope of the gains and broader applicability remain to be fully characterized.

submission: Recent advances in 3D generation have been remarkable, with methods such as DreamFusion leveraging large-scale text-to-image diffusion-based models to guide 3D object generation. Our experiments suggest that IPDreamer frequently produces 3D objects that align with both textual and complex image prompts, indicating promising capability, though further validation and broader testing are needed to fully establish its strengths and limitations.

title: Enhancing Transfer Learning with Flexible Nonparametric Posterior Sampling
submission: Transfer learning with deep networks relies heavily on priors for downstream data when performing Bayesian model averaging. Prior work centers priors around pretrained parameter solutions, which can struggle under distribution shift between upstream and downstream data. We propose nonparametric transfer learning (NPTL), a flexible posterior sampling approach based on nonparametric learning (NPL) ideas, intended to better handle such shifts. NPL uses a nonparametric prior for posterior sampling and is designed to be robust to model misspecification; we adapt this intuition to the transfer learning setting. Empirically, we report that NPTL outperforms several baselines in Bayesian model averaging metrics across a range of downstream tasks. The manuscript focuses on the high-level approach and empirical comparisons; specific algorithmic and implementation details are deferred, and we leave a fuller methodological exposition to follow work.

title: Encoding Unitig-level Assembly Graphs with Heterophilous Constraints for Metagenomic Contigs Binning
submission: Metagenomics studies genomic material from mixed microbial communities and binning aims to cluster subsequences from high-throughput sequencing into organismal bins. Mainstream binners rely on composition and abundance features and often fail on short sequences and noisy data. Several tools augment sequence features with assembly graph information from assemblers, but many existing graph-based binners simplify unitig-level graphs into contig-level graphs, thereby reducing connectivity resolution. We propose UnitigBin, a binning tool that performs representation learning directly on unitig-level assembly graphs while imposing heterophilous constraints derived from single-copy marker genes so that constrained contigs are prevented from being grouped together. UnitigBin leverages graph neural encodings together with marker-gene constraints to better preserve assembly graph signal; extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets indicate that UnitigBin substantially surpasses several state-of-the-art binning tools across standard benchmarks.

title: Independent-Set Design of Experiments for Estimating Treatment and Spillover Effects under Network Interference
submission: Interference is ubiquitous when conducting causal experiments over networks. Except for certain structures, causal inference with interference is challenging because treatment assignments and interference levels are entangled. We study causal inference under interference on an observed, sparse, connected network and propose a design of experiments based on selecting an independent set. The independent-set design concentrates on an independent subset and controls their interference exposure through assignments on the complementary (auxiliary) set. We provide a lower bound on the size of the independent set obtained from a simple greedy procedure and give theoretical guarantees characterizing estimator behavior under the proposed design. The approach is intended to enable estimation of both spillover effects and direct treatment effects under the adopted interference model. We include simulation studies to illustrate how the design behaves across a range of network instances and discuss practical considerations for implementation.

title: T2V-Turbo-v2: Enhancing Video Model Post-Training through Data, Reward, and Conditional Guidance Design
submission: In this paper, we focus on enhancing a diffusion-based text-to-video (T2V) model during the post-training phase by distilling a highly capable consistency model from a pretrained T2V model. Our proposed method, T2V-Turbo-v2, introduces a significant advancement by integrating various supervision signals, including high-quality training data, reward model feedback, and conditional guidance, into the consistency distillation process. Through comprehensive ablation studies, we highlight the crucial importance of tailoring datasets to specific learning objectives and the effectiveness of learning from diverse reward models for enhancing both the visual quality and text-video alignment. Additionally, we highlight the vast design space of conditional guidance strategies, which centers on designing an effective energy function to augment the teacher ODE solver. We demonstrate the potential of this approach by extracting motion guidance from the training datasets and incorporating it into the ODE solver, showcasing its effectiveness in improving the motion quality of the generated videos with the improved motion-related metrics from VBench and T2V-CompBench. Empirically, our T2V-Turbo-v2 establishes a new state-of-the-art result on VBench, **with a Total score of 85.13**, surpassing proprietary systems such as Gen-3 and Kling.

title: Interpreting and Editing Vision-Language Representations to Mitigate Hallucinations
submission: We study internal representations of vision–language models (VLMs) to tackle hallucinations, a persistent issue despite scaling. Projecting VLM image features onto the language vocabulary reveals that model output probabilities tend to be higher for real objects than for hallucinated ones; these probabilities can also be used to localize real objects spatially. Motivated by these observations, we introduce a knowledge erasure procedure that removes hallucinated content by linearly orthogonalizing image features with respect to features associated with hallucinated objects. Targeted edits to latent representations reduce hallucination rates and do so while largely preserving the model’s overall performance. The method also suggests new capabilities such as zero-shot segmentation via the same projection mechanism. Overall, analyzing and editing latent image–language alignments appears to be a practical avenue to improve reliability, though further evaluation across diverse benchmarks remains necessary.

title: Bayes Conditional Distribution Estimation for Knowledge Distillation Based on Conditional Mutual Information
submission: It is commonly assumed that in knowledge distillation (KD) the teacher should provide an estimate of the Bayes conditional probability distribution (BCPD) used to train the student. Conventionally this estimate is obtained by training the teacher with maximum log-likelihood (MLL). We introduce conditional mutual information (CMI) into BCPD estimation and propose a maximum CMI (MCMI) estimator that jointly maximizes log-likelihood and the teacher's CMI during teacher training. Maximizing the teacher's CMI is intended to help capture contextual information in images, and we use Eigen-CAM to visualize the learned contextual cues. In empirical studies across several KD frameworks, the use of an MCMI-trained teacher often leads to improvements in student classification accuracy in some settings, particularly in low-data regimes; in other settings gains are marginal or inconsistent. The observed outcomes are mixed, suggesting that MCMI can yield better BCPD estimates in certain scenarios but its advantages are context-dependent.

title: HyperPLR: Hypergraph Generation through Projection, Learning, and Reconstruction
submission: Hypergraphs are essential for modeling higher-order complex networks, especially collaboration networks where group interactions extend beyond pairwise links. Generative models for hypergraphs are a key tool to validate our understanding of such structures: if generators reproduce observed patterns, they support our interpretations. We introduce HyperPLR, a hypergraph generative paradigm composed of three phases: Projection, Learning, and Reconstruction. First, the hypergraph is projected onto a weighted graph. The model then learns this graph structure in a latent space while estimating a distribution between hyperedges and the projected graph. Finally, HyperPLR generates weighted graphs from the learned model and samples cliques, which are used to reconstruct hypergraphs via a clique cover procedure. We evaluated HyperPLR on real-world hypergraph datasets and found it to be effective; details of comparative metrics and ablations are discussed in the full text.

Applied to several popular MLLMs and benchmarks, γ-MoD is reported to yield efficiency gains with only minor performance change, though the experimental protocol and ablations supporting these claims are not fully described.

title: Learning in reverse causal strategic environments with ramifications on two sided markets
submission: Motivated by equilibrium models of labor markets, we formulate causal strategic classification where strategic agents can directly influence their outcomes. As an application, employers anticipate the strategic response of a labor force when designing hiring policies. We provide a theoretical analysis in the Coate-Loury labor market model and describe conditions under which performatively optimal hiring policies are beneficial. Empirically, we report that performative policies generalize in a general equilibrium labor market we construct, and we discuss several observed effects. Overall, the paper outlines modeling choices, theoretical observations, and empirical patterns that highlight both promise and potential harms of performative hiring.

title: Do as We Do, Not as You Think: the Conformity of Large Language Models
submission: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) revolutionize the field of intelligent agents, enabling collaborative multi-agent systems capable of tackling complex problems across various domains. However, the potential of conformity within these systems, analogous to phenomena like conformity bias and group-think in human group dynamics, remains largely unexplored, raising concerns about their collective problem-solving capabilities and possible ethical implications. This paper presents a comprehensive study on conformity in LLM-driven multi-agent systems, focusing on three aspects: the existence of conformity, the factors influencing conformity, and potential mitigation strategies. In particular, we introduce BenchForm, a new conformity-oriented benchmark, featuring reasoning-intensive tasks and five distinct interaction protocols designed to probe LLMs’ behavior in collaborative scenarios. Several representative LLMs are evaluated on BenchForm, using metrics such as conformity rate and independence rate to quantify conformity’s impact. Curiously, the metric-based scores and our qualitative case studies sometimes disagree: high conformity rates are reported while individual case analyses show clear independent rationales, indicating a mismatch between the chosen metrics and observed behaviors. Our analysis delves into factors influencing conformity, including interaction time and majority size, and we explore two mitigation strategies, i.e., developing enhanced persona and implementing a reflection mechanism. The empirical results and case studies yield several interesting but occasionally inconsistent findings regarding LLMs’ conformity. We hope these insights can pave the way for more robust and ethically-aligned collaborative AI systems. Our benchmark and code are available at BenchForm.

title: Reverse Forward Curriculum Learning for Extreme Sample and Demo Efficiency
submission: Reinforcement learning (RL) can learn policies through environment interaction but often requires large amounts of data to solve tasks with sparse rewards. Augmenting RL with offline demonstrations can help, yet prior work frequently demands many high-quality demonstrations that are difficult to obtain for domains like robotics. We present a method combining a reverse curriculum followed by a forward curriculum. Unlike prior approaches, our formulation leverages more than one demonstration by generating a per-demonstration reverse curriculum via state resets. The reverse curriculum yields an initial policy that performs well on a narrow initial distribution and alleviates hard exploration problems; a subsequent forward curriculum then expands that capability to the full initial distribution and aims to improve demonstration and sample efficiency. We describe algorithmic details for generating per-demo reverse curricula and for constructing the forward progression, outline practical implementation choices, and apply the approach (RFCL) to a set of robotic control tasks. Code and visualizations are available at the project website.

title: Selective Induction Heads: How Transformers Select Causal Structures in Context
submission: Transformers have exhibited strong capabilities in sequence modelling, leveraging self-attention and in-context learning. Induction heads—attention circuits that enable copying tokens based on previous occurrences—are central to this success, and prior work studies their formation via Markov chains. In contrast to fixed causal structures, natural language exhibits dynamic relationships, but whether the goal is to better predict tokens, to explain circuits, or to design new architectures is not stated explicitly here. We introduce a synthetic framework that varies causal structure through interleaved Markov chains with different lags while keeping transition probabilities fixed, and this setting reveals a mechanism we call Selective Induction Heads. Empirically, attention-only transformers trained in this setting learn to identify the correct lag and copy the corresponding past token, and we give a construction of a 3-layer transformer that implements the selective induction head. We provide an analysis indicating asymptotic convergence toward a likelihood-based solution, and we discuss implications for interpretability and modelling, leaving open precise practical objectives and evaluation paths.

title: TIPS: Text-Image Pretraining with Spatial awareness
submission: While image-text representation learning has become very popular in recent years, existing models tend to lack spatial awareness and have limited direct applicability for dense understanding tasks. For this reason, self-supervised image-only pretraining is still the go-to method for many dense vision applications (e.g. depth estimation, semantic segmentation), despite the lack of explicit supervisory signals. In this paper, we close this gap between image-text and self-supervised learning by proposing a general-purpose image-text model that can be used off the shelf for dense and global vision tasks. Our method, Text-Image Pretraining with Spatial awareness (TIPS), leverages two simple and effective insights. First, on textual supervision: replacing noisy web image captions by synthetically generated textual descriptions often boosts dense understanding performance, due to a richer signal for learning spatially aware representations. We propose an adapted training method that combines noisy and synthetic captions, which yields improvements across a range of dense and global understanding tasks. Second, on the learning technique: we combine contrastive image-text learning with masked image modeling to encourage spatial coherence. Building on these ideas, we scale a transformer architecture trained on a curated set of public images, and present experiments on multiple tasks that suggest improved off-the-shelf behavior, though further validation across broader benchmarks is warranted.

title: Gap-Dependent Bounds for Q-Learning using Reference-Advantage Decomposition
submission:
We study the gap-dependent bounds of two important algorithms for on-policy $Q$-learning for finite-horizon episodic tabular Markov Decision Processes (MDPs): UCB-Advantage (Zhang et al. 2020) and Q-EarlySettled-Advantage (Li et al. 2021). UCB-Advantage and Q-EarlySettled-Advantage improve upon the results based on Hoeffding-type bonuses and achieve the {almost optimal} $\sqrt{T}$-type regret bound in the worst-case scenario, where $T$ is the total number of steps. However, the benign structures of the MDPs such as a strictly positive suboptimality gap can significantly improve the regret. While gap-dependent regret bounds have been obtained for $Q$-learning with Hoeffding-type bonuses, it remains an open question to establish gap-dependent regret bounds for $Q$-learning using variance estimators in their bonuses and reference-advantage decomposition for variance reduction. We develop a novel error decomposition
framework to prove gap-dependent regret bounds of UCB-Advantage and Q-EarlySettled-Advantage that are logarithmic in $T$ and improve upon existing ones for $Q$-learning algorithms. Moreover, we establish the gap-dependent bound for the policy switching cost of UCB-Advantage and improve that under the worst-case MDPs. To our knowledge, this paper presents the first gap-dependent regret analysis for $Q$-learning using variance estimators and reference-advantage decomposition and also provides the first gap-dependent analysis on policy switching cost for $Q$-learning.

title: MVTokenFlow: High-quality 4D Content Generation using Multiview Token Flow
submission: In this paper, we present MVTokenFlow for high-quality 4D content creation from monocular videos. Recent advancements in generative models such as video diffusion models and multiview diffusion models enable creation of videos or 3D models, but extending these generative models for dynamic 4D content remains challenging because generated content must be spatially and temporally consistent. To address this, MVTokenFlow utilizes a multiview diffusion model to generate multiview images at different timesteps, attaining spatial consistency across viewpoints and enabling reconstruction of a coarse 4D field. MVTokenFlow then regenerates the multiview images using rendered 2D flows as guidance: the 2D flows associate pixels across timesteps and improve temporal consistency by reusing tokens in the regeneration process. The regenerated images are used to refine the coarse 4D field into a more coherent 4D representation. Project page: https://soolab.github.io/MVTokenFlow.

title: Linear SCM Identification in the Presence of Confounders and Gaussian Noise
submission: Noisy linear structural causal models (SCMs) with confounding are known to be identifiable under some classical non-Gaussianity assumptions, and unidentifiable when all latent and noise variables are Gaussian. The intermediary case where some variables are Gaussian has been less clear, and here we provide a set of identifiability statements. We show that, in the presence of Gaussian noise, a linear SCM is uniquely identifiable provided that (i) the number of confounders is at most the number of observed variables, (ii) the confounders lack any Gaussian component, and (iii) the causal structure of the SCM is known. If the causal graph is not given, the model becomes finitely identifiable: it belongs to a set of at most n! linear SCMs, where n is the number of observed variables, and the confounders in all these n! SCMs share the same joint PDF, which we derive analytically. For the extreme case where both noise and confounders are Gaussian, we revisit existing counterexamples to unidentifiability and show that any SCM with confounders can be represented as an SCM without confounders but with the same joint PDF. The proofs and derivations are detailed in the main text.

title: Framer: Interactive Frame Interpolation
submission: We propose Framer for interactive frame interpolation, targeting smoothly transitioning frames between two images as per user creativity. Concretely, besides taking the start and end frames as inputs, our approach supports customizing the transition by tailoring the trajectory of selected keypoints. Such a design has two benefits. First, incorporating human interaction mitigates issues arising from numerous possible transformations between images, enabling finer control of local motions. Second, as the most basic form of interaction, keypoints help establish correspondences across frames, improving handling of challenging cases (e.g., objects in the start and end frames differing in shape or style). Our system also offers an “autopilot” mode: a module estimates keypoints and refines their trajectory automatically to simplify practical use. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the appealing performance of Framer on applications such as image morphing, time-lapse generation, and cartoon interpolation. The code, model, and interface are available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/Framer.

title: LucidPPN: Unambiguous Prototypical Parts Network for User-centric Interpretable Computer Vision
submission: Prototypical parts networks combine deep learning with the explainability of case-based reasoning to make interpretable decisions. They follow the "this looks like that" reasoning, representing each prototypical part with patches from training images. However, a single image patch contains multiple visual features — color, shape, and texture — making it hard for users to know which feature the model relies on. To reduce this ambiguity, we introduce the Lucid Prototypical Parts Network (LucidPPN), a prototypical parts network that separates color prototypes from other visual features. Our approach uses two reasoning branches: one for non-color visual features operating on grayscale images, and another that focuses only on color. This separation clarifies whether decisions stem from color, shape, or texture, and identifies prototypical parts corresponding to semantic object parts, which can make class comparisons more intuitive (for example, belly color differences between bird species). We argue the two branches are complementary and that LucidPPN yields less ambiguous prototypes that improve user understanding.

title: MindSearch: Mimicking Human Minds Elicits Deep AI Searcher
submission: Information seeking and integration are complex cognitive tasks that consume substantial time and effort. Motivated by human problem solving, we introduce MindSearch, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that mimics aspects of human query decomposition and iterative search. A WebPlanner incrementally constructs a dynamic graph of atomic sub-questions, while a WebSearcher handles retrieval for each sub-question using hierarchical strategies. The agents interact to grow and refine the graph and to collect relevant passages from many web pages. The multi-agent design permits parallel seeking and aggregation from larger collections of pages than single-pass retrieval, and in preliminary evaluations it yields improvements in response depth and breadth on both closed- and open-domain QA. Results are preliminary and scoped: we report modest gains under limited conditions and discuss where the approach appears most useful and where further evaluation against stronger baselines is needed.

title: An Efficient Tester-Learner for Halfspaces
submission: We study learning halfspaces in the testable learning model of Rubinfeld and Vasilyan, where a learner must certify near-optimal accuracy whenever the training set passes an associated test. Focusing on Gaussian-like covariates and label noise regimes such as Massart or adversarial noise, we give an efficient tester-learner that integrates label-aware tests with moment-matching checks. Our approach builds on moment-based distribution testing and adapts recent SGD-based strategies for noisy halfspace learning. A key technical ingredient is a set of new label-dependent tests that complement empirical moment verification and make it possible to run a testable variant of existing algorithms for noisy halfspaces. We provide algorithmic descriptions and sketches of analysis, and outline how the tests can be implemented in polynomial time. Empirical evaluation and tight numerical guarantees are left for future work.

title: Efficient Low-Bit Quantization with Adaptive Scales for Multi-Task Co-Training
submission: Co-training can enable parameter-efficient multi-task models, but its interaction with quantization-aware training (QAT) is not well explored. We find that naively applying co-training to existing QAT methods leads to notable degradation, largely due to mismatched activation quantization scales across tasks. To address this, we propose Task-Specific Scales Quantization for Multi-Task Co-Training (TSQ-MTC). TSQ-MTC incorporates a task-specific learnable multi-scale activation quantizer (TLMAQ) to enrich shared features for different tasks, and introduces a structure-based layer-by-layer distillation (SLLD) to mitigate information distortion in deeper Transformer layers. These components together improve representational transfer under low-bit constraints. We evaluate TSQ-MTC in two co-training settings and find it effective and versatile. In one case we obtain a 4-bit quantized visual foundation model based on IPT that retains PSNR comparable to the full-precision model while providing about 7.99x compression for 4x super-resolution on Set5.

title: Zero-Shot Natural Language Explanations
submission: Natural Language Explanations (NLEs) aim to interpret a model’s decisions via textual sentences. Current NLEs are often unfaithful because a separate textual decoder is trained on annotated explanations, which can reflect annotator preferences more than the model’s internal reasoning. We take a first step toward generating more faithful NLEs for arbitrary visual classifiers without any explanation training data. Our approach models the relationship between class embeddings from a classifier and their class names via a lightweight MLP trained in seconds. After training, we map arbitrary text into the classifier space and measure its association with visual features to produce zero-shot explanations. We evaluate the approach across 38 vision models (CNNs and Transformers) and observe that it can produce plausible, class-aligned explanations while also enabling zero-shot classification and concept discovery. The results are preliminary and point to potential directions for faithful, training-free NLEs.

title: BarLeRIa: An Efficient Tuning Framework for Referring Image Segmentation
submission: Pre-training followed by full fine-tuning has gradually been substituted by Parameter-Efficient Tuning (PET) in the field of computer vision. PET has gained popularity, especially in the context of large-scale models, due to its ability to reduce transfer learning costs and conserve hardware resources. There has been extensive work on adapters, LoRA-style updates, and other PET variants across recognition benchmarks, and a growing body of literature focuses on efficiency, scalability and multi-modal alignment. However, existing PET approaches primarily focus on recognition tasks and typically support uni-modal optimization, while neglecting dense prediction tasks and vision–language interactions. To address this limitation, we propose a novel PET framework called Bi-directional Intertwined Vision Language Efficient Tuning for Referring Image Segmentation (BarLeRIa), which leverages bi-directional intertwined vision language adapters to fully exploit frozen pre-trained models' potential in cross-modal dense prediction tasks. In BarLeRIa, two different tuning modules are employed for efficient attention, one for global and the other for local, along with an intertwined vision–language tuning module for efficient modal fusion. Extensive experiments on RIS benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of BarLeRIa over prior PET methods, achieving an average improvement of 5.6%. The code is available at https://github.com/NastrondAd/BarLeRIa.

title: DexMove: Learning Tactile-Guided Non-Prehensile Manipulation with Dexterous Hands
submission: Non-prehensile manipulation with dexterous, multi-fingered hands is a promising alternative to pick-and-place, but learning such skills has been limited by the absence of large, contact-aware datasets and wrist–finger control policies. We present DexMove, a tactile-guided non-prehensile manipulation framework for dexterous hands that combines a scalable simulation pipeline for physically plausible wrist–finger trajectories with a wearable device that records multi-finger contact from human demonstrations using vision-based tactile sensors. From these data we train a flow-based policy to produce synergistic wrist–finger control for real-time non-prehensile manipulation of diverse tabletop objects. In real-world trials the method shows substantially better performance than simple baselines and demonstrates generalization to language-conditioned, longer-horizon tasks such as object sorting and desktop tidying. We include implementation details, dataset descriptions, and analysis of failure modes to facilitate reproduction.

title: Flash-Mono: Feed-Forward Accelerated Gaussian Splatting Monocular SLAM
submission: Monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM faces limitations in time efficiency, geometric accuracy, and multi-view consistency, largely due to time-consuming train-from-scratch optimization and inconsistent single-frame geometry priors. We advocate a feed-forward paradigm that leverages multi-frame context to predict Gaussian attributes directly. Flash-Mono comprises a recurrent feed-forward frontend that aggregates multi-frame visual features into a hidden state via cross-attention, a 2D Gaussian Splatting mapping backend, and a hidden-state-based loop-closure module. The frontend jointly predicts camera poses and per-pixel Gaussian properties, allowing the method to avoid per-frame optimization and achieve a substantial speedup while maintaining high-quality rendering. The recurrent hidden states also serve as compact submap descriptors to enable efficient loop closure with global Sim(3) optimization to mitigate drift. We report strong improvements in tracking and mapping quality in our evaluations, though direct comparisons to a wide range of baselines are limited in this version.

title: SiNGER: A Clearer Voice Distills Vision Transformers Further
submission: Vision transformers are prevalent as backbones for vision foundation models but tend to produce high-norm artifacts that hurt representation quality. When knowledge distillation transfers features from teacher to student, these high-norm artifacts can dominate the objective so students overfit to artifacts and underweight informative signals, reducing the benefits of larger teachers. Prior work attempted artifact removal but faced a trade-off between suppression and preserving teacher signals. We propose Singular Nullspace-Guided Energy Reallocation (SiNGER), a distillation framework that suppresses artifacts while preserving informative signals via principled teacher feature refinement. SiNGER uses a nullspace-guided perturbation to retain information while attenuating artifacts, implemented efficiently with a LoRA-style adapter. Experiments across downstream tasks show consistent improvements with SiNGER, though gains are modest in some settings and depend on student capacity. We include analyses of representation clarity and interpretability to better understand where SiNGER helps and where limitations remain.

title: Towards Multimodal Data-Driven Scientific Discovery Powered by LLM Agents
submission: Recent advances in large language models have enabled agents that aim to automate scientific discovery by interpreting data, generating analysis pipelines, and executing them with computational tools. We introduce MoSciBench, a benchmark for multimodal scientific discovery constructed from peer-reviewed studies through a four-stage pipeline. We evaluate several representative agent frameworks across LLM families and observe that multimodal discovery poses substantial challenges, largely driven by cross-modal alignment difficulties. Lightweight workflow scaffolding appears to help in some cases. We release the benchmark and evaluation framework as a practical resource for future work, though further validation and broader community use will determine its ultimate impact.

title: PASER: Post-Training Data Selection for Efficient Pruned Large Language Model Recovery
submission: Model pruning is a common way to compress large language models, but recovery of capabilities after pruning remains challenging and costly. We introduce PASER, a post-training data selection method for efficient recovery of pruned large language models. PASER uses manifold learning and spectral clustering to group candidate recovery instructions in semantic space, uncovering capability-specific clusters. We also include a filtering step to remove potentially conflicting or irrelevant recovery data. Extensive experiments show PASER outperforms conventional baselines while using a small fraction of post-training data. Code is provided in the anonymous repository.

title: DUET: Distilled LLM Unlearning from an Efficiently Contextualized Teacher
submission: LLM unlearning is a technique to remove the impacts of undesirable knowledge from the model without retraining from scratch, which is indispensable towards trustworthy AI. Existing unlearning methods face significant limitations: conventional tuning-based unlearning is computationally heavy and prone to catastrophic forgetting, while in-contextualized unlearning is lightweight but vulnerable to prompt removal or reverse engineering attacks. In response, we propose Distilled Unlearning from an Efficient Teacher (DUET), a distillation-based unlearning method that combines the merits of these two lines of work. DUET learns a student to imitate a prompt-steered teacher that refuses undesirable knowledge generation while preserving general domain knowledge. We report that DUET yields near-complete removal of targeted knowledge with no observable utility loss in held-out tasks. Extensive evaluations on standard benchmarks across a range of scenarios support these qualitative findings and indicate strong data efficiency for DUET.

title: Bayesian Post Training Enhancement of Regression Models with Calibrated Rankings
submission: Accurate regression models are essential for scientific discovery, yet high-quality numeric labels are scarce and expensive. Rankings, particularly pairwise, are often easier to obtain from experts or AI judges. We introduce RankRefine++, a plug-and-play method that improves a base regressor's prediction for a query by leveraging pairwise rankings between the query and reference items with known labels. RankRefine++ performs a Bayesian update combining a Gaussian likelihood from the regressor with the Bradley–Terry likelihood from the ranker, yielding a log-concave posterior with a unique maximum and fast Newton updates. We show that prior methods fall within our framework and identify a failure mode: Bradley–Terry likelihoods can suffer from scale mismatch and curvature dominance with many reference items. From this analysis we propose a calibration to adjust the information from rankings. Empirically, RankRefine++ provides notable improvements on several datasets when realistic rankers are used, though gains vary by setting.

title: OpenPros: A Large-Scale Dataset for Limited View Prostate Ultrasound Computed Tomography
submission: Prostate cancer is one of the most common and lethal cancers among men, making its early detection critically important. Ultrasound computed tomography (USCT) has emerged as an accessible and cost-effective method that reconstructs quantitative tissue parameters, which can serve as potential biomarkers for malignancy. Simulations are conducted under clinically realistic configurations using advanced finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) and Runge-Kutta acoustic wave solvers, both provided as open-source components. Through comprehensive benchmarking, we find that deep learning methods dramatically outperform traditional physics-based algorithms in inference efficiency and reconstruction accuracy, achieving near-clinical quality reconstructions and enabling immediate downstream clinical workflows. By publicly releasing OpenPros, we provide the community with a rigorous benchmark that not only enables fair method comparison but also accelerates translation to clinical deployment. The dataset is publicly accessible at https://open-pros.github.io/.

title: Training Dynamics Impact Post-Training Quantization Robustness
submission: Post-training quantization is widely used for deploying large language models, yet the relationship between training dynamics and quantization robustness is not fully understood. We analyze quantization degradation across open-source training trajectories up to 32B parameters and 15T tokens to examine how training hyperparameters influence quantization errors. A key observation is that, after learning rates decay, validation loss and quantization error tend to diverge, a pattern that appears largely independent of dataset scale. To explore interventions, we train controlled models up to 100B tokens and investigate how specific hyperparameter choices modulate quantization robustness. The manuscript documents these training runs, observed correlations, and a set of candidate interventions, though the overarching objective—whether to optimize for minimal quantization error, maximal accuracy, or deployment trade-offs—is discussed in a somewhat open-ended way to encourage follow-up work.

title: G4Splat: Geometry-Guided Gaussian Splatting with Generative Prior
submission: Generative priors from diffusion models have improved 3D scene reconstruction, but methods still struggle with weak geometric supervision and multi-view inconsistencies. We argue accurate geometry is a prerequisite for exploiting generative priors effectively. Our method derives metric-scale depth maps by leveraging planar structures to provide reliable supervision in both observed and unobserved regions. We incorporate geometry guidance through the pipeline to improve visibility masks, guide novel-view selection, and enhance consistency when inpainting with video diffusion models. Experiments on Replica, ScanNet++, DeepBlending, and Mip-NeRF 360 show consistent improvements over baselines in geometry and appearance reconstruction, especially for unobserved regions. Our approach naturally supports single-view inputs and unposed videos, generalizing across indoor and outdoor scenes. The project page includes code and additional qualitative results.

title: IDEAL: Data Equilibrium Adaptation for Multi-Capability Language Model Alignment
submission: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance after Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) on diverse instructional corpora. When training on multiple capabilities, the mixture dataset composition, governed by different domain volumes, strongly affects the final model. Rather than focus solely on data selection quality, we study how the compositional quantity of mixture SFT datasets relates to emergent capabilities. Given a high-quality multi-domain dataset, it is important to understand each domain’s impact on overall capabilities for preparing SFT data. We introduce IDEAL, a data equilibrium adaptation framework that optimizes domain volumes within mixture SFT via an iterative, gradient-based procedure that adjusts domain-specific data volumes according to downstream performance impact. IDEAL refines the data mix to yield a more balanced model and, across capability suites, shows improvement over uniform allocation by roughly seven percent in our multi-task evaluation. The framework is practical and can be integrated into existing SFT pipelines, though some implementation details can be tuned depending on datasets.

title: Calibrated Information Bottleneck for Trusted Multi-modal Clustering
submission: Information Bottleneck (IB) Theory is valued for learning compact, effective data representations and has promise for multi-modal clustering by removing redundancy while preserving discriminative information. Existing IB-based multi-modal clustering methods suffer from low-quality pseudo-labels and over-reliance on accurate mutual information estimation, which is challenging, and noisy pseudo-labels can yield overconfident clustering. We propose a Calibrated Information Bottleneck (CLIB) framework intended to produce more accurate and trustworthy clustering. The high-level idea is to use multiple heads to calibrate distortions introduced by biased MI estimation and to construct more reliable targets for IB from multiple modalities. We also allude to a dynamic pseudo-label selection strategy motivated by information redundancy theory to improve stability. Experimental validation, specific architectural details, training procedures, and quantitative results are not provided in this abstract and are deferred to the main text.

title: Latent Visual Reasoning
submission: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved notable gains in various tasks by incorporating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in language spaces. Recent work extends this direction by leveraging external tools for visual editing, thereby enhancing the visual signal along the reasoning trajectories. Nevertheless, these approaches remain fundamentally constrained: reasoning is still confined to the language space, with visual information treated as static preconditions. We introduce Latent Visual Reasoning (LVR), a new paradigm that enables autoregressive reasoning directly in the visual embedding space. A visual encoder first projects images into visual tokens within a joint semantic space shared with the language model. The language model is then trained to generate latent states that reconstruct key visual tokens critical for answering the query, constituting the process of latent visual reasoning. By interleaving LVR with standard text generation, our model achieves substantial gains on perception-intensive visual question answering tasks. In addition, we adapt the GRPO algorithm to conduct reinforcement learning on latent reasoning, further balancing LVR and textual generation.  We show that LVR substantially improves fine-grained visual understanding and perception, achieving 71.67\% on MMVP compared to 66.67\% with Qwen2.5-VL. Code base and model weights will be released later.

title: Frozen Policy Iteration: Computationally Efficient RL under Linear $Q^{\pi}$ Realizability for Deterministic Dynamics
submission:
We study computationally and statistically efficient reinforcement learning under the linear $Q^{\pi}$ realizability assumption, where any policy's $Q$-function is linear in a given state-action feature representation. title: Entropic Confinement and Mode Connectivity in Overparameterized Neural Networks
submission: Modern neural networks exhibit a striking property: basins of attraction in the loss landscape are often connected by low-loss paths, yet optimization dynamics generally remain confined to a single convex basin and rarely explore intermediate points. We resolve this paradox by identifying entropic barriers arising from the interplay between curvature variations along these paths and noise in optimization dynamics. Empirically, we find that curvature systematically rises away from minima, producing effective forces that bias noisy dynamics back toward the endpoints — even when the loss remains nearly flat. These barriers persist longer than energetic barriers, shaping the late-time localization of solutions in parameter space. Our results highlight the role of curvature-induced entropic forces in governing both connectivity and confinement in deep learning landscapes.

title: From Spatial to Actions: Grounding Vision-Language-Action Model in Spatial Foundation Priors
submission: Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models act in 3D real-world settings but are typically built on 2D encoders, leaving a spatial reasoning gap that limits generalization and adaptability. Recent 3D integration methods either require specialized sensors and transfer poorly, or they inject weak cues that lack geometry and degrade alignment. We introduce FALCON (From Spatial to Action), a paradigm that injects rich 3D spatial tokens into the action head by leveraging spatial foundation models to provide geometric priors from RGB alone. These design choices aim to address spatial representation, modality transferability, and alignment. title: Aligning Deep Implicit Preferences by Learning to Reason Defensively
submission: Personalized alignment is crucial for enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to engage effectively in user-centric interactions. Prior work has explored reward modeling and preference elicitation, and there are substantial open challenges in inferring users' unstated goals, semantic context, and risk tolerances. This paper emphasizes that existing pipelines often lack depth in preference inference and defensive reasoning, leading to superficial or brittle responses. To bridge this cognitive gap we propose Critique-Driven Reasoning Alignment (CDRA). We also introduce the DeepPref benchmark, a curated collection of 3000 preference-query pairs across 20 topics, built by simulating a multi-faceted cognitive council that annotates critique-based reasoning chains to deconstruct semantics and highlight latent risks. Complementing DeepPref, we present the Personalized Generative Process Reward Model (Pers-GenPRM), which frames reward modeling as a personalized reasoning task that generates critique chains to evaluate candidate responses before issuing a score. Finally, these components are integrated into a process-level online policy alignment algorithm that uses both numerical and natural language feedback. We provide dataset release details and discuss directions for applying CDRA to practical personalization problems.

title: Evoking User Memory: Personalizing LLM via Recollection-Familiarity Adaptive Retrieval
submission: Personalized LLMs require efficient memory retrieval to incorporate user histories without overwhelming the model. Drawing on the dual-process view from cognitive science, we propose RF-Mem, a Recollection–Familiarity dual-path retriever that adaptively switches between fast familiarity-based recognition and deliberate recollection-style reconstruction. Familiarity is measured via mean similarity and entropy: high-familiarity cases use direct top-K Familiarity retrieval, while low-familiarity cases trigger a Recollection path that clusters candidate memories and applies an α-mix with the query to iteratively expand evidence in embedding space. This design simulates human-like retrieval, avoids feeding full context into the model, and adapts retrieval effort to uncertainty. RF-Mem yields consistent, often large gains in personalization metrics across three benchmarks and multiple corpus scales—outperforming one-shot retrieval and full-context approaches and reducing latency and budget needs substantially. We provide algorithmic details, implementation notes, and pointers to our code in the reproducibility statement.

title: Neural Posterior Estimation with Latent Basis Expansions
submission: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is an amortized, likelihood-free variational inference approach that approximates posterior projections. Prior NPE variational families are either simple and interpretable (e.g., Gaussian) or flexible and black-box (e.g., normalizing flows). We propose parameterizing variational families via latent basis expansions: the log density is expressed as a linear combination of latent basis functions (LBFs) which may be fixed or adapted to the problem. This yields a family that aims to balance interpretability and flexibility while remaining tractable for NPE's marginalization. Training and inference are computationally efficient for high-dimensional latent spaces when only low-dimensional projections are needed. In experiments across several inference tasks, the LBF-based family often matches or exceeds baselines in approximating posterior projections, and we discuss optimization considerations and limitations. Future work will clarify the scope of problems where basis expansions offer clear advantages.

submission: Modeling single-cell gene expression across diverse biological and technical conditions is key to characterizing cellular states and simulating unseen scenarios. We introduce WebArbiter, a reasoning-first WebPRM that frames reward modeling as text generation: it produces structured justifications that conclude with a preference verdict and identify the action most conducive to task completion. We also release WebPRMBench, a benchmark spanning four web environments with high-quality preference annotations. The approach emphasizes interpretable verdicts and action recommendations, though integrating such models into large-scale web agents will require additional robustness work.

title: Towards Better Optimization For Listwise Preference in Diffusion Models
submission: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is effective for aligning text-to-image diffusion models with human preferences. Although Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is adopted for its efficiency and avoidance of explicit reward models, its diffusion-model applications have primarily used pairwise preferences. The precise optimization of listwise preferences remains largely unaddressed. In practice, human feedback often contains implicit ranked information, which can convey more precise preferences. We propose Diffusion-LPO, a framework for Listwise Preference Optimization in diffusion models using listwise data. Given a caption, we aggregate user feedback into a ranked list and derive a listwise extension of the DPO objective under the Plackett–Luce model. Diffusion-LPO enforces consistency across the entire ranking by encouraging each sample to be preferred over lower-ranked alternatives. While we report that Diffusion-LPO empirically outperforms pairwise DPO baselines across several tasks, the exact scope of gains, the specific training regimen, and how generative quality is measured are left high-level; the central contributions are presented in broad terms rather than as detailed, narrowly defined advances.

title: <SO$G_k$>: One LLM Token for Explicit Graph Structural Understanding
submission:
Large language models show great potential in unstructured data understanding, but still face significant challenges with graphs due to their structural hallucination. Existing approaches mainly either verbalize graphs into natural language, which leads to excessive token consumption and scattered attention, or transform graphs into trainable continuous embeddings (i.e., soft prompt), but exhibit severe misalignment with original text tokens. To solve this problem, we propose to incorporate one special token <SO$G_k$> 
to fully represent the \textbf{\underline{S}}tructure \textbf{\underline{O}}f \textbf{\underline{G}}raph
within a unified token space, facilitating explicit topology input and structural information sharing. Specifically, we propose a topology-aware structural tokenizer that maps each graph topology into a highly selective single token. Afterwards, we construct a set of hybrid structure Question-Answering corpora to align new structural tokens with existing text tokens. With this approach, <SO$G_k$> empowers LLMs to understand, generate, and reason in a concise and accurate manner. Extensive experiments on five graph-level benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our method, achieving a performance improvement of 9.9–41.4\% compared to the baselines while exhibiting interpretability and consistency. Furthermore, our method provides a flexible extension to node-level tasks, enabling both global and local structural understanding. The codebase is publicly available\footnote{The code of our project is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SOG-8432}{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SOG-8432}.}.

title: ProofOptimizer: Training Language Models to Simplify Proofs without Human Demonstrations
submission: Neural theorem proving has recently produced extremely long mechanically verified proofs that are hard for humans to read, so proof simplification is a pressing bottleneck. We introduce ProofOptimizer, a language model trained to simplify Lean proofs without requiring human demonstrations. ProofOptimizer is trained via expert iteration and reinforcement learning, using Lean to verify candidate simplifications and derive training signal; at inference time it runs an iterative proof-shortening workflow to progressively reduce proof length. On benchmarks produced by state-of-the-art provers, ProofOptimizer substantially compresses proofs, for example reducing proof length by 87% on miniF2F, 57% on PutnamBench, and 50% on Seed-Prover IMO 2025 proofs, and the simplified proofs also check faster in Lean and can be reused to improve downstream provers.

title: Human Behavior Atlas: Benchmarking Unified Psychological And Social Behavior Understanding
submission: Using intelligent systems to perceive psychological and social behaviors—the underlying affective, cognitive, and pathological states manifesting through observable behaviors and social interactions—remains challenging due to complexity, personalization, and multifaceted variation. Existing single-task datasets and specialized systems miss opportunities for scalability and cross-task transfer. To address this, we curate Human Behavior Atlas, a unified benchmark of diverse behavioral tasks to support foundation models for psychological and social behavior understanding. Human Behavior Atlas comprises over 100,000 samples spanning text, audio, and visual modalities across affective states, cognitive states, pathologies, and social processes. Our unification aims to reduce redundancy and cost, enable scalable multi-task training, and improve generalization across domains. We train three models—Omnisapiens-7B SFT, Omnisapiens-7B BAM, and Omnisapiens-7B RL—and observe improvements on many behavioral tasks, with some transfer benefits to novel datasets when using behavioral descriptors. We note that gains vary by task and that further work is needed to assess ethical and robustness considerations.

title: Teach to Reason Safely: Policy-Guided Safety Tuning for MLRMs
submission: Multimodal Large Reasoning Models (MLRMs) show strong capabilities on complex multimodal tasks, but we observe a trade-off: reasoning-focused models can be more prone to harmful content, degrading safety. We analyze this safety–reasoning trade-off and identify two main mechanisms of safety degradation: (i) visual attention drift, which reduces visual grounding and exacerbates overlooked cross-modal risks; and (ii) unsafe reasoning patterns, including flawed reasoning initiation and chain-of-thought attenuation, which erode safety awareness. To mitigate these issues, we propose Policy-guided Safety Tuning (PST), a two-stage alignment framework. First, Policy-Guided Supervised Fine-Tuning integrates explicit safety policies into reasoning to create a structured foundation for safer decisions. Second, Safety Reasoning Preference Optimization encourages safe, helpful, and informative outputs while reducing oversensitivity and homogenization. Experiments suggest PST can reduce harmful outputs across several multimodal safety benchmarks while maintaining competitive performance on general tasks, though gains vary by dataset and model size.

title: Barriers for Learning in an Evolving World:  Mathematical Understanding of Loss of Plasticity
submission: Deep networks perform well in stationary settings but often encounter loss of plasticity (LoP) in evolving environments. We offer a dynamical-systems perspective that frames LoP as entrapment of gradient dynamics within invariant sub-manifolds of parameter space. Two mechanisms are emphasized: frozen units from activation saturation and cloned-unit manifolds arising from representational redundancy. These mechanisms are argued to interact with common generalization-promoting factors such as low-rank compression, which may paradoxically steer networks into LoP manifolds. We present formal definitions and sketches of why gradient descent becomes constrained in these regions, and we illustrate dynamics with selected simulations. Finally, we outline several architectural interventions that could destabilize these manifolds to restore plasticity. While we motivate connections to continual learning and representation collapse, the precise conditions under which interventions reliably recover plasticity remain to be fully clarified in follow-up work.
