title: Evaluating GFlowNet from partial episodes for stable and flexible policy-based training
submission: Generative Flow Networks learn policies to sample combinatorial candidates by viewing generation as trajectories in directed acyclic graphs. Value-based training aligns with a Q-learning view enforcing flow balance over partial episodes, while policy-based training follows an actor-critic pattern that alternates between estimating policy divergence and updating the policy. A major challenge is reliably estimating divergence under DAG-structured generation. title: Internal Planning in Language Models: Characterizing Horizon and Branch Awareness
submission: How much decoder-only language models engage in planning—organizing intermediate computations for coherent long-range generation—is an important open question. We present a pipeline that compresses hidden states with vector-quantized variational autoencoders into compact summary codes to measure mutual information and probe computational structure. Using these codes, we study planning properties across synthetic grammars, path-finding tasks, and natural language datasets, focusing on planning horizon and the handling of alternative continuations. Our analyses characterize task-dependent planning horizons, preservation of unused correct continuations, and a tendency to draw most on recent computations while earlier blocks remain informative. The framework is broadly applicable for inspecting internal model dynamics.

title: On The Fragility of Benchmark Contamination Detection in Reasoning Models
submission: Leaderboards for large reasoning models (LRMs) have turned evaluation into a competition, incentivizing developers to optimize directly on benchmark suites. A shortcut to achieving higher rankings is to incorporate evaluation benchmarks into the training data, thereby yielding inflated performance, known as benchmark contamination. Despite that numerous contamination detection approaches have been proposed, surprisingly, our studies find that evading contamination detections for LRMs is alarmingly easy. We focus on the two scenarios where contamination may occur in practice: (I) when the base model evolves into LRM via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), we find that contamination during SFT can be originally identified by contamination detection methods. Yet, even a brief Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training can markedly \textbf{conceal contamination signals} that most detection methods rely on. Further empirical experiments and theoretical analysis indicate that Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) style importance sampling and clipping objectives are the root cause of this detection concealment, indicating that \textbf{a broad class of RL methods} may inherently exhibit similar concealment capability; (II) when SFT contamination with CoT is applied to advanced LRMs as the final stage, most contamination detection methods \textbf{perform near random guesses}. Without exposure to non-members, contaminated LRMs would still have more confidence when responding to those unseen samples that share similar distributions to the training set, and thus, evade existing memorization-based detection methods. Together, our findings reveal the unique vulnerability of LRMs evaluations: Model developers could easily contaminate LRMs to achieve inflated leaderboards performance while leaving minimal traces of contamination, thereby strongly undermining the fairness of evaluation and threatening the integrity of public leaderboards. This underscores the urgent need for advanced contamination detection methods and trustworthy evaluation protocols tailored to LRMs.

title: Local Entropy Search over Descent Sequences for Bayesian Optimization
submission: Searching large and complex design spaces for a global optimum can be infeasible and unnecessary. A practical alternative is to iteratively refine the neighborhood of an initial design using local optimization methods such as gradient descent. We propose local entropy search (LES), a Bayesian optimization paradigm that explicitly targets the solutions reachable by the descent sequences of iterative optimizers. The algorithm propagates the posterior belief over the objective through the optimizer, resulting in a probability distribution over descent sequences. It then selects the next evaluation by maximizing mutual information with that distribution, using a combination of analytic entropy calculations and Monte-Carlo sampling of descent sequences. Empirical results on high-complexity synthetic objectives and benchmark problems show that LES achieves strong sample efficiency compared to existing local and global Bayesian optimization methods.

title: DEAS: DEtached value learning with Action Sequence for Scalable Offline RL
submission: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables learning from fixed datasets but struggles with long-horizon sequential decision making. We introduce DEtached value learning with Action Sequence (DEAS), an offline RL framework that leverages temporally extended action sequences for value learning. By using action sequences, DEAS reduces the effective planning horizon and provides richer context than single-step actions. title: AnyBCQ: Hardware Efficient Flexible Binary-Coded Quantization for Multi-Precision LLMs
submission: LLM deployment faces memory and latency bottlenecks, motivating quantization that balances accuracy and efficiency. Recent multi-precision models let a single model run at multiple precisions depending on runtime. To support this, weights are stored as bit-planes, where hardware is more efficient when compute operates on bit-planes and activates only needed precision. We present AnyBCQ, a hardware-friendly multi-precision extension of Binary-Coded Quantization that supports direct bit-plane operations. By representing weights as binary bit-planes with scale factors, AnyBCQ enables bit-plane-level computation and maps to accelerator-friendly, bit-parallel arithmetic. Our progressive precision expansion refines scaling factors while reusing prior binary codes, yielding monotonic accuracy improvements as more bits are enabled. We also co-design a specialized kernel that exploits BCQ structure to support dynamic per-request precision selection with negligible overhead. Experiments on recent LLMs show AnyBCQ narrows accuracy drop in low-bit regimes and achieves significant throughput gains over baselines.

title: SeeDNorm: Self-Rescaled Dynamic Normalization
submission: Normalization layers are essential components in neural networks. In transformers, RMSNorm constrains vectors to a unit hypersphere and then rescales by a learnable coefficient gamma to retain representational capacity. RMSNorm discards input norm information in the forward pass, and a static gamma may not capture the variability of inputs or distributional shifts, which is particularly relevant in zero-shot scenarios for large language models. We propose SeeDNorm, which dynamically adjusts the scaling coefficient based on the input, aiming to preserve input norm information and enable data-dependent self-rescaled normalization. During backpropagation SeeDNorm keeps the property of adjusting gradients by input norm. We analyze training optimization and note potential instabilities, proposing mitigations. We evaluate SeeDNorm across pretraining sizes and vision tasks and report improved performance over RMSNorm, LayerNorm, and some activation-based alternatives, while introducing few parameters and limited overhead.

title: AtC: Aggregate-then-Calibrate for Human-centered Assessment
submission: Human-centered assessment often lacks verifiable ground truth and depends on human judgment. We propose Aggregate-then-Calibrate (AtC), a two-stage framework that combines comparative human judgments with model scores. Stage 1 aggregates heterogeneous judgments into a consensus ranking using a rank-aggregation model that accounts for annotator reliability. Stage 2 calibrates any predictive model's scores by an isotonic projection onto the consensus ordering, aiming to enforce ordinal consistency while preserving model information. We state theoretical claims about efficiency from modeling annotator heterogeneity, risk bounds for isotonic calibration under misspecification, and asymptotic advantages over model-only assessment. Empirically, AtC improves accuracy and robustness on semi-synthetic and real datasets. However, the concrete novelty and broader significance remain modest: AtC is presented as an integration of existing ideas and primarily offers a pragmatic recipe rather than a fundamentally new theory.

title: Beyond URLs: Metadata Diversity and Position for Efficient LLM Pretraining
submission: Incorporating metadata during LLM pretraining has been proposed to accelerate training, but prior work has mainly emphasized URLs as the useful signal. We broaden this view by investigating a wider range of metadata types, finding that other forms—such as fine-grained indicators of document quality—can also accelerate pretraining when prepended. We identify a common theme among effective metadata: they often encode finer-grained information. Beyond prepending, we experiment with metadata appending where predicting metadata is an auxiliary task, and with learnable meta-tokens trained with masked loss to induce latent structure that reflects quality. Using probing analyses, we explore how different metadata signals shape representations. Together, these results are intended to provide practical guidelines for integrating metadata into pretraining. Much of the discussion situates these approaches within existing literature on efficiency and representation, providing extended background and motivation.

title: MATRIX: Mask Track Alignment for Interaction-aware Video Generation
submission: Video DiTs have advanced video generation, yet they still struggle to model multi-instance or subject-object interactions. To study how these models internally represent interactions, we curate MATRIX-11K, a video dataset with interaction-aware captions and multi-instance mask tracks. Using this dataset, we conduct an analysis that formalizes two perspectives of video DiTs: semantic grounding, via video-to-text attention, which evaluates whether noun and verb tokens capture instances and their relations; and semantic propagation, via video-to-video attention, which assesses whether instance bindings persist across frames. We find both effects concentrate in a small subset of interaction-dominant layers. Motivated by this, we introduce MATRIX, a regularization that aligns attention in selected layers of video DiTs with multi-instance mask tracks from MATRIX-11K, which we show improves grounding and propagation. We further propose InterGenEval, an evaluation protocol for interaction-aware video generation. In experiments, MATRIX reduces drift and hallucination and we provide ablations that examine design choices.

title: Decoding Open-Ended Information Seeking Goals from Eye Movements in Reading
submission: When reading, people often pursue specific information in a text—experimental design details, whether a method actually works, or other text-specific curiosities. More broadly, readers approach texts with many possible goals that shape their eye-movement behavior. In this work we ask whether open-ended reading goals can be decoded solely from eye movements. To study this, we introduce goal decoding tasks and evaluation frameworks using large-scale English eye-tracking data with many text-specific information-seeking tasks and annotations of task-critical information. We develop and compare several discriminative and generative multimodal text-and-gaze LLMs. Our experiments show some success at selecting the correct goal among options and some progress toward free-form reconstruction of goal formulations. We also attempt to relate model performance to interpretable aspects of gaze behavior. Overall, the contributions are exploratory: we sketch frameworks, evaluate models, and point to possible applications in education and assistive tech, while leaving many concrete objectives and operational definitions deliberately open.

title: LingoLoop Attack: Trapping MLLMs via Linguistic Context and State Entrapment into Endless Loops
submission: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can be attacked by inducing excessive output, causing resource exhaustion. Prior energy-latency attacks broadly shift output distributions away from EOS, but they overlook token-level POS influences on EOS and sentence-level structural patterns on output counts. To address this, we propose LingoLoop, an attack to induce verbose and repetitive sequences. First, we show that a token's POS tag affects EOS likelihood and introduce a POS-Aware Delay Mechanism that adjusts attention to postpone EOS generation. Second, we identify that constraining output diversity sustains loops and introduce a Generative Path Pruning Mechanism that limits hidden-state magnitudes to encourage repetition. We evaluate on several contemporary MLLMs and find LingoLoop effectively causes prolonged generation and increased energy usage, though full quantitative comparisons and baseline ablations are not provided in this version. These findings highlight vulnerabilities in MLLMs' generative behavior.

submission: Reward models play a central role in post-training of language models by turning preference data into a training target across instruction following, reasoning, and safety tasks. This paper introduces RewardBench 2, a new multi-skill reward modeling benchmark built to provide more challenging accuracy-based evaluation. Compared to RewardBench, models score about 20 points lower on average on RewardBench 2, and the benchmark uses newly collected human prompts rather than reusing prompts from downstream tasks. We describe the benchmark construction process and report how existing models perform on it. While we aim to study correlations between benchmark accuracy and downstream utility, our empirical analysis produces mixed signals: in some settings higher RewardBench 2 accuracy aligns with downstream gains, whereas in others it does not reliably predict improvements for inference-time scaling or RLHF training. We discuss implications for reward model evaluation and future directions.

We report qualitative analyses that suggest different RA choices influence training dynamics and stability, and we offer discussion on why certain RA families may yield more stable behavior.

submission: Quantization methods such as BitsAndBytes, AWQ, and GPTQ are widely used to deploy large language models but can degrade accuracy in low-bit regimes. Low-rank corrections have been proposed to mitigate this, yet existing approaches restore layers individually and insert correction modules into every decoder block, increasing latency and memory. We propose GlowQ, a group-shared low-rank approximation that caches a single shared right factor per input-sharing group and restores only groups or layers that yield the highest benefit. GlowQ computes a high-precision projection once per input-sharing group and reuses it across modules, reducing parameter and memory overhead while preserving expressivity. We also introduce GlowQ-S, a selective variant that applies the cached module where it provides the largest benefit. The abstract focuses on high-level design and motivation; methodological details, optimization choices, and comprehensive empirical results are omitted here and provided in the paper.

title: Geometric-Mean Policy Optimization
submission: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced reasoning in large language models by optimizing the arithmetic mean of token-level rewards. However, GRPO can suffer unstable policy updates when tokens produce outlier importance-weighted rewards, which appear as extreme importance sampling ratios during training. We propose Geometric-Mean Policy Optimization (GMPO) to improve GRPO stability by suppressing token reward outliers: simply replace GRPO's arithmetic mean with the geometric mean of token-level rewards, since the latter is less sensitive to outliers. GMPO is plug-and-play. Analysis shows that both GMPO and GRPO are weighted forms of the policy gradient, while GMPO enjoys purportedly more stable weights. This, we argue, should benefit optimization. Experiments on several math reasoning benchmarks are reported; the connection between the stability analysis and empirical gains, however, is not fully consistent across tasks, and some results do not clearly corroborate the theoretical claims.

title: Medical thinking with multiple images
submission: Large language models perform well on many medical QA benchmarks, but real clinical reasoning is harder because diagnosis often requires integrating evidence across multiple images rather than interpreting a single view. We introduce MedThinkVQA, an expert-annotated benchmark for thinking with multiple images in which models must interpret each image, combine cross-view evidence, and solve diagnostic questions under intermediate supervision and step-level evaluation. The dataset contains 10,067 cases, including 720 test cases, with an average of 6.68 images per case, substantially denser than prior work. On the test set, state-of-the-art models still achieve only modest accuracy, revealing a fundamental failure mode: current VLMs cannot reliably extract, align, and compose evidence across views. Further analysis shows that adding expert single-image cues and integrating cross-image evidence helps, whereas relying on models’ self-generated intermediates harms performance. Step-level breakdown attributes most errors to image reading and cross-view integration. Together, these results show that the central, irreducible barrier to clinical-grade performance is poor grounded multi-image reasoning, and overcoming it requires fundamentally new grounding and alignment mechanisms.

title: HiFo-Prompt: Prompting with Hindsight and Foresight for LLM-based Automatic Heuristic Design
submission: This paper investigates the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in Automated Heuristic Design (AHD), where their integration into evolutionary frameworks reveals a significant gap in global control and long-term learning. We propose the Hindsight-Foresight Prompt (HiFo-Prompt), a novel framework for LLM-based AHD designed to overcome these limitations through two synergistic strategies: Foresight and Hindsight. Foresight acts as a high-level meta-controller, monitoring population dynamics to switch the global search between exploration and exploitation explicitly. Hindsight builds a persistent knowledge base by distilling successful design principles from past generations, making this knowledge reusable. This dual mechanism ensures the LLM is an active reasoner guided by a global plan while improving from cumulative experience. Empirical results demonstrate HiFo-Prompt dramatically outperforms state-of-the-art AHD methods, often discovering near-optimal heuristics and reducing query complexity by up to 10x in our suites. Our code is available at https://github.com/Challenger-XJTU/HiFo-Prompt.

title: Generative Human Geometry Distribution
submission:
Realistic human geometry generation is an important yet challenging task, requiring both the preservation of fine clothing details and the accurate modeling of clothing-body interactions. To tackle this challenge, we build upon Geometry distributions—a recently proposed representation that can model a single human geometry with high fidelity using a flow matching model. However, extending a single-geometry distribution to a dataset is non-trivial and inefficient for large-scale learning. To address this, we propose a new geometry distribution model by two key techniques: (1) encoding distributions as 2D feature maps rather than network parameters, and (2) using SMPL models as the domain instead of Gaussian and refining the associated flow velocity field. We then design a generative framework adopting a two-staged training paradigm analogous to state-of-the-art image and 3D generative models.
In the first stage, we compress geometry distributions into a latent space using a diffusion flow model; the second stage trains another flow model on this latent space. 
We validate our approach on two key tasks: pose-conditioned random avatar generation and avatar-consistent novel pose synthesis.
Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 57% improvement in geometry quality.

title: Imitating the Truth: Attention-aware Truth-Guided Enhancement for Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision-Language Models
submission: Large Vision-Language Models achieve impressive multimodal reasoning yet still hallucinate, producing content inconsistent with visual evidence. Many mitigation methods rely on auxiliary modules or coarse decoding-time adjustments and do not attend to the fine-grained dynamics that distinguish truthful tokens from hallucinated ones. We propose AGE (Attention-aware Truth-Guided Enhancement), a training-free framework that performs layer-wise interventions guided by attention behaviors associated with real tokens. Our analysis indicates that different token types exhibit distinct attention dynamics, and AGE applies simple interventions to encourage truth-like attention patterns. The approach is lightweight and can be applied to existing LVLMs without retraining. Overall, AGE illustrates a principle—imitating truth-grounded attention dynamics—that can reduce hallucinations and improve reliability of multimodal outputs.

title: Efficient Differentiable Contact Model with Long-range Influence
submission: Differentiable physics is increasingly used in model-predictive control, design optimization, and neural PDE solvers, but derivative information from differentiable simulators can be erratic or vanish, impeding gradient-based optimization. We argue that this problematic gradient behavior is linked to contact model design and propose a set of desirable properties for contact models to produce more stable derivatives. Building on these properties, we present a practical contact model for differentiable rigid-body simulation that aims to satisfy the proposed criteria while remaining computationally efficient. Empirical illustrations suggest that with such a contact model, gradient-based methods can uncover contact-rich control strategies from simple initializations across locomotion and manipulation tasks. We discuss practical trade-offs and potential integration paths into existing differentiable simulation toolchains.

submission: Hierarchical robot systems often separate high-level planners from low-level policies, enabling planners to be trained from action-free data (e.g., videos) while leaving grounding to policies. Our framework also supports policy acquisition from planners trained on cross-embodiment video data, suggesting potential for scalable robot learning. While specific algorithmic choices and ablations are left to the main text, the overall approach emphasizes online hindsight relabeling as a practical route to better grounding.

diction models, with a focus on MOIRAI (Woo et al., 2024). We study its ap-
proximation and generalization capabilities. First, we demonstrate that there exist
transformers that fit an autoregressive model on input univariate time series via
gradient descent. We then analyze MOIRAI, one of the state-of-the-art multivariate
time series prediction models capable of modeling arbitrary number of covariates.

with an arbitrary number of covariates, offering insights into its design and em-
pirical success. For generalization, we establish learning bounds for pretraining
when the data satisfies Dobrushin’s condition. Experiments support our theoretical
findings, highlighting the efficacy of using transformers for time series forecasting.

title: FAPO: Flawed-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient and Reliable Reasoning
submission: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) aims to improve reasoning in large language models by using rollouts with correct answers as optimization signals. However, many rollouts contain flawed patterns such as answer-guessing and jump-in-reasoning, which can be treated as positive signals and thus distort policy learning. In this work we study flawed-positive rollouts and present an approach, FAPO, that introduces a penalty for such rollouts so policies can benefit from early shortcuts while gradually emphasizing reliable reasoning. We also discuss using a generative reward model to detect process-level errors and localize reasoning flaws. Overall, we advocate for methods that account for flawed signals during policy optimization to improve stability and reasoning quality without increasing token budgets.

title: Mitigating Mismatch within Reference-based Preference Optimization
submission: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used for offline preference alignment, but its reliance on a reference policy creates tension. DPO regularizes updates relative to a reference, which stabilizes training but can cause problems on pessimistic pairs where the reference prefers the rejected response. For those pairs, DPO reduces the gradient once the policy margin exceeds the reference margin, even if the policy is still incorrect; we call this premature satisfaction. HyPO thus strengthens per-example learning signals on pessimistic pairs while keeping DPO’s form and cost. Empirically we observe improvements in inference-aligned metrics and pairwise win rates across alignment tasks. These findings suggest conditional debiasing of the reference can help, though broader evaluation and ablations against diverse baselines are left for future work.

title: QuaMo: Quaternion Motions for Vision-based 3D Human Kinematics Capture
submission: Vision-based 3D human motion capture from videos remains challenging due to temporal inconsistency that causes implausible, jittery motion. Kinematics-based capture estimates temporal transitions between poses rather than independent frames, but many existing kinematics methods rely on Euler angles, which suffer from discontinuities. We propose QuaMo, a Quaternion Motions formulation that uses quaternion differential equations (QDE) for human kinematics capture. QuaMo employs a state-space model with quaternion states and a QDE describing quaternion velocity; angular accelerations are produced by a meta-PD controller with an acceleration enhancement that adaptively regulates control signals during rapid pose changes. The QDE is solved under quaternion geometric constraints to promote continuity. Experiments on Human3.6M, Fit3D, SportsPose and a subset of AIST show QuaMo produces more continuous estimations with fewer implausible artifacts than comparable methods, and we provide code at https://github.com/cuongle1206/QuaMo for reproducibility. Results indicate promising gains, though further evaluation across more challenging scenarios is warranted.

title: Exploring the Design Space of Transition Matching
submission: Transition Matching (TM) generalizes diffusion, flow-matching, and continuous-state autoregressive models by using an internal generative model to implement expressive transition steps. To keep TM tractable, a large backbone and a smaller head module are used to execute transitions efficiently. We present a large-scale investigation into head design for time-continuous bidirectional TM, reporting comprehensive ablations across many head variants and sampler choices. We trained numerous text-to-image models and evaluated generation quality, training, and inference efficiency, finding that an MLP head with a particular time weighting and a high-frequency sampler yields top rankings across metrics, while a Transformer head with sequence scaling and low-frequency sampling excels at aesthetics. We summarize the design aspects likely to provide quality and efficiency gains and note which choices are unlikely to help further.

title: Plan and Budget: Effective and Efficient Test-Time Scaling on Reasoning Large Language Models
submission: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in complex reasoning tasks, but their inference remains computationally inefficient. We observe a common failure mode in many prevalent LLMs, overthinking, where models generate verbose and tangential reasoning traces even for simple queries. Recent work has tried to mitigate this by enforcing fixed token budgets; however, this can lead to underthinking, especially on harder problems. To formalize this inefficiency, we develop BAM (Budget Allocation Model), which models reasoning as a sequence of sub-questions with varying uncertainty, and introduce the E3 metric to capture the trade-off between correctness and computation efficiency. Building on theoretical results from BAM, we propose Plan-and-Budget, a model-agnostic, test-time framework that decomposes complex queries into sub-questions and allocates token budgets based on estimated complexity using adaptive scheduling. Unexpectedly, while the framework omits a concrete estimator specification, we report substantial empirical improvements—up to 70% accuracy gains, 39% token reduction, and 193.8% improvement in E3—demonstrating large efficiency gains without retraining. Code is available at https://github.com/junhongmit/P-and-B.

title: BEP: A Binary Error Propagation Algorithm for Binary Neural Networks Training
submission: Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) reduce computation and memory by constraining weights and activations to binary values, which is attractive for resource-constrained deployment. Training BNNs with gradient-based methods typically relies on surrogate gradients and latent full-precision parameters, losing binary efficiency during optimization. We introduce Binary Error Propagation (BEP), a discrete analog of the backpropagation chain rule that propagates error signals as binary vectors using only bitwise operations. BEP is conceived to support end-to-end binary computations, including backward passes, and is presented as the first principled mechanism for binary error propagation across layers. We validate BEP on multi-layer perceptrons and include preliminary evaluations on recurrent architectures. Results show clear gains on MLP benchmarks; however, RNN experiments are limited and suggest further work is needed to fully realize end-to-end binary training in recurrent settings. The algorithm and code are released to encourage follow-up studies.

title: Never Saddle for Reparameterized Steepest Descent as Mirror Flow
submission: How does the choice of optimization algorithm shape a model’s ability to learn features? To address this question for steepest descent methods --including sign descent, which is closely related to Adam --we introduce steepest mirror flows as a unifying theoretical framework. This framework reveals how optimization geometry governs learning dynamics, implicit bias, and sparsity and it provides two explanations for why Adam and AdamW often outperform SGD in fine-tuning. Focusing on diagonal linear networks and deep diagonal linear reparameterizations (a simplified proxy for attention), we show that steeper descent facilitates both saddle-point escape and feature learning. In contrast, gradient descent requires unrealistically large learning rates to escape saddles, an uncommon regime in fine-tuning. Empirically, we confirm that saddle-point escape is a central challenge in fine-tuning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that decoupled weight decay, as in AdamW, stabilizes feature learning by enforcing novel balance equations. Together, these results highlight two mechanisms how steepest descent can aid modern optimization.

title: Towards Faithful Reasoning in Remote Sensing: A Perceptually-Grounded GeoSpatial Chain-of-Thought for Vision-Language Models
submission: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in remote sensing often fail at complex analytical tasks, a limitation stemming from their end-to-end training paradigm that bypasses crucial reasoning steps and leads to unverifiable outputs. To address this limitation, we introduce the Perceptually-Grounded Geospatial Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), a framework that models remote sensing analysis as a verifiable, multi-step process. We instill this analytical process through a two-stage alignment strategy, leveraging Geo-CoT380k, the first large-scale dataset of structured Geo-CoT rationales. This strategy first employs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to instill the foundational cognitive architecture, then leverages Group Reward Policy Optimization (GRPO) to refine the model’s reasoning policy towards factual correctness. This capability yields dominant performance, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art models across a comprehensive range of tasks. The public release of our Geo-CoT380k dataset and RSThinker model upon publication serves as a concrete pathway from opaque perception towards structured, verifiable reasoning for Earth Observation.

submission: LLMs show strong reasoning in many domains, but applying explicit chain-of-thought in recommendation is limited by scarce CoT data and inference latency. The framework is compatible with different LLM-based recommendation backbones and aims to enable effective latent reasoning without explicit CoT supervision. Code and training details are provided to facilitate integration with existing systems.

title: Achieving low-bit Muon through subspace preservation and grid quantization
submission: Memory constraints make training large language models challenging, and the Muon optimizer—based on matrix orthogonalization—offers memory advantages by relying primarily on first moments. We investigate low-bit compression of Muon and analyze how orthogonalization amplifies quantization error. We identify the top singular subspace and outlier patterns in the moment matrix as primary sources of error and propose 4-bit-Muon-GRASP (GRid And Subspace Preserving), which applies grid quantization while preserving critical subspace structure with limited overhead. We describe implementation details and outline pre-training and fine-tuning setups across several model sizes. While we claim comparable accuracy to full-precision counterparts and reduced memory consumption, detailed numerical results and full training curves are not presented here; further evaluation is needed to verify robustness across tasks and scales. The codebase is made available for replication and extended study.

title: Feature segregation by signed weights in artificial vision systems and biological models
submission: Signed connectivity is fundamental to neural computation in brains (excitatory/inhibitory) and machines (positive/negative), yet the role of signed weights in shaping visual representations remains unclear. We show that ImageNet-trained ANNs exhibit a spontaneous, sign-specific “Dale-like” segregation in their output layers that correlates with accuracy, and that ablation and feature visualization reveal functional segregation: removing positive inputs mainly disrupts localized, object-related structure while removing negative inputs alters dispersed background textures. This segregation strengthens in adversarially robust and unsupervised models and disappears with non-rectified activations. We validate analogous patterns in macaque ventral visual cortex (V1, V4, IT) using encoding models and in vivo visualization; the features recovered in models qualitatively match those observed experimentally. These results indicate a general organizing principle — indeed a convergent strategy — across artificial and biological vision systems: positive weights emphasize object features and negative weights refine context, a finding that we argue should reshape how vision models and experiments are designed.

title: Confident and Adaptive Generative Speech Recognition via Risk Control
submission: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems frequently produce transcription errors due to acoustic variability, motivating post-processing correction methods. Recent approaches leverage large language models for generative ASR error correction using N-best hypotheses but typically use a fixed set size regardless of input difficulty and lack robust control over failure risk. We propose an adaptive framework that dynamically determines the number of hypotheses per input via risk control. Our mechanism leverages ASR confidence scores and applies Learn-Then-Test (LTT) to control expected relative word error rate degradation compared to the best achievable performance for a given model and hypothesis set. The approach furnishes probabilistic guarantees on risk and often requires fewer hypotheses on average, yielding computational savings under varied acoustic conditions. Empirical results on diverse acoustic settings indicate practical efficiency gains and improved robustness in many scenarios, though behavior can vary with ASR confidence calibration and model settings.

submission: Sheaf Neural Networks (SNNs) generalize Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) using algebraic topology and improve modeling of complex relational data. We report experiments on twelve real-world benchmarks showing DSNN consistently outperforms many baseline methods. The presentation includes construction details, theoretical motivation, and implementation notes. The source code is available at https://github.com/hakanaktas0/DSNN.

title: Healthcare Insurance Fraud Detection via Continual Fiedler Vector Graph Model
submission: Healthcare insurance fraud detection presents unique machine learning challenges: labeled data are scarce due to delayed verification, and fraudulent behaviors evolve rapidly, often manifesting in complex, graph-structured interactions. To address these issues, we propose the Continual Fiedler Vector Graph model (ConFVG), a fraud detection framework designed for label-scarce and non-stationary environments. To mitigate label scarcity, we develop a Fiedler Vector-guided graph autoencoder that leverages spectral graph properties to learn structure-aware node representations. The Fiedler Vector, derived from the second smallest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian, captures global topological signals such as community boundaries and connectivity bottlenecks that are frequently associated with collusive fraud. To handle evolving graph streams, we propose a Subgraph Attention Fusion (SAF) module that constructs neighborhood subgraphs and applies attention-based reweighting to emphasize emerging high-risk structures, combined with a Mean Teacher mechanism to stabilize online updates. Experiments on real-world medical fraud datasets indicate promising improvements in low-label and distribution-shift scenarios, suggesting ConFVG is a scalable, structure-sensitive approach for real-time fraud detection.

title: SparseD: Sparse Attention for Diffusion Language Models
submission: Diffusion language models (DLMs) present an alternative to autoregressive models, but open-source DLMs face high inference latency chiefly from attention’s quadratic complexity over context length. A natural strategy is to restrict attention to sparse patterns that retain the most relevant connections. We find three key properties in DLM attention: (1) patterns vary across heads, (2) patterns per head remain similar across denoising steps, and (3) early denoising steps are important for generation. Based on these observations, we propose SparseD, a sparse attention approach tailored to DLMs: pre-compute head-specific sparse patterns once and reuse them across steps, and apply full attention in early steps before switching to sparse attention later. SparseD is designed to avoid recomputing patterns each denoising step and to preserve generation quality. We outline implementation considerations and report measured speedups at long contexts, with code available to reproduce the timing experiments.

title: Black-Box Privacy Attacks on Shared Representations in Multitask Learning
submission: Multitask learning (MTL) trains multiple related tasks jointly by learning a shared representation that captures common structure. Although the shared representation is intended to be minimal, it may leak sensitive information about tasks. We study black-box task-inference attacks in which an adversary, given embedding vectors from querying the shared representation on samples from a task, aims to decide whether that task was present during MTL training. Motivated by tracing attacks on mean estimation in mixtures of Gaussians, we develop purely black-box attacks that exploit dependencies between embeddings from the same task without using shadow models or labeled reference data. The threat model and attack algorithms are described, and we discuss implications for personalization and multi-problem MTL deployments. Empirical evaluation details and quantitative success rates are omitted here and are provided in the experimental section.

title: QKV Projections Require a Fraction of Their Memory
submission: The Multi-Head Attention mechanism is central to LLM operation, and multiple works target its compute and memory efficiency during training. While most efforts focus on approximating the scaled dot product, the memory consumption of the linear projections that compute the Q, K, and V tensors from the input x receives less attention. We propose Point-Approximate Matrix Multiplication (PAMM), a tensor compression technique that compresses activations of the Q,K,V projections by large factors, effectively reducing their memory footprint while preserving training dynamics. PAMM is designed to be composable with efficient attention methods such as FlashAttention, making it a complementary approach for memory-efficient LLM training. We describe the compression scheme, discuss implementation considerations, and analyze its effect on optimization and model perplexity. Empirical evaluation details and quantitative results are presented in the full paper, focusing on trade-offs between compression ratio and final task performance.

title: DASH: Deterministic Attention Scheduling for High-throughput Reproducible LLM Training
submission: Determinism is essential for reproducibility in large language model (LLM) training, but it often incurs a steep throughput cost. In common attention implementations (e.g., FlashAttention-3), the deterministic backward pass requires serialized gradient accumulation to guarantee numerical consistency, which can lead to hardware underutilization. We cast the deterministic attention backward pass as a scheduling problem on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and derive scheduling principles that aim to reduce the critical path length. Based on this view, we propose DASH (Deterministic Attention Scheduling for High-Throughput), which combines two complementary strategies: Descending Q-Tile Iteration, a reversed query-block traversal intended to shrink pipeline stalls in causal attention, and Shift Scheduling, a schedule derived within the DAG model to reduce stalls for full and causal masks. We describe implementation considerations for GPU kernels and report that empirical evaluations on modern hardware indicate improved throughput of the attention backward pass compared to a baseline deterministic implementation. Detailed experimental procedures, microbenchmarks, and ablations are deferred to the full version as this abstract focuses on the scheduling formulation and high-level strategies.

title: AbdCTBench: Learning Clinical Biomarker Representations from Abdominal Surface Geometry
submission: We introduce AbdCTBench, a large-scale dataset of 23,506 CT-derived abdominal surface meshes from 18,719 patients, paired with numerous comorbidity labels, diagnosis codes, and CT-derived biomarkers. Our central insight is that external surface geometry predicts internal tissue composition, enabling lower-cost screening via consumer devices. We benchmark seven architectures (ResNet-18/34/50, DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-B0, ViT-Small, Swin-Base) on 2D mesh projections and show models can learn surface-to-biomarker representations. Top models achieve clinically relevant accuracy for age, mortality, and diabetes detection. We note smaller architectures often match larger ones, and that domain-specific or self-supervised pretraining yields competitive results. While we report performance numbers, we do not provide extensive baseline comparisons to existing diagnostic pipelines here; AbdCTBench mainly provides a large resource and standardized protocols to spur future work. The dataset and code will be released after review.

title: Learning multimodal dictionary decompositions with group-sparse autoencoders
submission: The Linear Representation Hypothesis asserts that the embeddings learned by neural networks can be understood as linear combinations of features corresponding to high-level concepts. Based on this ansatz, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently become a popular method for decomposing embeddings into a sparse combination of linear directions, which have been shown empirically to often correspond to human-interpretable semantics. However, recent attempts to apply SAEs to multimodal embedding spaces (such as the popular CLIP embeddings for image/text data) have found that SAEs often learn ``split dictionaries,'' where most of the learned sparse features are essentially unimodal, active only for data of a single modality. In this work, we study how to effectively adapt SAEs for the setting of multimodal embeddings while ensuring multimodal alignment. We first argue that the existence of a split dictionary decomposition on an aligned embedding space implies the existence of a non-split dictionary with improved modality alignment. Then, we propose a new SAE-based approach to multimodal embedding decomposition using cross-modal random masking and group-sparse regularization. We apply our method to popular embeddings for image/text (CLIP) and audio/text (CLAP) data and show that, compared to standard SAEs, our approach learns a more multimodal dictionary while reducing the number of dead neurons and improving feature semanticity. We finally demonstrate how this improvement in alignment of concepts between modalities can enable improvements in the interpretability and control of cross-modal tasks.

title: HEIST: A Graph Foundation Model for Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics Data
submission: Single-cell transcriptomics and proteomics have become a great source for data-driven insights into biology, enabling the use of advanced deep learning methods to understand cellular heterogeneity and gene expression at the single-cell level. With the advent of spatial-omics data, we have the promise of characterizing cells within their tissue context as it provides both spatial coordinates and intra-cellular transcriptional or protein counts. Beyond transcriptomics, proteomics offers a complementary view by directly measuring proteins, which are the primary effectors of cellular function and key therapeutic targets. However, existing models either ignore the spatial information or the complex genetic and proteomic programs within cells. Thus they cannot infer how cell internal regulation adapts to microenvironmental cues. Furthermore, these models often utilize fixed gene vocabularies, hindering their generalizability to datasets with different genes than pretraining. In this paper, we introduce HEIST, a hierarchical graph transformer foundation model for spatial transcriptomics and proteomics. HEIST models tissues as hierarchical graphs. The higher level graph is a spatial cell graph, and each cell in turn, is represented by its lower level gene co-expression network graph. Rather than using a fixed gene vocabulary, HEIST computes gene embeddings from its co-expression network and cellular context. HEIST  achieves this by performing both intra-level and cross-level message passing to utilize the hierarchy in its embeddings and can thus generalize to novel datatypes including spatial proteomics without retraining. HEIST is pretrained on 22.3M cells from 124 tissues across 15 organs using spatially-aware contrastive and masked autoencoding objectives. Unsupervised analysis of HEIST embeddings reveals spatially informed subpopulations missed by prior models. Downstream evaluations demonstrate generalizability to proteomics data and state-of-the-art performance in clinical outcome prediction, cell type annotation, and gene imputation across multiple technologies.

title: AgentGym-RL: An Open-Source Framework to Train LLM Agents for Long-Horizon Decision Making via Multi-Turn RL
submission: Training LLM agents for complex multi-turn decision-making tasks requires extensive exploration within their environment; reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural way. We introduce AgentGym-RL, a modular and decoupled framework designed for RL-based agents in multi-turn decision-making tasks. It offers flexibility and extensibility, supports mainstream RL algorithms, and spans a broad range of realistic scenarios. We also propose ScalingInter-RL, a staged training approach intended to stabilize long-horizon RL by starting with short-horizon interaction to establish foundational policies and progressively expanding them to encourage deeper exploration. The write-up describes components of the framework, the staged training intuition, and a set of environments used in our experiments. Extensive experiments are reported showing agents trained with our approach perform competitively with commercial counterparts across a collection of tasks. We release the full framework, including code and datasets, to support further community work: https://github.com/WooooDyy/AgentGym-RL.
